body: Arabic has twenty-eight letters. The first table of Qaida Noorania usually prints twenty-nine or thirty entries, because it lists the hamza ء on its own line and adds لا at the end. لا is not a letter: it is simply how ل and ا are drawn when they meet. The hamza is a genuine question, and grammarians differ over whether it counts as a letter separate from the alif; tajweed sidesteps the argument by treating them as two sounds, because they are made in two different places. The hamza shuts the deepest part of the throat completely. The alif does nothing but lengthen, and never carries a vowel at all.

Everything in this course rests on one idea: a letter IS its place in the mouth. English lets you shift a consonant a centimetre and still be understood, so an English ear hears the difference between س and ص as a matter of style. It is not. They are two letters, the way b and p are two letters, and swapping them swaps the word. قَلْب with a ق means a heart; كَلْب with a ك means a dog. The distance between those two letters in the mouth is small, and the distance in meaning is not.

Six confusions cause almost all of the trouble. Four of them are light-and-heavy partners, and three of those four are true twins: the tip of the tongue sits in exactly the same place for ت and ط, for ذ and ظ, and for س and ص, and what separates the two letters is whether the BACK of the tongue rises toward the roof of the mouth. That rising is called isti'la. On س and ص, and on ذ and ظ, it is the whole difference. On ت and ط it is the difference you have to make deliberately, and the voice and the qalqalah bounce come with it. Pressing harder with the front of the tongue does not make a ط; it makes a loud ت.

The fourth of those partners is the trap. د and ض sound to a foreign ear like a light and a heavy version of one letter, and they are nothing of the kind: ض is not a heavy د. The د is a tip letter, made at the roots of the upper front teeth alongside ت and ط. The ض is made along the EDGE of the tongue, pressed against the upper molars, and the sound runs along that edge before it is released. Two different exits, two unrelated letters, and no amount of weight added to a د will ever produce one.

The last two confusions are in the throat, and there the pairing and the mix-up run in different directions. By exit the four letters make two pairs: ء and ه share the deepest point of the throat, ع and ح share the middle. Inside each pair the two letters behave oppositely: ء shuts the air off completely while ه is a soft open breath, and ع is a narrowing the voice keeps running through while ح is the same place squeezed tighter with the voice switched off. What learners actually confuse, though, runs across the two exits: ه against ح, heard as a soft h and a strong h when the real difference is depth, and ء against ع. Learn all four by feel, one hand on the throat, rather than by comparing them to any English sound, because English has none of them.

Work through the alphabet in twos, not straight down the list. Say ت then ط, س then ص, ه then ح, back and forth, until the two letters sound different to you without any effort. That is the point at which the letter has been learned. Until then you know its shape, which is a different thing.

definition.technical: The twenty-eight letters of Arabic, each identified in tajweed by its makhraj, the exact point where its sound is produced, and by the qualities that sound carries. The name of a letter and the sound of a letter are two different things.

drills.caption: The first fourteen letters, one at a time, unhurried.
drills.text: ا ب ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ر ز س ش ص
drills.translit: alif ba ta tha jim hha kha dal dhal ra zay sin shin sad

drills.caption: The second fourteen. Together these two rows are the whole alphabet.

drills.translit: sin sad / ta tah / dhal dha

drills.caption: The fourth partner, and the odd one out. The د is at the tip; for the ض the tongue moves to its edge, against the upper molars.
The two throat exits themselves: the deepest pair, then the middle pair. Same place each time, voice on then voice off.
Now across the exits, which is where the mix-ups live: deepest, then middle. Keep a hand on your throat.

examples.focus: ه from the deepest throat in هُوَ, then ح from the middle throat in أَحَدٌ. One region apart, two different letters.
Two thin س in يُوَسۡوِسُ, then a heavy ص in صُدُورِ. Same tip of the tongue, different shape of the tongue body.
A hamza closing one word and a ع opening the next, a breath apart. The hamza stops the air dead; the ع narrows the throat and keeps the voice running through it.

keyPoints: Twenty-eight letters. لا is a ligature, not a twenty-ninth.
A letter is its place in the mouth. Change the place and you have said a different letter.
Three true twins: ت/ط، ذ/ظ، س/ص. Same place, and only the back of the tongue moves.
د and ض are not twins. ض is made along the edge of the tongue, not at the tip.
Two throat pairs by exit: ء/ه deepest, ع/ح in the middle. The mix-ups run across them: ه against ح, ء against ع.
The name of a letter is not its sound. بَاء is the name, b is the sound.

mistakes.right: Leave the tip where it is and raise the BACK of the tongue toward the roof of the mouth.
mistakes.why: Heaviness in Arabic is produced at the back of the tongue. Extra pressure at the front only produces a forceful ت, which is still a ت.
mistakes.wrong: Making ط by pressing the tip of the tongue harder against the same spot as ت.

mistakes.right: Squeeze the middle of the throat and keep the voice running through the squeeze.
mistakes.why: The hamza closes the airway completely; the ع never closes. This is the commonest substitution among non-Arab readers, and it replaces one letter with another rather than colouring it.
mistakes.wrong: Saying ع as a hamza, or as a vowel with a small catch in it.

mistakes.right: The name is بَاء, the sound is a single b. Names belong to the table, sounds belong to words.
mistakes.why: A reader who only learned names spells words out letter by letter instead of reading them, and that habit is slow to undo later.
mistakes.wrong: Reading a letter's NAME where its SOUND is meant, so ب inside a word comes out as 'baa'.

mistakes.right: Put the side of the tongue against the upper molars and let the sound run along it before releasing.
mistakes.why: ض is the only letter made along the side of the tongue and it is held longer than د. Arabic is called the language of the ض precisely because no neighbouring language has it.
mistakes.wrong: Treating ض as a heavy د, which is what most non-Arab readers produce.

The back of the tongue rises toward the roof of the mouth
It is said with more breath

quiz.explain: ه is made at the deepest part of the throat and ح at its middle, so depth is the whole difference. س/ص and ذ/ظ do share one place in the mouth and differ only by whether the back of the tongue rises. د and ض differ by place as well, but in the mouth rather than the throat: ض is made along the edge of the tongue.
quiz.prompt: Which two letters are separated by depth in the throat rather than by heaviness?

lessons.summary: Twenty-eight letters, each fixed to one place in the mouth. A letter said from the wrong place is not an accent; it is a different letter.

table.title: Six confusions worth drilling

body: A letter's core shape never changes. What changes is what is attached to it: a connector reaching back to the letter before, a connector reaching forward to the letter after, or a tail when nothing follows. So ب alone is ب, at the start of a word it is بـ, between two letters it is ـبـ, and at the end it is ـب. Four shapes, one letter. There are twenty-eight letters in Arabic, not a hundred and twelve.

Six letters break the pattern: ا، د، ذ، ر، ز، و. Each of them accepts a join from the letter before it, but never gives one to the letter after it. In right-to-left writing the next letter sits to the LEFT, so when the pen reaches one of these six it lifts, and a gap opens up in the middle of the word. Those six therefore have only two shapes each, not four: standing alone, and attached on the right.

This gap is the single biggest obstacle for a beginner who already knows all twenty-eight letters. It looks exactly like a space, so the eye reads one word as two or three. ٱلۡكَوۡثَرَ is one word, but it is drawn in three joined runs: ٱ, then لكو, then ثر, because the alif and the waw refuse to join forward. The ra is a non-connector too, but it ends the word, so nothing follows it to refuse and all you see is its closing shape. Two letters refusing forward is what opens two gaps and leaves three runs. The cue is width: the space between two real words is noticeably wider than a gap inside one.

The six are easiest to hold as three pairs. د and ذ are the same shape with and without a dot. ر and ز are the same shape with and without a dot. The alif and the waw are the two odd ones out, and both of them will turn up again in the last lesson of this chapter as madd letters.

Dots do most of the identifying work, and they matter most in the middle of a word. Written between two joins, ب، ت، ث، ن، ي are all the same small tooth: one dot below is ب, two above is ت, three above is ث, one above is ن, two below is ي. The same is true of ج ح خ, of د ذ, of ر ز, of س ش, of ص ض, of ط ظ, of ع غ, and of ف ق. Reading the dots carefully is not fussiness; it is most of what reading Arabic actually is.

Two more things you will see on the page. When ل is followed by ا the two fuse into لا, which is why Noorania gives that shape its own entry in the table. And in a printed mushaf a letter is sometimes stretched sideways so the line ends flush with the margin. That stretch is typography, not sound: it adds nothing to hold and nothing to say.

definition.technical: The positional forms a letter takes once it is written inside a word: standing alone, opening the word, sitting between two letters, or closing it. Qaida Noorania gives these their own lesson immediately after the isolated letters, because recognising a letter in isolation does not yet let anyone read a line.

drills.caption: The same ب: alone, opening, in the middle, closing.
Three of the six non-connectors. Two shapes each, because nothing may attach on their left.
drills.text: ر ـر   /   د ـد   /   و ـو

drills.caption: Lam meeting alif fuses into one shape. Noorania gives it its own line in the table.

examples.focus: One word in three joined runs: ٱ, then لكو, then ثر. The alif and the waw open the two gaps by refusing to join forward. The ra is a non-connector as well, but it ends the word, so it opens nothing.
Three pieces again in a single word: أ, then عو, then ذ. Read it as one word with no pause at either gap.

keyPoints: Four positions: alone, opening, middle, closing. The core of the letter never changes.
Six letters never join forward: ا د ذ ر ز و.
A gap after one of those six is not a space. Do not read the word as two.
Between two joins, ب ت ث ن ي are one shape and the dots are the letter.
لا is ل and ا drawn as one shape, not an extra letter.

mistakes.right: Look for the space, not for the gap. A real space between words is visibly wider.
mistakes.why: This is the most common reason a learner who knows every letter still cannot read a line of the mushaf out loud.
mistakes.wrong: Reading the gap after ا د ذ ر ز و as a word break, so ٱلۡكَوۡثَرَ becomes three words.

mistakes.right: Learn the core shape once, then notice only what the join adds.
mistakes.why: Treating the forms as separate items makes the alphabet look four times larger than it is, and it slows recognition rather than helping it.
mistakes.wrong: Memorising each positional form as though it were a separate letter.

mistakes.right: Check how many dots there are and whether they sit above or below, before saying the letter.
mistakes.why: Between two joins these five letters are drawn identically. The dots are the entire difference between one word and another.
mistakes.wrong: Glancing past the dots mid-word, so ب ت ث ن ي blur together.

choices: It is three short words written close together
ا, و and ر do not join to the letter that follows them
The mushaf stretches letters to fill out the line
A gap is always printed before a heavy letter
quiz.explain: ا و and ر are three of the six non-connectors. They accept a join from the right but never give one to the left, so the pen lifts and a gap appears inside the word. Here the two gaps come after the alif and after the waw; the ra is a non-connector too, but it ends the word, so nothing follows it to be cut off.
quiz.prompt: Why does ٱلۡكَوۡثَرَ look like three separate pieces?

choices: The height of the letter
Only the dots
The vowel it carries
Its position in the word
quiz.explain: All five are drawn as the same small tooth. One dot below is ب, two above is ت, three above is ث, one above is ن, two below is ي.
quiz.prompt: Between two joined letters, what tells ب apart from ت, ث, ن and ي?

lessons.summary: Arabic is joined writing. Each letter has up to four shapes, and six letters refuse to join to what follows, which is why one word can look like three.

body: Arabic writes consonants; the short vowels are marks added above and below them. There are three, and between them they carry every short vowel sound in the language. The fatha is a small slanted stroke above the letter and the jaw drops for it. The kasra is the same stroke below the letter, and the tongue rises toward the front while the corners of the mouth pull back. The damma is a small waw above the letter, and the lips round and push slightly forward.

The names describe what the mouth is doing rather than what the mark looks like. Fatha means opening, and the mouth opens. Kasra means breaking, for the way the jaw is broken downward and the sound pulled forward. Damma means drawing together, and the lips are drawn together. If you cannot remember which mark is which, make the mouth shape first and the name follows.

Order matters and it is one direction only: the vowel is heard AFTER its letter, never before. بَ is ba, never ab. English speakers sometimes reverse this on a letter that would end a syllable in English, and the result is a word with its letters in the wrong order.

One count. A count, حركة, is the time it takes to say one vowelled letter at your own steady pace, roughly the time to lower one finger. It is not a fixed number of milliseconds and it does not have to match anyone else's. What matters is that all of your counts are the same length as each other, because every longer measurement in tajweed is defined as a multiple of this one.

The most common beginner fault, by a wide margin, is stretching. A fatha held too long turns بَ into بَا, which is a two-count madd and frequently a different word: قَتَلَ, he killed, is not قَاتَلَ, he fought. This is exactly what the Noorania drill is for. Take one letter, run it through all three vowels, keep every one of them short and equal, then change the letter and do it again.

One last observation about the page. In a fully vowelled mushaf almost every letter carries something: a haraka, a tanween, a sukoon, or a shaddah with a vowel on top of it. The letters that carry nothing at all are the madd letters, and their blankness is deliberate. They are the subject of the last lesson in this chapter.

definition.technical: A vowel mark written above or below a letter and sounded after it, held for one count. The name is literal: a letter carrying a haraka moves, as opposed to a letter carrying sukoon, which rests.

drills.caption: One letter through all three vowels. This is the core Noorania drill.
The same pattern on three more letters. Same three sounds, same short length.
drills.text: تَ تِ تُ  /  جَ جِ جُ  /  دَ دِ دُ
drills.translit: ta ti tu / ja ji ju / da di du

drills.caption: Three fathas in a row, and nothing stretched.
Damma, then kasra, then fatha, on the very same three letters.

examples.focus: All three vowels inside a few syllables: fatha on ح, damma on د, kasra on the first ل and on ب. Every one of them is a single count.
No kasra anywhere in this ayah, only fathas and dammas. Keep each to one count and the rhythm settles by itself.

keyPoints: Three marks: fatha above (a), kasra below (i), damma above (u).
One count each. Two counts is a madd, which is a different thing entirely.
The vowel is sounded after the letter, never before it.
A count is your own steady beat; what matters is that all your counts match.
A letter left with no mark at all is a madd letter, not an oversight.

mistakes.right: Cut the vowel at one count and move straight to the next letter.
mistakes.why: Two counts is a natural madd. Stretched short vowels are the most common fault in beginner recitation, and they change words: قَتَلَ is not قَاتَلَ.
mistakes.wrong: Holding the fatha long enough that بَ turns into بَا.

mistakes.right: Round the lips but keep it short, nearer the vowel in 'put' than the one in 'boot'.
mistakes.why: 'oo' is already two counts long. The damma is the short partner of that sound, not the sound itself.
mistakes.wrong: Reading the damma as an English 'oo'.

mistakes.right: Pull the corners of the mouth back and keep the tongue high and forward.
mistakes.why: A flattened kasra is heard as a fatha. At the end of a word that is a different grammatical case, and often a different meaning.
mistakes.wrong: Rushing the kasra until it flattens into a neutral 'uh'.

choices: Half a count
One count
Two counts
As long as the reciter's breath allows
quiz.explain: Every haraka is one count. Two counts is the length of a natural madd, which is why a stretched fatha is heard as an alif and can change the word.
quiz.prompt: How long is a fatha held?

choices: Before the letter, as 'ib'
After the letter, as 'bi'
At the same moment as the letter
Only when the word is connected to the next one
quiz.explain: A haraka is always sounded after its letter. The mark sits below the ب, but the order in speech is consonant first, then vowel.
quiz.prompt: Where is the vowel heard in بِ?

ruleCard.action: Say the letter from its own place, then release it into the vowel.
ruleCard.hold: One count. Long enough to be heard, short enough that no alif, waw or ya appears after it.
ruleCard.trigger: A fatha, kasra or damma written on a letter.

lessons.summary: Fatha, kasra and damma each last exactly one count. Stretching one of them into two is the first habit a new reciter has to break.

body: A haraka tells you to move; a sukoon tells you to stop. The letter is produced at its own place in the mouth and then released, and nothing comes out after it. The KFGQPC mushaf you are reading writes it as a small dotless خ head above the letter, ۡ, that is, the head of a خ with its dot taken off, where many other prints use a small circle, ْ. They mean the same thing.

Practically, the test is what happens at the end. With a haraka the airflow continues into a vowel; with a sukoon it does not. قُلۡ is qul, and it ends on the ل: no faint 'uh' after it, no puff of breath. Beginners almost always add something, because the mouth wants to finish the gesture, and hearing that addition in your own recitation is the first real diagnostic skill in tajweed.

One structural fact follows from this: no Arabic word can begin on a sakin letter. There is nothing for the sound to lean on. That is why words such as ٱقۡرَأۡ are written with an extra alif at the front carrying a starting vowel, an alif that vanishes the moment the word is connected to what comes before it. That mark has its own lesson later; for now, notice only that a sakin letter always has a vowelled letter in front of it.

Now the reason this lesson matters more than its length suggests. Read the definition of any rule in this course and the same word appears: sakin. The four rules of nun sakin need a نْ. The three rules of mim sakin need a مْ. Qalqalah fires only on a sakin ق ط ب ج د. Idgham is a sakin letter falling into the vowelled letter after it. Even the three madd letters are sakin letters. A vowelled letter is finished in itself; a sakin letter is not, and what happens next is the whole subject of tajweed.

Finally, stopping. When you stop on a word, its last letter is read as though it carried sukoon, whatever vowel or tanween is actually written on it. ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ read to a stop is ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينۡ. Two entire rules exist because of this. A natural madd that suddenly has a sukoon after it becomes madd 'arid, held at two, four or six counts by the reader's choice, kept consistent through a sitting. And a ق ط ب ج د that suddenly becomes sakin at a stop bounces, which is the strong qalqalah.

definition.technical: The state of a letter carrying no vowel. The letter is sounded from its own articulation point and released, with nothing following it. Its opposite is the haraka, which is why a vowelled letter is called mutaharrik, moving, and a vowelless one sakin, still.

drills.caption: Vowel, then a hard close. Nothing at all after the sakin letter.
The same letter vowelled and then sakin, so the mouth feels the difference.
Real words with a sakin letter inside. Read them slowly and cut each one clean.

examples.focus: The clearest sukoon in the mushaf: a damma on ق, nothing on ل. Say qul and stop the ل dead.

Four written sukoons in four words. The two د bounce, because a sakin ق ط ب ج د always does. The و of يُولَدۡ is sakin too, but it carries no mark because it is a madd letter, which is the last lesson of this chapter.
Written with a fatha on the ن. Stop on it and that ن becomes sakin, which stretches the madd before it to two, four or six counts.

keyPoints: Sukoon means no vowel: make the letter and release it, with nothing after.
This mushaf writes it as a small dotless خ head (ۡ); other prints use a small circle (ْ).
No Arabic word begins on a sakin letter.
Nearly every rule in tajweed is triggered by a sakin letter.
At a stop the final letter is read as though it carried sukoon.

mistakes.right: Close the sound off at the letter itself.
mistakes.why: The added vowel is an extra sound that is not in the text. On the qalqalah letters it is the difference between a clean bounce and a whole extra syllable.
mistakes.wrong: Letting a faint vowel escape after the sakin letter, so قُلۡ comes out as 'qulu'.

mistakes.right: Close the letter and let the sound end there, then breathe separately.
mistakes.why: Breath after the last letter adds an audible ه that nobody wrote. It comes from breathing at the stop rather than after it.
mistakes.wrong: Releasing a breath after the final letter at a stop, so ٱلۡفَلَقِ ends with an audible 'huh'.

mistakes.right: Drop it. The final letter takes sukoon at a stop.
mistakes.why: Sounding the vowel fully is simply not stopping. There are two refined ways of hinting at a final vowel at a stop, rawm and ishmam, and they are taught separately with their own conditions.
mistakes.wrong: Pronouncing the written vowel in full on the word you are stopping on.

choices: Its written vowel is read as normal
It is read as though it carried sukoon
It takes a small nasal hum
It is lengthened to two counts
quiz.explain: Stopping means the word ends, and a word does not end on a vowel at a stop. The written damma, fatha or kasra is dropped and the letter is closed. This is exactly why madd 'arid and the strong qalqalah exist.
quiz.prompt: What happens to the last letter of a word when you stop on it?

choices: Sakin letters are rare, so they are worth singling out
A letter with no vowel of its own has to lean on whatever comes next
Sakin letters only ever occur at the end of a word
The mushaf prints them in colour
quiz.explain: A vowelled letter is complete in itself. A sakin letter is not: its sound has to go somewhere, so the following letter decides whether it stays clear, merges, hides, bounces or stretches.
quiz.prompt: Why do so many tajweed rules begin by naming a sakin letter?

ruleCard.action: Say the letter from its own place and release it. Nothing follows: no vowel, no escaping breath, no hum unless a rule puts one there.

fragments.caption: sukoon on م and on د
stop on it and the ن becomes sakin

ruleCard.hold: Zero counts. A sakin letter has no length of its own.
ruleCard.trigger: A letter written with ۡ (a small dotless خ head) in this mushaf, or ْ in other prints. Also the final letter of any word you stop on.

lessons.summary: A sukoon is the absence of a vowel. The letter is made and released with nothing after it, and almost every rule in this course is triggered by a letter in that state.

body: A shaddah is not an instruction to say the letter louder. It stands for two letters written as one shape. رَبِّ is ra, then a sakin ب, then a ب with a kasra. Because the first of the pair is sakin, you do not let go between them: the tongue arrives at the ب once, stays there under pressure, and releases once, into the vowel. What the ear hears is weight, not repetition.

Some shaddahs belong to the word itself, like the one in رَبِّ. Many others are the record of a merge that the mushaf has already written into the page. The commonest is the ل of ٱل disappearing into a sun letter: ٱلصَّمَدُ has a shaddah on the ص precisely because the ل is written but not read. The same logic produces the shaddahs of idgham in the nun sakin chapter, where مِّن رَّبِّهِمۡ carries no sukoon on the noon at all, because the noon is not going to be pronounced.

Now the rule that makes this lesson worth its own place. ن and م are the two nasal letters of Arabic, and wherever either of them carries a shaddah, a nasal hum of two counts is obligatory. Inside a word, at the end of a word, connecting or stopping, there is no exception and no shortening. Scholars call this غنّة مشدّدة and rank it the fullest ghunnah there is, which is a useful way to hear it: it is the yardstick against which the humming in ikhfa and idgham is measured.

The mirror of that rule is just as important. No other doubled letter hums. A doubled ب, ل, ر or ك is held and released completely dry, with the nose out of it. Once a learner has been taught ghunnah, nasalising every shaddah in sight becomes the standing error, and a nasal ب is not an Arabic sound at all.

A shaddah also changes the length of what comes before it. When a madd letter runs straight into a letter carrying a shaddah in the SAME WORD, the madd is stretched to six counts, with no choice in the matter. وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ at the close of al-Fatiha is the example every reciter knows: the alif of ضَآ is followed immediately by a doubled ل, so it is six counts, and only then is the doubled ل itself held. This is madd lazim, and it is rare. This app's ground-truth index marks it on 119 words in the entire mushaf, which is why it is worth learning to recognise on sight.

That same phrase carries the trap, so read it twice. The alif of وَلَا also stands immediately in front of a shaddah, the doubled ض of ٱلضَّ, and it takes no length at all. Joined to the next word, the connecting hamza of ٱل falls away, the alif then runs into the sakin first half of that ض, and the alif is dropped outright. The condition is what saves you: the madd letter and the shaddah have to sit inside one word. Across a word boundary a following shaddah lengthens nothing.

One last case, for when you stop. Stopping on a word whose final letter is a doubled ق ط ب ج د leaves a doubled letter with sukoon. Hold it, then release it with a single bounce. Not two bounces: the doubling is heard as extra weight before the release. Most teachers rank this the strongest degree of qalqalah there is.

definition.technical: A mark written above a letter to show that the letter is doubled: the first of the two carries sukoon, the second carries the vowel written with the shaddah, and the pair is produced as one held press rather than as two separate letters.

drills.caption: What a shaddah actually is: a sakin ب, then a ب with a fatha, said as one press.
Doubled noon and doubled mim. Two counts of hum on each, no exceptions.
Doubled letters that never hum. Hold each one dry.

examples.focus: A doubled ن: two counts of hum before the alif, every time the word appears in this surah.
A doubled م. The lips stay shut for two counts while the nose carries the whole sound.
This shaddah is a merge: the ل of ٱل is written but never read, and the ص is held in its place.
A madd running straight into a shaddah: six counts on ضَآ, and only then the doubled ل.

keyPoints: A shaddah is a sakin letter plus a vowelled letter, drawn as one.
Press once and hold. Do not let a vowel escape between the halves.
A doubled ن or م takes an obligatory two-count hum. No other doubled letter does.

mistakes.right: Hold the closure through both halves and release once, into the written vowel.
mistakes.why: The first half is sakin. A vowel escaping there turns one doubled letter into two syllables and adds a sound the text does not have.
mistakes.wrong: Letting the first half of the doubled letter go before the second, so a tiny vowel appears between them.

mistakes.right: Only نّ and مّ hum. Everything else is held dry.
mistakes.why: The nose is involved only when the letter itself is nasal. This is the standard over-correction once ghunnah has been taught.
mistakes.wrong: Humming on every doubled letter, so رَبِّ comes out nasal.

mistakes.right: Two counts every time, whatever pace you are reading at.
mistakes.why: The ghunnah on a doubled noon or mim is obligatory rather than decorative, and a listener notices its absence immediately.
mistakes.wrong: Shortening the hum on نّ or مّ when the line is moving quickly.

mistakes.right: Six counts, because a shaddah follows the madd immediately, inside the same word.
mistakes.why: This is madd lazim. Unlike muttasil, munfasil and 'arid, madd lazim inside a word leaves the reader nothing to choose: six counts.
mistakes.wrong: Reading ٱلضَّآلِّينَ at two counts because the alif looks like an ordinary madd.

body: The word tanween means adding a noon, and that is exactly what the mark is. The vowel at the end of the word is written twice, and the second half of it stands for a noon sakin that is heard but never spelled out. أَحَدٌ is read ahadun, كُفُوًا is kufuwan, قُرَيۡشٍ is qurayshin. There is no letter on the page to look for. The doubled mark is the letter.

Once you accept that the trailing sound is a noon sakin, an entire chapter of this course comes free. All four rules of nun sakin apply to tanween without a single change: the following letter decides whether the hidden noon is said clearly, merged away, turned into a mim, or hidden behind a hum. The only structural difference is position. A written noon sakin can sit anywhere in a word; a tanween is always at the end of one, so a rule it triggers always reaches across into the next word.

This mushaf will usually tell you which rule is coming before you have worked it out. The two marks are printed level with each other when the hidden noon is to be pronounced plainly, and staggered or otherwise altered when it is about to be hidden or merged; where the rule is iqlab, a small م is printed in place of one of the marks. You do not need to know the four rules yet. You do need to start noticing that the shape of the tanween changes, because that change is the mushaf giving you the answer.

Stopping on a tanween is where the three marks part company, and this is the part beginners are most often never told. Stop on a dammatan or a kasratan and the tanween simply disappears, leaving the final letter with sukoon: أَحَدٌ becomes أَحَدۡ, قُرَيۡشٍ becomes قُرَيۡشۡ. Stop on a fathatan and it turns into a long alif of two counts: كُفُوًا becomes كُفُوَا. That is why an alif is usually already printed after a fathatan; it is not an extra letter, it is there for the stop.

One exception to the fathatan rule, and it is common enough to matter. A fathatan on a ta marbuta ة is stopped on as a silent ه, not as an alif: رَحۡمَةً is stopped as رَحۡمَهۡ. The ta marbuta is only a ت while the word is connected; at a stop it reverts to the ه it is drawn from, and the tanween goes with everything else.

Two places in the Qur'an print what looks like a fathatan on a verb: لَنَسۡفَعَۢا in Surat al-'Alaq and وَلَيَكُونٗا in Surat Yusuf. Grammatically that is a light noon of emphasis rather than a tanween, but it is read the same way and stopped on the same way, as an alif. Nothing new to learn there, just a spelling worth recognising when you meet it.

definition.technical: An extra noon sakin sounded at the end of a word in connected reading, written by doubling the final vowel mark rather than by writing a letter, and altered or dropped entirely when the reader stops on that word.

drills.caption: Each doubled mark is its own vowel plus an unwritten noon sakin.
Connected, then stopped. The noon and the vowel both go.

examples.focus: Dammatan at the end of an ayah. Read on and a noon appears; stop here and the word is simply أَحَدۡ.

The hidden noon of كِرَامٗا meets ك, so it is concealed behind a two-count hum. Two words, one rule.
Nearly the same word, now standing before ب. Look for the small م printed where the second mark would be.

mistakes.why: Every rule of the nun sakin chapter fires on tanween exactly as it does on a written ن, and tanween sits at the end of a very large share of the phrases you will read.
mistakes.wrong: Looking for a written noon, not finding one, and concluding the rule does not apply.

mistakes.right: Drop it and close the د.
mistakes.why: Tanween belongs to connected speech. Sounding it at a stop is the same error as sounding any other final vowel at a stop.
mistakes.wrong: Sounding the tanween when the recitation stops there, so أَحَدٌ ends 'ahadun'.

mistakes.right: Stop on it as كُفُوَا, with a clear two-count alif.

mistakes.wrong: Stopping on كُفُوًا as 'kufuwan', or cutting it short as 'kufuw'.

mistakes.right: Stop it as رَحۡمَهۡ, with a silent ه.
mistakes.why: The ta marbuta only sounds as ت while the word is connected. At a stop it reverts to ه, and there is no alif to add.
mistakes.wrong: Turning a fathatan on a ta marbuta into an alif, so رَحۡمَةً is stopped as 'rahmataa'.

body: There are three madd letters and each is tied to one vowel: ا comes after a fatha, a sakin و after a damma, a sakin ي after a kasra. The pairing is not a convention to memorise, it is the mechanism. A madd letter is its own vowel held on, with the mouth frozen in the position that vowel has already put it in. The fatha opens the mouth and the alif keeps it open; the damma rounds the lips and the waw keeps them rounded; the kasra spreads them and the ya keeps them spread. That is why the mouth does not move at all during a madd, and why any movement during the hold is audible as a fault.

و and ي have to earn the title. They must be sakin, and the vowel in front of them must be the matching one. If the و carries a vowel of its own it is an ordinary consonant. If it is sakin but a FATHA precedes it, it is not a madd letter at all but a leen letter, a soft letter: خَوۡف, قُرَيۡش. Leen letters are not stretched while you read on. They take length only at a stop, and that is a separate rule with its own lesson. The alif has no such condition to meet: it is always sakin and always preceded by a fatha, so an alif is always a madd letter.

Two counts, which is exactly twice the one count you measured out in the harakat lesson. Test yourself on بَ against بَا. If those two do not sound clearly different in length when you say them back to back, no later madd will be reliable either, because four counts and six counts are defined as multiples of this one.

On the page, a madd letter is the letter carrying no mark at all. In a fully vowelled mushaf that blankness is the signal. There is one variant to recognise: the dagger alif, a small vertical stroke standing in for an alif that was never written into the skeleton of the word, as in ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ and ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ. It is a full madd letter and is held for the same two counts as any other alif.

The natural madd grows longer only when something follows it. A hamza after the madd letter, or a sukoon after it, produces the derived madds, and those have a chapter of their own. It is worth knowing now where Hafs actually leaves you a choice, because reciters differ audibly and it confuses learners. Through the tariq of ash-Shatibiyyah, Hafs reads both the joined madd (madd muttasil, where the hamza sits in the same word) and the separated madd (madd munfasil, where the madd ends one word and a hamza opens the next) at four or five counts. The two-count separated madd you will hear from many reciters comes through a different tariq, at-Tayyibah. Both are sound; take the one your teacher gives you and hold to it consistently within a sitting.
The natural madd itself is not one of those choices. It is two counts, and it is the most frequently applied length in the whole mushaf: this app's ground-truth index marks it on 8,572 words.

definition.technical: Holding the sound of one of the three madd letters for two counts, when nothing follows that would call for more. Also named المد الأصلي, the original madd, because the length belongs to the letter itself rather than being added by a hamza or a sukoon coming after it.

drills.caption: The three madds on one letter. Two counts each, and all three the same length.

Waw after a damma in دُو. The lips round for the damma and stay rounded right through the hold. The word sits in the middle of the ayah and a vowelled ن follows the waw, so nothing can add to those two counts.
Ya after a kasra in مِي. The lips stay spread and the tongue stays high for the whole two counts.
Not a madd. The ي is sakin, but a fatha precedes it, so this is a leen letter and reading on you do not stretch it at all.

و and ي must be sakin. After a fatha they are leen letters, not madd letters.
Two counts, connecting or stopping.

One count is a haraka, two counts is a natural madd. Everything longer is built on that.

mistakes.wrong: Stretching a natural madd to three or four counts because it sounds more beautiful.

mistakes.right: A sakin و or ي after a fatha is a leen letter. Connecting, it takes no length at all.

mistakes.right: Freeze the position and let the sound run out flat.
mistakes.why: A sliding madd produces a diphthong, which is an English habit rather than an Arabic sound.

body: The word comes from the root ج و د, which carries the sense of quality. The second form جوّد means to make something good, so تجويد is the act of improving: taking a recitation that is merely readable and bringing it to the shape it is supposed to have.

That shape was not designed. Every rule in this course is a description of how the Qur'an was recited by the Prophet, taken from him by his companions, and passed down through an unbroken chain of reciters to the teachers alive today. None of the letter rules was derived from Arabic grammar and none was invented for beauty. The one place scholarly judgement genuinely enters is where a reciter may stop, and the chapter on stopping says so plainly. When this course says a noon is hidden before ف, that is a report about how the word has always been read, and the reason it is worth learning precisely is that it is a report.

The science has two halves and they are not interchangeable. The first is theory: the terms, the letter sets, the counts, the conditions. It fits in a book, and this course is that half. The second is التلقي, taking the sounds face to face from a teacher who took them from a teacher. The difference between a ض and a ظ, or between a full two-count hum and a lazy one, is something your ear has to be corrected on, because nobody hears their own mouth from the outside. Ibn al-Jazari put it in one line: وليس بينه وبين تركه إلا رياضة امرئ بفكه, there is nothing between mastering tajweed and abandoning it except a person exercising his mouth.

The ruling comes in two levels, and confusing them is the usual source of anxiety. Learning the science as a science, and keeping it alive by teaching it, is فرض كفاية: if enough of the community carries it, the obligation lifts from the rest. Applying enough of it that your own recitation is free of لحن جلي, the clear error that breaks a letter or a vowel, is فرض عين on anyone who recites, because that error changes the words. Beyond that line lie the fine points: the exact hold of a ghunnah, the degrees of ikhfa. Most scholars treat falling short there as a deficiency rather than a sin; some, reading Ibn al-Jazari's couplet وَالأَخْذُ بِالتَّجْوِيدِ حَتْمٌ لازِمُ / مَنْ لَمْ يُجَوِّدِ القُرْآنَ آثِمُ broadly, take a stricter line. The next lesson draws that boundary concretely.

One thing to fix before starting. Everything in this course is Hafs عن عاصم by the tariq of ash-Shatibiyyah, the reading the mushaf in this app prints. Where Hafs himself is transmitted with a choice, such as the length of a separated madd, the lesson says so instead of presenting one option as the only reading.

lessons.summary: Tajweed is the science of giving every letter of the Qur'an its due. Half of it is knowledge you can read off a page; the other half only ever transfers from one mouth to one ear.

body: حق الحرف is what a letter is before any context touches it: its makhraj, the place in the mouth or throat where it is made, and its permanent صفات, the attributes that travel with it everywhere. Say ص on its own, in any word, in any position, and it is still voiceless, still emphatic, still whistling. Nothing a neighbouring letter does can take that away, and nothing you will be asked to do in this course changes it.

مستحق الحرف is what the letter is owed because of where it happens to sit. The noon of مِن is an ordinary noon said in isolation; put ب after it and it becomes a mim hidden behind a hum. The alif of مَا is two counts alone; put a hamzah after it at the head of the next word and Hafs holds it four or five. Nothing about the letter itself changed, only its neighbourhood. Every rule from the Nun Sakin chapter onward lives in this second category; the two chapters before it, Articulation Points and Letter Qualities, are the haqq half of the same pair. That is exactly why none of the neighbour rules appear in an alphabet chart and all of them appear the moment letters stand next to each other.

One word can show both dues at once. In ٱلضَّآلِّينَ the ض is haqq: the side of the tongue presses against the upper molars and the sound runs along that side before it releases, and that is true of the ض wherever you meet it. The six counts of madd held on the alif after it are mustahaqq: they are owed because a doubled letter follows a madd letter, and if that alif stood somewhere else the six counts would not follow it. Both dues have to be paid, and paying one does not cover the other. Qalqalah sits right on the boundary and is worth naming: the bounce is a permanent attribute of ق ط ب ج د, but you only hear it when one of them carries sukoon, which is why the books list it under haqq while you practise it in context. Ghunnah sits on the same boundary: the nasal sound itself is a permanent attribute of ن and م, issuing from the khayshoom, while its two-count measure is owed by the neighbour.

Now the errors. لحن جلي, the clear error, is a break in the letters or in the vowels: substituting one letter for another, adding or dropping a letter, changing a harakah, turning a sukoon into a vowel or a vowel into a sukoon. It is called clear because a trained reader hears it at once and an untrained listener often does too. Its ruling is that it is forbidden and must be corrected, and persisting in it knowingly is sinful. The classification goes by what broke, not by how bad the outcome sounds, so a wrong harakah is jali whether or not it lands on another real word.

The consequence can be very large. أَنۡعَمۡتَ in the Fatiha, read with a damma on the ت, turns those upon whom You bestowed favour into a claim about the reciter, inside the surah recited in every rak'ah. In 9:3, وَرَسُولُهُۥ read with kasras instead of dammas moves the Messenger from the side of the disavowal to its object, and that is the incident traditionally credited with prompting the invention of the vowel marks in the first place.

لحن خفي, the hidden error, is what is left when the letters and vowels are all correct but a due went unpaid: a ghunnah dropped, a madd cut short or stretched past its measure, an ikhfa said as a clear noon, a ر made heavy where it should be light. It is called hidden because only an ear schooled in the science catches it, and some manuals divide it again into what an ordinary student of tajweed hears and what only a specialist does. On its ruling the scholars genuinely differ: the majority treat it as disliked and a deficiency in the recitation rather than a sin, while some hold it prohibited on the strength of the same couplet of Ibn al-Jazari. Nobody holds that it can be left alone.

That difference in ruling is the practical use of the whole distinction, because it tells you what to repair first. A learner whose ض still comes out as a د should be spending time there and not on the third degree of ikhfa: one of those two is changing the words being recited and the other is not.

definition.literal: to bend away, to incline off the straight
definition.technical: An error entering the recitation. It is جلي, clear, when a letter or a vowel is broken, and خفي, hidden, when the letters and vowels are correct but a tajweed due went unpaid.

drills.caption: Say each one alone, with no word around it. Everything you hear is haqq al-harf, and the next two chapters are about nothing else. Not one of the neighbour rules applies yet.
The same noon by itself and in company. Only the second one has a neighbour, and only the second one changes.

examples.focus: Both dues in one word: the ض is haqq al-harf, the six counts on the alif after it are mustahaqq.
Fatha on the ت. A damma here is lahn jali and changes who bestowed the favour.
Damma on the ل and the ه: wa rasuluhu. Kasras there attach the disavowal to the Messenger himself.
Two counts of hum on the doubled م. Cutting it short breaks nothing, and is still an unpaid due.
Held four or five counts in the tariq this course follows. Shortening it is lahn khafi, not a broken word.
The noon is hidden behind a hum. Saying it clearly leaves every letter intact and still misses a due.

keyPoints: حق الحرف: makhraj plus permanent sifat. It never leaves the letter.
مستحق الحرف: what the neighbours require. Every rule from the Nun Sakin chapter onward lives here.
Lahn jali breaks a letter or a vowel. It is forbidden, and it is repaired first.
Lahn khafi drops a due. Most call it a deficiency, some call it prohibited, none call it fine.
Knowing which one you committed is what tells you how urgent it is.

mistakes.right: Fatha on the ت: an'amta. The verb is addressed to Allah.
mistakes.why: This is lahn jali in the surah recited in every rak'ah, and it moves the favour from the One who gave it to the one reciting.
mistakes.wrong: Reading أَنۡعَمۡتَ with a damma on the ت.

mistakes.right: Press the side of the tongue against the upper molars and let the sound run along that side before releasing it.
mistakes.why: Substituting a letter is lahn jali by definition, and ض and ظ are two different letters made in two different places.
mistakes.wrong: Letting ٱلضَّآلِّينَ come out with a د or a ظ in place of the ض.

mistakes.right: Repair in ruling order: the clear error first, the hidden one after it.
mistakes.why: Both are worth fixing, but only one of them is currently changing the words you recite.
mistakes.wrong: Polishing ghunnah counts while a letter is still coming out as the wrong letter.

mistakes.right: Ask what broke. A wrong harakah is jali even when it lands on nothing meaningful; a missing ghunnah is khafi even when it sounds glaring to you.
mistakes.why: The two categories are defined by which part of the reading failed, not by the size of the consequence.
mistakes.wrong: Assuming that an error which does not change the meaning must be lahn khafi.

choices: The two counts held on a noon hidden before ف
The makhraj of the ض
Hiding a noon before ف
The four counts Hafs gives a separated madd
quiz.explain: Haqq is what the letter is on its own: where it is made, and the attributes that never leave it. The other three exist only because of a neighbouring letter, which makes them mustahaqq.
quiz.prompt: Which of these belongs to حق الحرف rather than مستحق الحرف?

choices: Lahn khafi: a tajweed due went unpaid
Lahn jali: a vowel is broken, and it must be corrected
Not an error, only a different qira'ah
A matter of personal style
quiz.explain: Changing a harakah is lahn jali by definition, and here it also changes the meaning. The ruling is that it is forbidden and has to be fixed, which is why it outranks any refinement work.
quiz.prompt: A reciter reads أَنۡعَمۡتَ with a damma on the ت. What is it, and what follows?

choices: Because only one of them is audible
Because they carry different rulings, and so different urgency
Because hidden errors only occur in long surahs
Because clear errors are limited to al-Fatiha
quiz.explain: Both are audible to someone. The split exists because jali is forbidden and must be repaired first, while khafi is treated by most scholars as a deficiency and by some as prohibited.
quiz.prompt: Why do the scholars separate lahn jali from lahn khafi at all?

lessons.summary: A letter owes two things: what it is by itself, and what its neighbours make of it. Every error in recitation is a failure of one or the other, and the two failures do not carry the same ruling.

rows: Its makhraj and permanent sifat: hams, jahr, shiddah, isti'la, itbaq, safir, qalqalah, istitalah
Madd lengths, the measured hold of a ghunnah in idgham, ikhfa and iqlab, tafkheem and tarqiq, and the rules of stopping
table.title: The two dues of every letter

body: تحقيق is the slowest deliberate pace: every letter given its full measure, every optional madd taken at its longest permitted value, nothing hurried. It is the pace of teaching and of drilling, and it is where a new rule gets installed. تدوير is the middle pace, and it is where most recorded murattal recitation sits. حدر is fast, used for revision and for covering large portions, with every rule still applied.

What does not change with speed is the rules. Hadr is not permission to thin out a ghunnah or clip an ikhfa, and a fast reading that loses them is not hadr, it is a fast reading with mistakes in it. The honest test is to record a page at your fastest and listen back for the two-count hums. If a rule disappeared, the speed is past your competence rather than the rule being optional up there.

What does change is the durations Hafs actually leaves open, and only within their permitted values. Three of them matter now. The separated madd, مد منفصل, is held four or five counts (a count is one vowelled letter at your own steady pace, the unit from the Harakat lesson) in the tariq of ash-Shatibiyyah, which is what this course teaches; the two-count reading of it is authentically transmitted for Hafs, but it comes through the tariq of at-Tayyibah, so it is a different route into the same riwayah and is not blended into a Shatibiyyah reading. The joined madd, مد متصل, is four or five counts and never drops to two, and the separated madd is never held longer than the joined one. The madd that exists only because you stopped, مد عارض للسكون, may be taken at two, four or six counts as you choose, and in practice tahqiq takes six, tadwir four and hadr two.

Whichever values you choose, the requirement is that you keep them. Holding one separated madd at four and the next at two is itself the fault, more than either number would be alone, because it means the reading is not following any single transmitted route.

That leaves the word tartil, which the Qur'an uses of the command in 73:4 and of the revelation itself in 25:32. Most teaching today treats tartil as the standard rather than a speed: correct, unhurried, understood recitation, which any of the three paces has to meet. Some classical works do list it as a level of its own, beside tahqiq and distinguished from it by being for worship rather than for drilling. Both usages are in circulation, the practical content is identical, and the count is not worth an argument. What matters is Ali's definition: the letters given their dues, and the stopping places known.

definition.literal: to arrange evenly and without crowding; teeth set in an even row are called رتل
definition.technical: Ali ibn Abi Talib's definition, which the tajweed books adopted as their own: تجويد الحروف ومعرفة الوقوف, giving the letters their dues and knowing where to stop.

drills.caption: Read it three times: tahqiq, tadwir, hadr. The four counts on جَآءَ have to survive all three.
Stop on ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ at two counts, then four, then six. All three are permitted; the sitting gets one of them.

examples.focus: Unhurriedly, at intervals. The Qur'an describes its own delivery in terms of pace.
A separated madd: the madd letter ends فِيهَآ and a hamzah opens the next word. Four or five counts, chosen once.
A joined madd inside جَآءَ. Four counts at the very least, at any speed, hadr included.
This madd exists only because you stopped here. Two, four or six counts are all permitted; pick one for the sitting.

keyPoints: Tahqiq, tadwir, hadr: three paces, every rule applied at each of them.
Tartil is the standard a pace has to meet, not a fourth pace.
Separated and joined madd: four or five counts by ash-Shatibiyyah.
The separated madd is never held longer than the joined one.
If a rule vanishes when you speed up, slow down until it survives.

mistakes.right: Drop back to tadwir until the rule holds, then rebuild the speed on top of it.
mistakes.why: Hadr is defined as fast recitation with the rules intact, so a hadr that loses them has simply left the definition.
mistakes.wrong: Reading fast and letting the hums and the hidden noons thin out.

mistakes.right: Choose one length and hold it for the whole sitting.
mistakes.why: Each value is defensible on its own, but they come from different routes, and mixing them inside one reading is the fault itself.
mistakes.wrong: Taking a separated madd at four counts in one ayah and two in the next.

mistakes.right: Tahqiq is deliberate, not detached. The word stays one word however slowly it is read.
mistakes.why: Over-slow reading breeds its own errors: an invented sukoon, a madd where there is none, a bounce on a letter that never carried one.
mistakes.wrong: Slowing down so far that words come apart and vowels appear between letters.

choices: The slowest of the three paces
The standard of correct, measured recitation that any pace must meet
A style of melodic recitation
Reciting with the eyes on the mushaf rather than from memory
quiz.explain: Ali's definition, giving the letters their dues and knowing the stops, describes a standard rather than a speed. Some classical works do list tartil as a level beside tahqiq, and the requirements come out the same either way.
quiz.prompt: What is tartil, in the way most teachers use the word?

choices: Vary it line by line for expressiveness
Keep it at four for the rest of the sitting
Shorten it to two as you pick up speed
Match whatever the reciter you are listening to does
quiz.explain: Four and five are the two values ash-Shatibiyyah transmits for Hafs, and the choice is made once. The two-count reading is authentic for Hafs but comes by a different tariq, so it is not blended into this one.
quiz.prompt: You take the separated madd at four counts on the first line of a page. What now?

lessons.summary: Tahqiq, tadwir and hadr are three paces. Tartil is not a fourth one: it is the thing that has to be true at all three.

table.title: The three paces

body: Start with the intention, because it is the one part nobody else can audit. Recitation is worship, and the intention is for Allah. The practical form of that check is simple: if reading in front of other people changes how you read, that is worth noticing before anything else in this lesson. Beside it sits tadabbur, the reflection asked for in 47:24, and that is what actually sets your pace. A page read slowly and followed is worth more than a juz passed over.

Purity is where casual advice does the most damage, so here are the lines. Touching a printed mushaf requires wudu according to all four madhhabs; they lean on the letter of the Prophet to Amr ibn Hazm, لا يمس القرآن إلا طاهر, whose chain the scholars discuss, together with 56:79, whose primary sense most commentators take to be the angels and the preserved Book rather than a ruling about paper. A minority, including the Dhahiris, permit touching without wudu. Reciting from memory does not require wudu at all, and most contemporary councils hold that a phone displaying the text is not a mushaf for the purposes of that ruling, since nothing is written on the device. That last point matters here, because you are almost certainly reading this on one.

Two further states deserve stating honestly. After janabah and before ghusl, the majority prohibit recitation. During menstruation the majority position across the madhhabs is that sustained recitation is not permitted, while a substantial number of scholars, classical and contemporary, permit it, particularly for a woman who is memorising or teaching. That is a live disagreement rather than a fringe view, and the right move is to follow your teacher or your madhhab rather than a paragraph in an app.

The setting is lighter than people assume. Facing the qiblah, sitting with composure, and cleaning the mouth with siwak are recommended, not conditions, and recitation while walking or lying down is valid and is reported of the Prophet's household. Reciting aloud and reciting quietly are both established; for tajweed work specifically, recite aloud, because an error you cannot hear is an error you cannot fix.

On portion, 73:20 says فَٱقۡرَءُواْ مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنَ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ, so read what is manageable of it. A small daily portion held for years beats a burst that ends in three weeks, and for a tajweed learner one page read consciously with this week's rule applied is worth ten pages read on autopilot.

Correcting someone else is where the ego usually enters, and three rules cover it. Be certain first, because a reading you do not recognise may not be an error at all: Hafs reads مَٰلِكِ يَوۡمِ ٱلدِّينِ, and so does Shu'ba, the other narrator from Asim, but the riwayat of Nafi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr that this app carries all read مَلِكِ, and a reciter using one of them is reading, not slipping. Second, correct at the stop rather than across the ayah, say the word correctly once, and add nothing to it; a person corrected in front of a room tends to stop reciting in front of rooms. Third, inside salah the follower prompting the imam is established practice and not an interruption, so there you prompt at once and briefly.

Last, the prostration of recitation, in passing. The mushaf this app renders prints the sign ۩ at fifteen places. When you recite one, say Allahu akbar, make a single prostration, say in it what you say in the sujud of salah, then rise and carry on; outside prayer there is no tashahhud, and the madhhabs differ over the tasleem: the Hanafis and Malikis say none is said, the Shafi'is and Hanbalis that it is. Follow your madhhab; nothing hangs on it. A listener follows the reciter. How many of the fifteen count as prostrations of recitation is disputed: the Malikis hold eleven, dropping the three in the mufassal and the second one in al-Hajj, and the other madhhabs land on fourteen or fifteen, the two contested places being that same one in al-Hajj and the one in Sad, which some count as a prostration of thanks instead. On the ruling itself the Hanafis call it wajib and the other schools call it a confirmed sunnah.

definition.technical: The conduct the scholars attach to reciting: the intention behind it, the state of the reciter, the handling of the mushaf itself, and the etiquette of a gathering in which the Qur'an is read.

examples.focus: The etiquette of the gathering: when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.
The ayah the jurists cite for touching the mushaf. Most commentators read it of the angels and the preserved Book.
Reflection is the point of the reading, and it is what should be setting the pace.
Read what is manageable. The portion you can hold is the portion that counts.
The ۩ at the end of this ayah marks a prostration: takbir, one sajdah, then continue.

keyPoints: Intention first: recitation is worship, not performance.
Wudu is for touching a mushaf. A screen is not a mushaf for that ruling.
Read what you can keep. A page followed beats a juz skimmed.
Not every unfamiliar reading is an error: Hafs is one riwayah among several.
Fifteen ۩ marks in this mushaf; the madhhabs count eleven, fourteen or fifteen of them.

mistakes.right: Check whether it is another riwayah before you speak. Nafi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr all read مَلِكِ.
mistakes.why: Correcting a transmitted reading teaches the person that your corrections are unreliable, which costs you the ones that matter.
mistakes.wrong: Correcting a reciter who says مَلِكِ يَوۡمِ ٱلدِّينِ.

mistakes.right: Wait for the stop, say the word once, and stop talking. In salah, prompt the imam at once and briefly.
mistakes.why: The purpose is the ayah, not a demonstration of who noticed.
mistakes.wrong: Correcting loudly, in front of the gathering, in the middle of the ayah.

mistakes.right: Recite from memory or from a screen now. The condition you are avoiding attaches to touching the pages.
mistakes.why: Most people who believe they are not allowed to read are applying the ruling for handling a mushaf to recitation itself.
mistakes.wrong: Waiting to be in a perfect state, and so going days without reading.

mistakes.right: Takbir, one prostration, the tasbih of sujud, then rise and continue reading.
mistakes.why: It is a short act, and hesitating over its details costs more than any of the differences between the madhhabs about it.
mistakes.wrong: Skipping the sajdah because the procedure feels uncertain.

choices: Not permitted: a device holding the text takes the ruling of a mushaf
Permitted: the requirement of wudu attaches to touching a written mushaf
Permitted only if you do not scroll the page
Disliked, but allowed once a day
quiz.explain: Recitation itself never required wudu, and most contemporary councils hold that a screen displaying the text is not a mushaf for the ruling about touching. The condition applies to the pages of a printed copy.
quiz.prompt: You are reading the Qur'an in this app, on your phone, without wudu. What is the majority position?

choices: Correct them, since Hafs reads مَٰلِكِ
Say nothing: مَلِكِ is the reading of several canonical riwayat
Ask them to stop reciting
Correct them quietly once the prayer has ended
quiz.explain: Hafs and Shu'ba, both from Asim, read مَٰلِكِ with the alif. Nafi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read مَلِكِ. A different transmitted reading is not a mistake, which is why certainty comes before correction.
quiz.prompt: A reciter beside you reads مَلِكِ يَوۡمِ ٱلدِّينِ. What should you do?

lessons.summary: What to intend, what state you have to be in, how much to read, how to correct someone without wounding them, and what to do when the page carries a ۩.

rows: All four madhhabs; a minority including the Dhahiris permit it without
Reading from a phone or a screen
Most contemporary councils do not give a device the ruling of a mushaf
Minor impurity does not prevent recitation itself
Qur'anic words said as du'a or dhikr are treated separately
Most of the madhhabs prohibit sustained recitation; many scholars permit it, especially for memorisation
table.title: Purity: where scholars agree and where they do not

body: The wording comes from 16:98: فَإِذَا قَرَأۡتَ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ فَٱسۡتَعِذۡ بِٱللَّهِ مِنَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ. The reciters take the chosen form, الصيغة المختارة, straight out of the ayah: أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم. Other wordings are reported and permitted, such as adding السميع العليم, and a student is better served drilling the chosen one until it needs no thought. The ayah reads literally as when you recite, seek refuge, which the great majority understand as when you intend to recite, so it comes before the reading; a minority took it at face value and placed it after, and that opinion is recorded without being practised. As for its ruling, the majority hold the isti'adhah recommended and a minority hold it obligatory for recitation.

Whether it is said aloud is a question about the listeners rather than about you. Say it aloud when you are reciting aloud in front of people and you are the one opening the recitation, because the isti'adhah is what tells a gathering that recitation has begun and it is time to fall silent. Say it quietly in the four situations the manuals list: reciting alone, reciting silently, reciting in salah, and taking your turn in a circle where someone has already begun.

The basmalah is written at the head of one hundred and thirteen of the one hundred and fourteen surahs; at-Tawbah alone has none. Whether it counts as an ayah of each surah is an old disagreement among the jurists and the reciters both, and the numbering this mushaf uses, the Kufan count that travels with Hafs, settles it one way: the basmalah is ayah 1 of al-Fatiha and is not numbered in any other surah. It also appears once inside a surah as part of an ayah, in Sulayman's letter at 27:30, where it is read as part of the ayah and is not an opening at all.

At-Tawbah takes no basmalah, whether you begin the surah directly or arrive from the end of al-Anfal. Scholars offer several explanations, among them that the companions were not certain whether al-Anfal and Bara'ah were one surah, and the report from Ali that the basmalah is safety while Bara'ah came down with the sword; they differ about the reason and agree entirely about the practice. Coming across that seam from al-Anfal there are three transmitted ways: waqf, stopping and taking a breath; sakt, a brief pause with no breath taken; and wasl, joining straight through. None of the three inserts a basmalah.

At every other seam between two surahs there are four conceivable ways to place the basmalah, and three of them are read. You may cut all three apart: stop at the end of the surah, stop again after the basmalah, then begin the next surah. You may join all three: the last ayah, the basmalah and the first ayah in one breath. You may cut and then join: stop at the end of the surah, then carry the basmalah forward into the first ayah, which is the most common practice and the one most reciters use. The fourth, joining the last ayah of the finished surah to the basmalah and then stopping before the next surah begins, is not read.

The reason is worth understanding rather than memorising. The basmalah belongs to the surah that is starting, not to the one that has ended. Attach it backward to the last ayah and then cut it off from what follows, and it lands where it does not belong: it sounds like the closing verse of the surah you just finished. The qurra call that wajh مُمْتَنِع, prevented, for exactly that reason. The short way to hold it: the basmalah may look forward, or stand on its own, but it may never look only backward. Note that the same four combinations exist between the isti'adhah, the basmalah and the first ayah when you open a surah, and there all four are permitted, because nothing in that sequence can be mistaken for the end of something else.

Starting in the middle of a surah, which is what happens whenever you open this app on your last-read ayah, works like this. The isti'adhah is said wherever you begin. The basmalah is optional there, and both saying it and leaving it out are transmitted. The one place scholars differ is starting in the middle of at-Tawbah: many of the reciters allow the basmalah there, on the grounds that what was omitted was the surah's opening, while others avoid it anywhere in that surah at all. Either practice is defensible and neither is worth an argument.

definition.literal: to take shelter with someone, to seek protection
definition.technical: Saying أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم before beginning to recite, so that the reading opens by taking refuge with the One whose speech is about to be read.

drills.caption: Say it once at your reading pace, not faster than the reading it opens.
Only when you begin a surah at its beginning. Optional in the middle of one.
All three joined in one breath: one of the four ways of opening a surah, and all four of those are read.
drills.text: أَعُوذُ بِٱللَّهِ مِنَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ  بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ  ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ

examples.focus: The wording of the isti'adhah is lifted straight out of this ayah.
The basmalah as ayah 1. In the Kufan numbering this mushaf uses, only al-Fatiha numbers it.
The one basmalah inside a surah: part of Sulayman's letter, read as part of the ayah.
At-Tawbah begins here, with no basmalah before it, however you arrive.
The last ayah of al-Anfal. From here into at-Tawbah: stop, pause without breathing, or join straight through.

keyPoints: أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم is the transmitted wording, taken from 16:98.
Aloud when you are opening for listeners; quietly alone, in salah, or mid-circle.
The basmalah heads 113 surahs. At-Tawbah has none, from either direction.
Three of the four seams between surahs are read. Joining it backward then stopping is not.
Starting mid-surah: isti'adhah always, basmalah as you wish.

mistakes.right: Either stop before the basmalah, or carry it forward into the surah that is starting.
mistakes.why: The basmalah opens what follows it. Hung on the end of the previous surah it reads as that surah's closing verse.
mistakes.wrong: Joining the basmalah to the end of the surah you just finished, then pausing before the next one.

mistakes.right: Say the isti'adhah, then begin with بَرَآءَةٞ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ, with nothing between them.
mistakes.why: No chain transmits a basmalah at that place. The omission is itself part of what was passed down.
mistakes.wrong: Saying the basmalah before Surat at-Tawbah because starting without it feels wrong.

mistakes.right: Say it quietly and begin.
mistakes.why: The isti'adhah is raised in order to announce that recitation has started. Mid-circle everyone already knows.
mistakes.wrong: Raising the isti'adhah when the reading has just been handed to you in a circle.

mistakes.right: Say it wherever you begin. It is the basmalah that is optional there, not the isti'adhah.
mistakes.why: The command in 16:98 attaches to reciting, not to opening a surah.
mistakes.wrong: Dropping the isti'adhah because you are starting in the middle of a surah.

choices: Stop after the surah, then join the basmalah to the next one
Join the last ayah, the basmalah and the next surah in one breath
Join the basmalah to the surah you just finished, then stop
Stop after the surah, stop after the basmalah, then begin
quiz.explain: The basmalah opens the surah in front of it. Joined backward and then cut off from what follows, it reads as the closing verse of the surah that ended, so the reciters call that way prevented. The other three are all transmitted.
quiz.prompt: Which way of handling the basmalah between two surahs is not read?

choices: Always, in every situation
When you are reciting aloud to listeners and you are the one beginning
Only inside salah
Only when reciting a complete surah
quiz.explain: It is raised so listeners know recitation has begun and fall silent. Alone, silently, in salah, or when someone else in a circle has already opened, it is said quietly.
quiz.prompt: When is the isti'adhah said aloud?

choices: Nothing, since you are not starting a surah
The isti'adhah, and the basmalah if you wish
The basmalah only
The isti'adhah, and the basmalah is required

body: A letter in Arabic is not a shape on a page. It is a sound with an address, and the address is the makhraj: the spot where the air is stopped, narrowed, or shaped. Change the spot and you have changed the letter, whatever you intended to say. This is why makharij come before every rule in this course: the rules govern what happens between letters, and none of that helps if the letters themselves land in the wrong place.

There are five general regions, and everything you will ever pronounce comes out of one of them: الجوف, the empty space inside the mouth and throat; الحلق, the throat; اللسان, the tongue; الشفتان, the two lips; and الخيشوم, the nasal passage.

Inside those five regions sit seventeen specific exits: one in the jawf, three in the throat, ten on the tongue, two at the lips, one at the nose. One plus three plus ten plus two plus one is seventeen. The letters divide very unevenly across them. The tongue alone produces eighteen of the twenty-nine letters, which is why its lesson is the longest in this chapter, while the nasal passage produces none at all. Twenty-nine rather than twenty-eight, because tajweed counts the hamza and the alif as two separate letters. The table below adds up to thirty-one rather than twenty-nine, because و and ي each appear twice: once as a madd letter in the jawf, and once as a consonant at its own exit, the lips for the waw and the middle of the tongue for the ya. Thirty-one slots, twenty-nine letters.

The number seventeen is not unanimous, and it is worth knowing why. Seventeen is the count of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, and it is the one Ibn al-Jazari chose in his Muqaddimah, so it is what nearly every tajweed course teaches, this one included. Sibawayh counted sixteen: he did not treat the jawf as an exit, placing the alif in the deepest throat beside ء and ه and assigning the madd waw and ya to the exits of their consonants. A third group, among them al-Farra', counted fourteen by dropping the jawf and treating ل، ن and ر as one exit instead of three. The disagreement is about how finely to divide the mouth, not about how any letter is actually pronounced.

There is a classical way to find a letter's makhraj yourself, and it takes about five seconds. Put the letter in sukoon, prefix a hamza carrying a fatha, and say it slowly: أَقْ، أَبْ، أَسْ. Listen for the point where the sound is cut off. That point is the exit. For letters whose sound trails away instead of stopping cleanly, double the letter instead and feel where the friction sits: أَسّ، أَشّ. Ibn al-Jazari gives exactly this method, and it beats any diagram, because it is your own mouth reporting rather than someone else's description.

Knowing the makhraj is not by itself knowing the letter. ط، د and ت share one exit; so do ص، ز، س, and so do ظ، ذ، ث. What separates the members of those groups is not place but sifat, the attributes: whether the voice runs or stops, whether air escapes, whether the sound is heavy or light. Makhraj tells you where, sifat tell you how, and a letter is wrong if either one is wrong.

definition.literal: the place of exit, where a thing comes out
definition.technical: The precise point in the throat, mouth, or nasal passage where a letter's sound is produced, and by which it is separated from every other letter.

body: Every other letter in the language is made by putting something in the way of the air: a tongue against a palate, lips against lips, a throat squeezed to a slit. The jawf letters are made by getting everything out of the way. The mouth simply holds the shape the preceding vowel gave it, and the sound continues through the empty space until it is stopped on purpose.

The three are ا، و and ي, but each only in one specific state: the alif always with a fatha before it, the waw sakinah with a damma before it, the ya sakinah with a kasra before it. Say each one slowly and you will notice that the letter is nothing but its own vowel held open. That matching of vowel to letter is what the books mean by مجانسة, homogeneity, and it is the condition for a letter being a jawf letter at all. The alif is the strictest case: it never carries a vowel of its own and never appears with a sukoon written on it, because it is only ever a stretched fatha.

The three are gathered in the word نُوحِيهَا, which is real Qur'anic Arabic rather than an invented string: the waw after a damma, the ya after a kasra, the alif after a fatha, in that order. Teachers have used it as the mnemonic for centuries.

Because nothing touches, nothing ends the sound except you. A ب ends when the lips open; an alif ends when you decide it ends. That is the entire reason madd is measured in counts (حركات) and why the natural madd is fixed at two: left alone, these letters would have no length of their own. Two counts is roughly the time to fold two fingers at your own reciting pace, so the count is relative to your tempo, not to a clock.

Two letters look like jawf letters and are not. When و or ي is sakin after a FATHA, as in فَوۡقَكُمۡ or بَيۡت, it is a letter of leen, softness, and not a letter of madd. It keeps a contact point of its own, the lips for the waw and the middle of the tongue for the ya, so it belongs to those exits. While you are reading on, it is said softly and briefly and is not stretched. Filing these two under the jawf is what produces the drawn-out khaawf that marks a beginner.

One last property follows from having no contact: the alif has no weight of its own. It takes the heaviness of whatever came before it, so it is full and thick in طَابَ and thin in تَابَ. There is nothing in the mouth doing anything to make it either, which is why the alif is never listed among the heavy letters or among the light ones.

definition.literal: the hollow, the inside of a thing
definition.technical: The empty space running up through the throat and mouth. It is the exit of the three madd letters, which touch nothing and end only when the reciter ends them.

mistakes.right: Say leen letters softly and briefly while you are reading on.
mistakes.why: They are not jawf letters. Only a madd letter sitting after its matching vowel is held.
mistakes.wrong: Stretching a leen letter: reading خَوۡف as khaawf or بَيۡت as baayt.

mistakes.right: Set the mouth on the vowel, then hold it perfectly still for the full two counts.
mistakes.why: A jawf letter is shaped by mouth position alone. If the position changes mid-letter, the sound changes with it and a listener hears two vowels.
mistakes.wrong: Letting the mouth move during the madd, so the vowel drifts partway through.

mistakes.right: Two counts at whatever pace you are reading, fast or slow.
mistakes.why: Arabic separates words by vowel length. A madd letter given one count has stopped being a madd letter.
mistakes.wrong: Cutting the natural madd short when reading quickly.

mistakes.right: Let the preceding fatha simply continue. Nothing new begins.
mistakes.why: A catch inserts a hamza, which is a throat letter with a complete closure, into a letter defined by having no closure at all.
mistakes.wrong: Starting the alif with a small catch in the throat, as if a hamza were attached to it.
