lessons.summary: One exit, three letters, and no contact anywhere in the mouth. These are the only letters whose length has to be counted, which is why the whole madd chapter rests on this lesson.

body: Take the six in the order the throat produces them, from the bottom up: ء and ه from the deepest part (أقصى الحلق), ع and ح from the middle (وسط الحلق), غ and خ from the part nearest the mouth (أدنى الحلق). Recited in that order, ء ه ع ح غ خ walks the throat from bottom to top. Recited alphabetically they teach you nothing about where they are.

There is a pattern inside the pairs worth noticing immediately: in each pair, the second letter is the breathy one. ه، ح and خ all let air escape audibly, an attribute the books call hams, while ء، ع and غ do not. So each exit gives you a full-voiced sound and its whispered neighbour, made in the very same place. Once you hear that, the throat stops being six unrelated sounds and becomes three positions with two settings each.

The hamza is a complete closure. The vocal folds shut, pressure builds behind them, and the release is a clean click. It is the most tightly stopped letter in the language. Two errors sit on either side of it: softening it into a plain vowel onset, so that أَحَدٌ begins the way an English word beginning with a would, and over-releasing it so that it bounces like a qalqalah letter. It stops, then it opens, and there is no echo after it.

The ه is made in the same place with the opposite setting: the throat stays wide open and a quantity of air passes without friction anywhere. It is the emptiest sound in the language, which is exactly why speed erases it, especially in the pronoun endings هُۥ and هِۦ. If a listener cannot hear it, you did not say it.

ع and ح share the middle throat, and this is the pair learners most often collapse. For ع the throat narrows to a point where the sound is neither a clean stop nor a free flow, and the voice keeps running through the narrowing; classically it is one of the letters described as sitting between shiddah and rakhawah. For ح the same place is squeezed tighter and the voice is switched off, so what you hear is hot air rasping through a narrow gap. Put a hand flat on the front of your neck: ع vibrates, ح does not.

غ and خ are made at the part of the throat nearest the mouth (أدنى الحلق), just behind the point where the tongue's own letters begin. Phoneticians describe a tongue-root gesture here as well, but the makhraj the classical books give is the throat itself: ق and ك are the pair made BY the tongue against the palate, and غ and خ are made in the throat behind them. Both are heavy letters, so they fill the mouth rather than thinning it. Again the pair splits by voice: غ vibrates and rolls, خ is dry and rasping. The two commonest substitutions are a French r for غ and a hard k for خ, and both come from dragging the sound forward into the mouth. It belongs in the throat.

The ه and ح confusion deserves its own paragraph, because beginners hear the two as a soft h and a strong h, which is not what they are. They are made in different places. ه sits at the very bottom of the throat with everything relaxed; ح sits a step higher with the throat squeezed. Say أَهْ then أَحْ with a hand on your neck and feel the squeeze arrive on the second one. That physical difference is what you are training, not a difference in effort.

One connection to keep: these six letters are the trigger set for idh-har in the nun sakin chapter. The reason given there is distance, because the noon is made at the tip of the tongue and these six are made as far from it as the mouth allows, so nothing can blend. That reason is this lesson.

definition.technical: The passage from the top of the chest to the back of the mouth. It holds three exits, two letters each, and its six letters are exactly the six that leave a nun sakin clear.

lessons.titleEn: The Throat: Three Exits, Six Letters

body: The classical books divide the tongue into four zones and place the ten exits inside them: the deepest part (أقصى اللسان) holds two, the middle (وسط اللسان) holds one, the edges (حافة اللسان) hold two, and the tip (طرف اللسان) holds five. Learn the four zones first and the ten exits then have somewhere to live.

Exits one and two, the deepest part of the tongue. ق is made by lifting the very back of the tongue against the soft palate above it: a complete stop, released with a bounce when it carries sukoon. ك is the same movement a short step forward, where the soft palate gives way to the hard. The two are called اللهويتان, the uvular pair, because they are made beside the uvula. The single most useful thing to know about them is that they are one small step apart and that ك releases a puff of air while ق does not. A ق that hisses has become a ك.

Exit three, the middle of the tongue. ج، ش and ي are made by pressing or approaching the middle of the tongue against the hard palate above it, and they are called الشجرية. The ي meant here is any ya that is not a madd letter: the vowelled ya, and the leen ya, sakin after a fatha, as in بَيۡت. Only the ya sakinah after a kasra is from the jawf. The three differ entirely in what happens at the contact: ج closes completely and releases with a bounce, ش releases air that spreads sideways across the mouth, and ي only approaches, never obstructing.

Exit four, the edge of the tongue. ض is made by pressing one edge of the tongue, or both, against the upper molars from the inside, and letting the sound run forward along that edge. Ibn al-Jazari allows the left edge, the right, or both together, and commentators note the left is the easier and commoner. ض is the hardest letter in the language to place, it is unique to Arabic, and it is the reason Arabic is called لغة الضاد. It is heavy, and it carries an attribute of its own, istitalah: the sound travels along the edge instead of stopping at a point.

Exit five, the same edge further forward. ل uses the forward portion of the tongue's edges, running to the tip, against the gum above the upper front teeth and the teeth beside them. It is the broadest exit on the tongue, which is why a lam is easy to say and just as easy to say sloppily: if only the very tip touches, the letter thins out and loses its body.

Exits six and seven, the tip alone. The nun is made with the tip against the gum just above the two upper front teeth, a hair below where the lam touched, with the nasal passage open, which is why the nun and the khaishum are inseparable. The ra is made at the same gum but slightly further in, with the tip curled a little toward the palate, and it carries takrir, a readiness to roll. The instruction for ra is to allow one contact only. A rolled Spanish rr is an error of degree rather than of place, and Ibn al-Jazari's own wording is to conceal the takrir, not to display it.

Exit eight, the tip with the base of the upper front teeth. ط، د and ت come from exactly the same point, where the tip meets the gum at the roots of the two upper incisors, and they are called النطعية. Since the exit is identical, only the attributes separate them: ط is the heavy one, with the tongue sealed up against the palate, while د and ت are both light, and د keeps the voice where ت is whispered. If you can hear the difference between these three, you are hearing sifat, not makharij.

Exit nine, the tip with the front teeth, whistling. ص، ز and س come from a narrow channel between the tip of the tongue, resting just above the two lower front teeth, and the upper front teeth in front of it. All three whistle, an attribute called safir, and they are called الأسلية. ص is the heavy one; ز and س are light, and ز keeps the voice where س is whispered. The whistle is the test: if there is no whistle at all, the tongue is sitting too far back.

Exit ten, the tip with the edges of the upper teeth. ظ، ذ and ث are made with the tip protruding very slightly to touch the biting edges of the two upper incisors, and they are called اللثوية. ظ is the heavy one; ذ and ث are light, and ذ keeps the voice where ث is whispered. Substituting ز for ذ and س for ث is the commonest makhraj error in the language, and it is a slip of exactly one exit: the tongue stayed behind the teeth instead of coming out to touch them.

Count the exits and their letters and the arithmetic comes out at 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 3 + 3, which is ten exits and eighteen letters. Notice that three of the ten hold three letters each. Those nine letters are where the sifat chapter earns its keep, because place alone cannot tell them apart.

definition.technical: The largest of the five regions: ten exits producing eighteen letters, counted from the back of the tongue forward and described in four zones, the deepest part, the middle, the edges, and the tip.

drills.caption: One step apart at the back of the tongue. The ك releases a puff of air; the ق does not.
Edge at the molars, tip at the teeth edges, tip at the gum. Three exits that beginners collapse into one.
Tip out on the teeth, then tip back behind them. If the second of each pair whistles and the first does not, both are right.
One exit, three letters. Move nothing but the weight and the voice.

examples.focus: ق and ك from the deepest tongue a few letters apart, then ز at the teeth and ج at the middle of the tongue.
ش from the middle of the tongue against ط from the tip, twice over. The tongue travels its whole length between them.
ض from the edge of the tongue at the molars, then ظ from the tip at the edges of the upper teeth. Two heavy letters, two different exits.
A doubled ض and a doubled ل in one word: the same edge of the tongue, back at the molars and then forward at the gum.
ن and ر from neighbouring points on the same gum, the ر a little further in and heavy here.
ط from the tip at the base of the upper teeth, ك from the back of the tongue, ث from the tip at their edges.
Two sins, both whistling through the narrow channel between the tip of the tongue and the front teeth.

keyPoints: Four zones: deepest, middle, edges, tip. Ten exits inside them, 18 letters.
ق then ك from the back, one small step apart; only ك releases air.
ج ش ي from the middle of the tongue against the hard palate.
ض from the edge against the molars; ل from the same edges further forward.
Three exits hold three letters each (ط د ت / ص ز س / ظ ذ ث), so only sifat separate them.

mistakes.right: Press the EDGE of the tongue against the upper molars and let the sound run forward along it.
mistakes.why: Tip contact produces a د or a ظ. ض is the only letter made with the edge against the upper molars, and the only one whose sound runs along the length of that edge, the attribute called istitalah. It is the letter Arabic is named after.
mistakes.wrong: Saying ض as a heavy د, with the tip of the tongue against the gum.

mistakes.right: Let the tip come out and touch the biting edges of the upper front teeth.
mistakes.why: This is a one-exit slip: the tongue stayed behind the teeth. The whistle it produces is the giveaway.
mistakes.wrong: Replacing ذ with ز and ث with س.

mistakes.right: One contact only. Takrir is a tendency to be restrained, not an instruction to trill.
mistakes.why: Ibn al-Jazari's wording is to conceal the takrir. A trill multiplies one letter into several, which changes the word's shape.
mistakes.wrong: Rolling the ر like a Spanish rr.

mistakes.right: Use the forward part of the tongue's edges against the gum, so the contact is wide.
mistakes.why: A thin, tip-only lam loses the letter's body and tends to drag the following vowel thin with it.
mistakes.wrong: Letting the lam touch with the very tip of the tongue alone.

table.title: Three exits that hold three letters each

body: The lips hold two exits and four letters, and they are the only makharij you can watch in a mirror. Use one. Lip letters are the easiest of all to diagnose and the easiest to leave uncorrected, because nothing in the sound alone tells you what your face is doing.

The first lip exit is not both lips. ف is made by bringing the inside of the lower lip up against the tips of the two upper front teeth and letting air run through the gap. The lower lip does the moving; the upper lip does nothing at all. The usual error is to make ف with the two lips pressed together, which produces something between ف and a p and is audible immediately to a trained ear.

The second exit is الشفتان, the two lips, and it holds ب، م and و. The three are not made the same way, and the difference is worth stating precisely. For ب the lips press shut firmly and the release is a bounce. For م the lips close as well, but more lightly, and the sound leaves through the nose rather than the mouth. For و the lips never close at all: they round and push forward, leaving an opening for the sound to pass through. Two closures and one rounding, from a single exit.

That و is any waw that is not a madd letter: the vowelled waw, as in وَتَبَّ, and the leen waw, sakin after a fatha, as in فَوۡقَكُمۡ. The waw of madd, sakin after a damma, is the one not counted here: the lips do hold their rounded shape for it, but nothing touches and nothing obstructs, so its exit is the jawf. Same lips, two different makharij, decided by what the waw is doing in the word.

م is the hinge between the two regions in this lesson. Its lips close, so the mouth is blocked, and the sound has to leave somewhere: it leaves through the nose. That nasal component is the ghunnah, and it is why ن and م are called the letters of ghunnah.

الخيشوم is the seventeenth exit and the only one that produces no letter. What it produces is the ghunnah: the nasal resonance that accompanies ن and م in every state they occur in. It earns a place in the list because a sound genuinely comes out of it, and you can prove that in one second by pinching your nose while saying مَمْ or نَنْ. The sound is choked off, because you have closed its only exit.

Nearly every rule in the nun sakin and mim sakin chapters is this exit carrying the sound while the mouth does something else. In ikhfa the tongue leaves the noon's place and the nose holds the sound for two counts. In iqlab the lips take a mim shape without sealing and the nose does the rest. In idgham with ghunnah the noon is gone entirely and the hum is what survives it. When you learn those rules, you are learning to route sound through this exit deliberately.

The ghunnah is longest and clearest when the ن or م carries a shadda, as in ثُمَّ and ٱلۡجِنَّةِ, and shortest when those letters carry an ordinary vowel. Scholars rank the states in between, and that ranking has its own lesson. What matters here is that the nose is always slightly open for these two letters, never open only sometimes.

definition.literal: the inner nose, the nasal cavity
definition.technical: The passage above the roof of the mouth opening into the nose. It produces no letter of its own; the only sound that issues from it is the ghunnah, which belongs to ن and م.

drills.caption: The four lip letters in front of a mirror. Only the ف uses the teeth, and only the و leaves the lips open.
Pinch your nose halfway through each one. The sound chokes off, which is the khaishum proving itself.

examples.focus: Both lip exits inside the second word: the و rounds without touching, then the ف lifts the lower lip to the upper teeth. The tanween ending the first word merges into that و with ghunnah, so the lips round while the nose is already humming.
The ب of لَهَبٖ, then a و that only rounds, then the doubled ب of وَتَبَّ. Watch the lips in a mirror.
A mim merging into a mim: the lips close once and the nose carries the sound across the word boundary.
The doubled م of ثُمَّ is the khaishum at its clearest: lips shut, everything through the nose, two counts.
The same nasal hold on a doubled ن. The tongue sits at the gum, but the sound is leaving through the nose.

keyPoints: ف: the inside of the lower lip against the tips of the upper front teeth. Never both lips.
ب، م and و share one exit: ب closes firmly, م closes lightly and vents through the nose, و only rounds.
Only the madd waw is from the jawf; the vowelled waw and the leen waw are both lip letters.
The khaishum produces no letter, only the ghunnah of ن and م.
Pinch your nose during مَمْ: the sound chokes. That is the proof the exit is real.

mistakes.wrong: Producing the ghunnah in the mouth: a nasal-sounding vowel rather than a nasal hum.

table.title: One exit, three lip settings

body: The table below is the whole chapter on one screen, ordered the way the mouth is built: from the empty space and the bottom of the throat, out along the tongue, to the lips, with the nasal passage last because it sits above all of them. Read down it once a day for a week and the order stops being a list and becomes a map.

The order is the part that matters. Neighbouring rows are the letters you are most likely to confuse, because they are made a few millimetres apart: ق and ك are neighbours, ه and ح are neighbours, ذ and ز are neighbours. Almost every substitution a learner makes is a jump to an adjacent row rather than a random error.

So use the table like this when a teacher tells you a letter is wrong. First, isolate the letter with the sukoon test: a vowelled hamza plus the letter with sukoon, repeated slowly. Second, find its row. Third, look at the rows immediately above and below and say those letters the same way, because one of them is almost certainly what you are actually producing. Fourth, alternate the two deliberately, ten times, paying attention to where the contact moves rather than to how it sounds. The correction is a change of place, and place is something you can feel long before you can hear it.

If the letter you are missing shares its exit with the letter you are producing, the table has already done its job and the problem is not place at all. ط، د، ت sit on one row; so do ص، ز، س, and so do ظ، ذ، ث. Confusing letters inside one of those rows is a sifat problem: weight, voice, or escaping air. That is the next thing to study, and no amount of moving your tongue will fix it.

One practical habit is worth more than the rest of this lesson. Record thirty seconds of your own recitation and listen for the rows rather than for the words. Almost every reciter has one or two rows that are consistently soft, and hearing your own ض or your own ه in isolation is far more instructive than being told about it.

drills.caption: Three neighbouring pairs. Alternate each pair ten times and track where the contact moves.
drills.text: أَقْ  أَكْ  /  أَهْ  أَحْ  /  أَذْ  أَزْ

drills.caption: One row, three letters. If these are hard, the work is in the sifat chapter, not in this one.

examples.focus: ض and ظ in consecutive words: the edge of the tongue at the molars, then the tip at the teeth. If they sound identical, two rows have collapsed into one.
Three commonly softened rows in two words: ص whistling at the teeth, خ rasping in the throat, ش spreading air at the middle of the tongue.

Three regions and five exits inside one word: ب at the lips, ع in the middle throat, ث at the edges of the upper teeth, then ر and ت at two further points on the tongue. A useful word to record and check row by row.

keyPoints: Seventeen rows, ordered from the deepest exit outward to the lips, nose last.
Confusions are almost always with an adjacent row, not a distant one.
Isolate with the sukoon test, find the row, drill the neighbour against it.
If the two letters share a row, the problem is sifat, not makhraj.
Record yourself and listen for rows rather than for words.

chapters.title: Articulation Points

body: The makharij chapter answers where. Press the tip of the tongue against the gum ridge behind the upper front teeth and you have located ت, د and ط at once, because all three are made in exactly that spot. Say them one after another and they are plainly not the same letter. What separates them is not location; it is everything that happens at the location.

Take the three apart. ت is said with the vocal cords still, so the breath keeps running out after the tongue releases. د is said with the vocal cords vibrating, so the breath is blocked. ط is classed jahr like د, meaning the breath is cut off rather than left to run, and it adds a third thing: the body of the tongue rises and presses flat against the roof of the mouth, which fills the sound out and makes it heavy. A caution on that classification: on ط the vibration classical writers described is not what a modern throat test finds, so reach for ب or د when you want to feel jahr for yourself. One exit, three sets of instructions, three letters.

That is what a sifah is, and it is why makharij and sifat are always taught as a pair. A learner who has the makharij but not the sifat produces a recitation in which every letter lands in roughly the right place and half of them are still the wrong letter. That is the usual shape of a non-Arab reciter's accent, and it is fixed one quality at a time rather than by trying harder.

Scholars do not agree on how many sifat there are. Seventeen is the count you will meet most often: ten that come in opposing pairs, and seven that stand alone with no opposite. Others count sixteen, or fourteen, and some classifications run past forty by splitting the categories more finely. The disagreement is about how to file the qualities, not about how the letters are pronounced, so learn one list rather than collecting them.

One further distinction earns its keep early. Some sifat are strong (قوية) and some are weak (ضعيفة). Jahr, shiddah, isti'la, itbaq, ismat and the standalone group apart from lin are strong; hams, rakhawah, istifal, infitah, idhlaq and lin are weak, and tawassut sits between the two. Lin is the one standalone quality counted weak, which is worth knowing before you meet the seven. A letter built mostly from strong qualities holds its shape under pressure. A letter built from weak ones is the first thing a tired reciter loses, which is why a long session tends to flatten ص into س rather than the other way round.

definition.literal: a quality, a description of a thing
definition.technical: The manner in which a letter's sound comes out of its articulation point: whether the breath keeps running, whether the sound stops or flows, whether the back of the tongue is raised, whether the tongue clamps against the roof of the mouth.

examples.focus: Two trios in one phrase: ص against the س of the next word, and ط against its ت.
ح and ع come from the same middle-throat exit. The ح is breathed and runs; the ع is voiced and half held.
ذ and ظ, identical in place and a whole letter apart in sound. The doubled ظ is the ذ with the tongue clamped.
The ز is the voiced member of the whistling trio س ز ص. Same channel, voice switched on.

keyPoints: A makhraj says where the letter is made; a sifah says what happens there.
ت د ط share one exit. Only their sifat make them three letters.
Seventeen is the usual count: ten in five opposing pairs, seven standing alone.
Strong sifat hold their shape; weak ones are the first to go when you tire.

mistakes.right: Press the body of the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, then release with the tip.
mistakes.why: A heavier-sounding ت is still ت. The clamp is not decoration on the letter; it is the letter.
mistakes.wrong: Saying ط as a thickened ت, with the tongue in the same shape.

mistakes.right: ذ flows between the tongue and the tips of the front teeth, ز whistles through a narrow channel, ظ is ذ with the tongue clamped.
mistakes.why: English has no ذ and no ظ, so an untrained tongue substitutes the nearest sound it already owns, and three letters become one.
mistakes.wrong: Letting ذ, ز and ظ all arrive as one z-like sound.

mistakes.right: Read each sifah as a physical action and test it on one letter: a hand at the mouth for hams, fingers on the throat for jahr on ب, د or ز.
mistakes.why: A quality you cannot demonstrate on a single letter in isolation will not survive a whole ayah.
mistakes.wrong: Treating the sifat as terminology to memorise rather than instructions to carry out.

lessons.titleEn: Why Two Letters Can Share an Exit

body: Before the lists, run the five questions on one letter. Take ط. Does the breath keep running? No: it is jahr. Does the sound stop dead? Yes: shiddah. Is the back of the tongue raised? Yes: isti'la. Does the tongue clamp against the palate? Yes: itbaq. Is it one of the six fluent letters? No: ismat. Five answers, and ط is completely described.

الهمس against الجهر is a question about the vocal cords. In a hams letter they do not vibrate, so nothing holds the air back and the breath goes on flowing after the letter is formed. There are ten, collected in فَحَثَّهُ شَخۡصٌ سَكَتۡ. In a jahr letter the cords vibrate and the breath is cut off; the remaining eighteen letters are jahr, counting the alphabet at twenty-eight as this course does. Manuals that count the alif as a twenty-ninth letter give nineteen, and every complement below shifts by one for the same reason. The test is a hand held a few inches from the mouth: say سْ and you feel a stream of air, say دْ and you feel almost nothing.

الشدة against الرخاوة is a question about the sound rather than the breath, and it has a middle rank. Say a letter with sukoon and try to hold it. A shiddah letter cannot be held for an instant, because the makhraj is shut and the sound stops dead; there are eight, in أَجِدۡ قَطٍ بَكَتۡ. A rakhawah letter can be held as long as your air lasts, because the makhraj is left slightly open and the sound runs through the gap; the remaining fifteen letters are rakhawah. Between them sit five letters of tawassut, لِنۡ عُمَرَ, which can be held for a moment but not indefinitely.

الاستعلاء against الاستفال is a question about the back of the tongue. Seven letters, خُصَّ ضَغۡطٍ قِظۡ, are said with the back of the tongue lifted toward the soft palate, which enlarges the space the sound fills and makes it heavy. The other twenty-one are said with the tongue lying low, and are light. This one pair is the whole foundation of tafkheem and tarqeeq, which the next lesson takes up on its own.

الإطباق against الانفتاح is a second, narrower question about the tongue, and it operates inside the isti'la group. Four letters, ص ض ط ظ, do not merely raise the back of the tongue: they press the body of the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth so the sound is trapped between two surfaces. The other twenty-four leave a gap. This is why ص ض ط ظ are audibly heavier than the other three isti'la letters خ غ ق, and why they are the four that collapse into س د ت ذ the moment the clamp goes missing.

الإذلاق against الإصمات is the odd one out, because it is not something a reciter performs. The six idhlaq letters, فَرَّ مِنۡ لُبٍّ, are made at the tip of the tongue or at the lips, the two most mobile parts of the mouth, so they leave their makhraj faster and with less effort than any others. The grammarians used this as a test of vocabulary: a genuine four- or five-letter Arabic root nearly always contains at least one of the six, and a word of that length with none was suspected of being borrowed. There is nothing here for a reciter to perform, and no single holding test can isolate it either, because the six cut straight across the other pairs: ب is shiddah, ر ل ن م are tawassut, and ف is rakhawah and can be held as long as any other flowing letter.

definition.literal: the qualities that contradict one another
definition.technical: The sifat that come in opposing pairs, such that every letter carries exactly one member of each pair. A letter cannot be both breathed and voiced, or both stopped and flowing.

drills.caption: One exit, three letters. Breath on the first, voice on the second, clamp on the third.
Try to hold each one. The first runs as long as your air; the second cannot be held at all.

examples.focus: Three ranks in one phrase: ب and ق are shiddah, ر and ل are tawassut, ف is rakhawah. Only the sakin ل of ٱلۡ can be heard leaning here, since every other letter carries a vowel, and if you stop on ٱلۡفَلَقِ the ق does not stop dead at all: it bounces, because it is one of the five.
The ب is jahr, so the breath is blocked. The final ت is hams, so it releases a puff of air.
A run of hams letters: ك, then the sakin ص, then ف. Hold a hand at the mouth and you feel each one.
ش and س lie low (istifal). The ض raises the tongue and clamps it, so it is heavy where the first word was thin.
Itbaq against infitah twice over: ص against س, ط against ت, same exits and opposite tongues.

keyPoints: Five questions, and every letter in the alphabet answers all five.
Hams (فحثه شخص سكت) lets the breath run; jahr blocks it. Test with a hand at the mouth.
Shiddah (أجد قط بكت) stops dead, rakhawah flows, five tawassut letters (لن عمر) sit between.
Isti'la (خص ضغط قظ) raises the tongue; itbaq (ص ض ط ظ) also clamps it flat.
Idhlaq (فر من لب) is the one pair with nothing to pass or fail.

mistakes.right: Shut the makhraj and stop. Only the five qalqalah letters get a released bounce, and even that carries no vowel.
mistakes.why: A leaked vowel invents a syllable the word does not have, and on ء, ك and ت there is nothing at all to release.
mistakes.wrong: Leaking a small vowel after a sakin shiddah letter, so أَكْ comes out as أَكَ.

mistakes.right: Raise the back of the tongue and leave the voice where it is.
mistakes.why: Growling makes a light letter sound heavy without making it heavy, and every heavy letter afterwards becomes the same undifferentiated rumble.
mistakes.wrong: Producing tafkheem by pushing the voice down into the chest.

mistakes.right: Flatten the body of the tongue against the palate first, then release.
mistakes.why: Itbaq is what makes these four the heaviest letters in the alphabet. Without it the letter has changed, not merely weakened.
mistakes.wrong: Saying ص ض ط ظ with the tongue tip alone and no clamp, which turns them into س د ت ذ.

mistakes.right: Give the letter its breath, then close. The airflow ends when the letter does.
mistakes.why: An over-long puff is the mirror of releasing no breath at all, and it is just as audible to a listener.
mistakes.wrong: Letting a final hams letter's breath run on so long that it becomes an extra sound.

body: The five paired sifat sort the entire alphabet. These seven do the opposite: each picks out a small group of letters and names something peculiar to them. Nothing carries their opposite because there is nothing to oppose.

الصفير, the whistle, belongs to ص س ز. All three drive air through a narrow channel between the tongue tip and the front teeth, and the channel is tight enough that the air whistles on its way out. It is the sharpest, highest sound in the alphabet. س is the plain whistle, ز is the same whistle with the voice switched on, and ص is the whistle with the tongue clamped, which drops its pitch and thickens it.

القلقلة, the bounce, belongs to ق ط ب ج د, gathered in قُطۡبُ جَدٍ. Six letters are shiddah and jahr at once, ء ج د ق ط ب: the breath is blocked and the voice is blocked, so when one of them carries a sukoon there is literally nothing left to make it audible. The hamza is the one left out, because its makhraj is a closure of the throat itself and detaching it sharply produces nothing but another hamza, which leaves the five that can be bounced. The only way to hear those five is to detach the makhraj sharply, and that detachment is the bounce. It must carry no vowel colour at all: a sakin ق is a clean release back into silence, not قَ and not قُ.

اللين, softness, belongs to و and ي when they carry a sukoon and the letter before them has a fatha, as in خَوۡف and بَيۡت. In that one position the two letters come out with no effort from the tongue and no true stretch. They are what makes a stop on a word like خَوۡف sound rounded instead of clipped.

الانحراف, deviation, belongs to ل and ر. Both begin at the tongue tip and then let the sound leave somewhere else: ل sends it off the sides of the tongue, and ر lets it roll back over the tip. Neither sound comes straight out of the place it started, which is what the name is pointing at.

التكرير, repetition, belongs to ر alone, and it is the one sifah on this list you are taught in order NOT to do. The tongue tip is springy against the gum ridge, so a ر left to its own devices trills like a rolled Spanish rr. Ibn al-Jazari's instruction is that takrir is learned so that it can be avoided. Press the tip firmly to the ridge and let it strike once. A doubled ر, as in ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ, is one strike held twice as long, never two strikes and never a roll.

التفشي, spreading, belongs to ش. The air does not stay in a channel; it spreads out through the whole mouth as it leaves. ش shares the middle of the tongue with ج and ي, and the spread is what separates it from them: ج shuts the makhraj completely, ي only approaches it, and ش lets the air escape sideways across the whole mouth. The whistling س is made at the other end of the tongue entirely, so it is the spread and not the place that keeps the two apart.

الاستطالة, extension, belongs to ض. The sound runs along the edge of the tongue, from the back molars forward toward the place where ل is made. The extension is in distance, not in time: ض is not held longer than any other letter, it simply travels further inside the mouth. It is the hardest letter in the alphabet to produce, and the reason Arabic is called لغة الضاد.

definition.literal: the qualities that have no opposite
definition.technical: Sifat carried by particular letters only, which no other letter carries the reverse of. A letter either whistles or it does not; there is no anti-whistle to be the other side of the pair.

The other lin letter, and it sits mid-ayah, so the ي is a plain ease after the fatha. Stop on a leen letter instead, as you must at the end of a surah, and the madd chapter's counts take over.

Istitalah on the doubled ض: the sound runs along the tongue's edge toward the place of the ل that follows it.

table.title: The seven, and what each one is

body: There are three populations of letters, and it is worth fixing them before any detail. Seven letters are heavy every time they appear, in every word, under every vowel: خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ, the isti'la letters. Most of the remaining letters are light every time they appear. Three do not settle: alif, the lam of the name of Allah, and ra. Those three are the only places where a reciter has to decide anything, and the last two get a lesson each.

Heavy does not mean loud and it does not mean low. Tafkheem is a single movement: the back of the tongue rises toward the soft palate, which enlarges the chamber the sound resonates in, so the letter comes out full and rounded. Nothing else changes. Your pitch stays where it was, your volume stays where it was, and the letter takes exactly as long as it did. A reciter who manufactures weight by dropping into a chest voice has made a light letter sound heavy without making it heavy, and every heavy letter after that will be the same undifferentiated rumble.

The four itbaq letters ص ض ط ظ do more than raise the tongue: they press it flat against the palate so the sound is trapped between two surfaces. That is why they are heavier than خ, غ and ق, and why they are the ones that collapse into س, د, ت and ذ when the clamp is missing.

Alif is not heavy or light on its own account. It has no consonantal makhraj to speak of, so it takes whatever the letter before it has: the alif of قَالَ is heavy because the ق is, and the alif of كَانَ is light because the ك is. The drill at the end of this lesson puts those two words side by side, and hearing the same alif come out full and then thin is the whole skill. وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ is where the heavy one is easiest to catch, on the alif after the ض. Do not listen for a light alif in لَا beside it: that alif is sakin, it meets the sakin first half of the doubled ض, and it drops out altogether where the two sakins meet.

The heavy letters are not all equally heavy. Weight rises and falls with the vowel the letter carries, and most manuals arrange this into five levels: heaviest is an isti'la letter with a fatha followed by an alif, then a fatha alone, then a damma, then a sukoon, then a kasrah at the bottom. Even at the bottom the letter is still heavy: the ص of ٱلصِّرَٰطَ carries a kasrah and is nothing like the س of ٱلۡمُسۡتَقِيمَ. Not everyone gives five levels or this order. Some give three or four, and some rank a sakin isti'la letter by the vowel before it rather than fixing it fourth. The top of the list and the bottom are not disputed.

The last thing to say is negative, and it matters more than any of the above. Tafkheem does not spread. A heavy letter does not make its neighbours heavy, and failing to keep the neighbours thin separates a trained reciter from an untrained one more reliably than any single rule. In ٱلۡمُسۡتَقِيمَ the ق is heavy and the س, ت, م and ي are not. In قَدۡ أَفۡلَحَ the ق is heavy and the د, ف, ل and ح are all light. Keep the light letters thin right up against the heavy one.

examples.focus: The alif after the ض is as heavy as an alif gets, since an alif takes the weight of the letter before it. The alif of لَا in front of it is not pronounced at all: it meets the sakin first half of the doubled ض and drops.
Level two: ق with a fatha. The د, ف, ل and ح around it all stay thin.
The fatha on the waw of هُوَ makes the lam of the name heavy, which is the last lesson of this chapter in miniature.
Level four: ق with a sukoon. Heavy and bounced at once, with no vowel in the bounce.
Level five: the ص carries a kasrah and is still plainly heavy. So is the ق of ٱلۡمُسۡتَقِيمَ, which carries the same kasrah, while the sakin س between them stays thin.

lessons.summary: Seven letters are heavy every time, most of the rest are light every time, and three swing between the two. The heavy ones also come in five degrees, set by the vowel the letter carries.

body: Start with the balance of the thing. ر is an istifal letter by class, and yet it is heavy far more often than it is light: the app's ground-truth engine marks heavy ra on 9,600 words of the mushaf and light ra on 2,757. Treat heavy as the resting state and light as the case that has to be earned.

Heavy when the ra carries a fatha or a damma, or the tanween of either: رَبِّ, ٱلۡكَوۡثَرَ, نَذِيرٞ. A shadda changes nothing, because a doubled letter is one letter held twice as long, and both halves take the weight of the vowel written on it.
Light when the ra carries a kasrah or a kasratan: شَرِّ, غَيۡرِ, رِزۡقٗا. Again the shadda is irrelevant: شَرِّ is doubled and light throughout.

A sakin ra is judged by the vowel on the letter before it. Fatha before it, heavy: مَرۡيَمَ. Damma before it, heavy: ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ. Kasrah before it, light: فِرۡعَوۡنَ. That one sentence covers most sakin ra in the mushaf, and the three refinements below are the whole of the rest.

Refinement one: the kasrah has to be original. A kasrah that exists only because of a hamzat al-wasl is incidental, and it does not lighten the ra. ٱرۡجِعُوٓاْ begins with a connecting hamza; read into it and the vowel you hear before the ra is a kasrah, but it is a joining vowel rather than part of the word, so the ra stays heavy. أَمِ ٱرۡتَابُوٓاْ and رَّبِّ ٱرۡحَمۡهُمَا work the same way. A kasrah sitting at the end of the previous word does not lighten the ra either: the vowel must be original and inside the same word.

Refinement two: an isti'la letter after the ra pulls it back to heavy. If a sakin ra follows an original kasrah but is itself followed, in the same word, by one of the seven isti'la letters, the ra is heavy: قِرۡطَاسٖ, مِرۡصَادٗا, لَبِٱلۡمِرۡصَادِ. The manuals enumerate a short list of such words. Two conditions decide it. The isti'la letter has to be in the same word, so in فَٱصۡبِرۡ صَبۡرٗا the ص belongs to the next word and the ra stays light; and the isti'la letter must not itself carry a kasrah, which is exactly what makes فِرۡقٖ the disputed word it is.

Refinement three: stopping re-opens the question. When you stop on a word ending in ر, the ra loses its vowel and becomes sakin, so it has to be judged again by what now stands before it. If that letter carries a vowel, the vowel decides in the ordinary way, so a stop on ٱلۡكَوۡثَرَ leaves a ra after a fatha and it stays heavy. If that letter is itself sakin, look one step further back. A ya sakinah before the ra always keeps it light, whatever came before that: نَذِيرٞ, قَدِيرٞ and غَيۡرِ all stop light. Any other sakin letter hands the decision to the vowel before it, so وَٱلۡفَجۡرِ is light when you read on and heavy when you stop, while ٱلذِّكۡرِ is light either way because the ك is preceded by a kasrah.

Finally, the words with two accepted wajhs. Hafs by the tariq of ash-Shatibiyyah reads a small number of words either way, and a reciter chooses one without being wrong. فِرۡقٖ in Surat ash-Shu'ara puts a sakin ra after an original kasrah and follows it with the isti'la letter ق, but that ق carries a kasratan of its own which weakens its pull; both readings are transmitted and the manuals differ over which they prefer. Stopping on مِصۡرَ and stopping on ٱلۡقِطۡرِ are the classic pair, since both leave the ra after a sakin isti'la letter that follows a kasrah: both accept either weight, with most texts preferring heavy for مِصۡرَ and light for ٱلۡقِطۡرِ. And the words whose final ya was dropped in writing, يَسۡرِ, أَسۡرِ and نُذُرِ, accept both when stopped on, with most giving preference to light out of regard for the ya that is no longer there.

definition.technical: A letter of istifal that is nevertheless heavy in most of its positions. Its weight is decided by the vowel it carries; when it is sakin, by the vowel before it, and sometimes by the letter after it.

body: This is a one-word rule. Every ل in Arabic is light, in every word, with one exception: the ل of the name ٱللَّه. Say قُلۡ or ٱلۡحَمۡدُ and the lam is thin. Say قَالَ ٱللَّهُ and it is not.

The trigger is the vowel on the sound immediately before the name, and there are only three possibilities. A fatha makes it heavy: وَٱللَّهُ, إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ, and هُوَ ٱللَّهُ too, where the sound immediately before the name is the fatha on the waw. A damma makes it heavy: نَصۡرُ ٱللَّهِ. A kasrah makes it light: بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ, بِٱللَّهِ, لِلَّهِ. And when you begin on the name with nothing before it, the hamza is opened with a fatha and the lam is heavy, as at the start of ayat al-Kursi.

Note carefully how this differs from the ra, because learning the two together invites a specific mix-up. For the ra, only an original kasrah lightens it and an incidental one does not. For the lam of the jalalah, any kasrah lightens it, original or not. قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ carries a kasrah on the ل of قُلۡ that exists purely to keep two sukoons from meeting, and it lightens the lam all the same. The two rules are shaped alike and are not the same rule.

The heaviness itself is ordinary tafkheem: the back of the tongue rises, the sound fills the mouth, and nothing gets longer. Because the lam is doubled, the weight has to be held across both halves of the shadda. A common half-measure is to start heavy and let the second half thin out, which produces a lam that is neither one thing nor the other.

Two closing notes. The rule follows sound, not spelling, which is why the same name is heavy in وَٱللَّهُ and light in بِٱللَّهِ. And it belongs to this name alone: words that merely share its shape, such as ٱلَّيۡلِ or ٱلَّذِينَ, keep an ordinary light lam no matter how heavy the letters near them are.

definition.technical: The name ٱللَّه. Its doubled lam is said heavy when the sound immediately before it is a fatha or a damma, and light when that sound is a kasrah. Every other lam in Arabic is light.

drills.caption: Kasrah, fatha, damma. The vowel before the name is the whole rule: light, heavy, heavy.
The prefix لِ carries a kasrah, so the first is light. The fatha on قَالَ makes the second heavy.

examples.focus: The kasrah at the end of بِسۡمِ lightens the lam. Keep the tongue low through both halves of the shadda.
The fatha on the waw of هُوَ makes the lam heavy; the damma on the haa is one sound too far back to count. Raise the back of the tongue as you reach the shadda.
Heavy after the damma of نَصۡرُ. The kasrah at the END of the name changes nothing; only what comes before it counts.
Light, because مَرۡضَاتِ ends on a kasrah. Note it, then read on to the next example in the same ayah.
Heavy, one word later. The وَ carries a fatha, and that is the entire difference.
The kasrah on قُلِ is only there to separate two sukoons, and it still lightens the lam.

keyPoints: One word only: ٱللَّه. Every other lam in Arabic is light.
Fatha or damma immediately before it: heavy. Kasrah: light.
Beginning on the name, the lam is heavy.
Unlike the ra, an incidental kasrah lightens it too: قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ is light.
Hold the weight across the whole shadda, not just its first half.

mistakes.right: Listen to the vowel before it. بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ and لِلَّهِ are light.
mistakes.why: This is a phonetic rule like any other. Reading the basmala with a heavy lam is simply an error, and it is the commonest one in this lesson.
mistakes.wrong: Making the lam heavy every time, out of reverence for the name.

mistakes.right: After a fatha or a damma it is heavy. وَٱللَّهُ is heavy.

mistakes.wrong: Making the lam light every time, because lam is a light letter.

mistakes.right: Carry one weight through both halves of the doubled lam.
mistakes.why: A doubled letter is one letter held twice as long, not two letters that are free to differ.
mistakes.wrong: Making the first half of the shadda heavy and letting the second half thin out.

mistakes.right: Any kasrah before the name lightens the lam, incidental or not.
mistakes.why: The two rules look parallel and are not. This is the usual cross-contamination between them.
mistakes.wrong: Importing the ra's original-kasrah condition, so قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ comes out heavy.

chapters.title: Letter Qualities

body: There is only one question to ask, and you ask it every single time: what is the very next letter? The answer sorts the 28 letters of the alphabet into four groups, and each group has one behaviour. Nothing else about the word matters.

Six letters keep the noon clear (idh-har). Six letters swallow it (idgham). One letter turns it into a mim (iqlab). The remaining fifteen hide it behind a nasal hum (ikhfa). Six plus six plus one plus fifteen is twenty-eight: the four rules account for the entire alphabet with nothing left over, which is why this chapter is the one most reciters learn first.

Tanween rides along for free. A tanween is written as a doubled fatha, kasra, or damma, and the extra mark is an unwritten noon sakin: كِتَابٌ is read kitaabun, كِتَابًا is kitaaban, كِتَابٍ is kitaabin. Because that trailing sound is a noon sakin, whatever rule the next letter triggers for نْ, it triggers identically for the tanween.

One difference is worth noting up front. A noon sakin can sit inside a word or at the end of one. A tanween only ever sits at the end of a word, so a rule triggered by tanween always reaches across into the next word.

definition.literal: the vowelless noon, and the doubled ending
definition.technical: A noon carrying sukoon, whether inside a word or at its end, and the n-sound produced by a doubled vowel at the end of a word. Both are the same sound to the ear, so both obey the same four rules.

examples.focus: The noon of مِّن vanishes straight into the ر, with no hum left behind.
The noon before ف is hidden: you hear a hum, not a noon.

keyPoints: The next letter decides everything. Nothing else does.
6 letters -> idh-har, 6 -> idgham, 1 -> iqlab, 15 -> ikhfa. That is all 28.
Tanween is an unwritten noon sakin, so it takes the exact same four rules.
A tanween is always at the end of a word; a noon sakin can be anywhere.

body: The trigger set is not arbitrary. All six letters come from the throat, which is as far as you can get from the tip of the tongue where the noon is made. Two sounds made that far apart cannot blend, so nothing happens: the noon is simply said, then the throat letter is simply said.

That distance is also why idh-har is the baseline rather than a rule in its own right. It is the sound of a noon with nothing done to it. Everything you will learn in the next three lessons is a departure from this, so your ear needs to know this shape first.

The six letters divide by throat depth, and it is worth learning them in that order rather than alphabetically: ء and ه from the deepest throat, ع and ح from the middle, غ and خ from the part nearest the mouth. Reciting the six in depth order trains the throat itself, not just the rule.
Idh-har happens both inside a word and across two words. أَنۡعَمۡتَ in Surat al-Fatiha is a single word with the noon and the ع inside it; مِنۡ هَادٖ is two words. The rule does not care.

definition.literal: to make apparent, to show plainly
definition.technical: Pronouncing the noon sakin or tanween from its own articulation point, complete and unaltered, without lengthening its ghunnah, when one of the six throat letters follows.

body: In the mushaf, idgham is written into the page: the noon or tanween loses its sukoon mark, and the letter that follows gains a shadda. If you can see a shadda on ي، ن، م or و right after a noon-less noon, you are looking at idgham, and the shadda is the instruction to double it.

There is a distinction inside this rule that is easy to miss and worth having from the start. When the noon merges into ن or م, the merge is complete (إدغام كامل): the noon is gone entirely, letter and ghunnah alike, and the ghunnah you hear belongs to the ن or م that swallowed it. When it merges into ي or و, the merge is incomplete (إدغام ناقص): the body of the noon is gone but its ghunnah survives on top of the ي or و, which is why those two keep a distinctly nasal colour.

This rule needs two separate words. A noon sakin followed by ي or و inside a single word is never merged: it is read clear instead. That exception has only four words in the whole Qur'an, and it has its own lesson at the end of this chapter.

The two counts are the same two counts as every other ghunnah in tajweed, roughly the time it takes to lower and raise a finger at a steady recitation pace. Consistency matters more than the exact duration: the hum on مَن يَقُولُ should measure the same as the hum on مِنكُمۡ.

definition.literal: to insert one thing into another
definition.technical: Joining a vowelless letter to the vowelled letter after it so the two become one doubled letter, pronounced with a single push of the tongue.

body: This is the same mechanism as the previous lesson with one thing removed: the hum. The noon vanishes, the ل or ر doubles, and the nasal passage stays shut. Everything you would do for مَن يَقُولُ, do for مِّن رَّبِّهِمۡ, except the humming.

ل and ر are both made at the tip of the tongue, very close to where the noon itself is made. Letters that near each other merge readily and completely, which is why nothing of the noon survives here, not even its ghunnah.
Like the previous rule, this one only operates across two words. And like the previous rule, the mushaf tells you it is happening: no sukoon on the noon, a shadda on the ل or ر.
Practically, the test is your nose. Pinch it lightly and read مِّن رَّبِّهِمۡ: if the sound changes, you are humming where you should not be.

definition.technical: A complete merge of the noon sakin or tanween into a following ل or ر, in which both the letter and its ghunnah are removed.

Complete merge, and no nasal hum whatsoever.

body: Iqlab is the only rule of this chapter with a single trigger letter, and the only one the mushaf marks with a symbol of its own. Look for a small ميم printed above the noon or above the tanween: that little م is the instruction, and it is printed exactly where the sound changes.

The reason for the rule is physical. The noon is made at the tip of the tongue, the ب at the lips. Getting from one to the other while carrying a nasal sound is awkward, so the noon moves forward to the lips and becomes a mim, which is the nasal letter that already lives there. The sound then flows into the ب without the tongue having to travel.

The critical detail is that the mim is concealed, not complete. The lips come together lightly and do not seal. If you press them shut you produce a full mim, which is a different rule (idgham shafawi) and the wrong sound here. Think of the lips as resting against each other while the nose does the work.
Iqlab only ever fires in one direction: noon then ب. A ب followed by a noon is not iqlab, and neither is a mim followed by a ب, which has its own rule in the mim sakin chapter.

definition.literal: to turn a thing over, to flip it
definition.technical: Converting a noon sakin or tanween into a mim that is concealed rather than fully closed, accompanied by ghunnah, when ب follows.

body: Ikhfa is the largest of the four rules by a wide margin: fifteen letters, more than half the alphabet. It is also the one learners get wrong most often, because it is defined by what you do not do. You do not touch the tongue to the noon's place, and you do not double the next letter. You do something in between.

Here is the mechanism concretely. For a clear noon, the tip of the tongue presses the gum ridge behind the upper front teeth. For ikhfa, it does not. Instead the tongue moves toward the position of the letter that is coming, hovering there while the nasal passage carries the sound for two counts. Then the letter is released. The hum is not an ornament added to the noon; it is what is left of the noon once its mouth position is taken away.

The fifteen letters are simply the remainder: everything that is not a throat letter, not one of يرملون, and not ب. That is the honest way to hold them in memory, and it is why the overview lesson insists on the arithmetic. The classical line صِفْ ذَا ثَنَا... exists so you can check the list quickly, not so you can derive it.

The hum takes its colour from the letter it is leading into. Before the heavy letters ص ض ط ظ ق the hum is full and thick; before the rest it stays thin. Reciters describe three degrees of closeness as well: ikhfa before ط د ت is the closest to idgham because those letters are nearest the noon's own place, ikhfa before ق and ك is the farthest and closest to idh-har, and the remaining ten sit in the middle. You do not need to name the degrees to recite correctly, but you do need to let the following letter shape the hum instead of humming identically every time.

definition.literal: to conceal, to hide something from view
definition.technical: Pronouncing the noon sakin or tanween in a state between idh-har and idgham, stripped of its shadda, with the ghunnah retained for two counts.

The tongue never touches the noon's articulation point.

body: Idgham with ghunnah has one structural condition that is easy to state and easy to forget: the noon must end one word and the trigger letter must begin the next. When a noon sakin is followed by ي or و inside the same word, the merge does not happen and the noon is read clear.
There are exactly four such words in the Qur'an: دُنْيَا، بُنْيَان، صِنْوَان، قِنْوَان. That is the entire list, so this is a lesson you can finish memorising in a minute.

The reason is meaning, not sound. Arabic marks a doubled root letter with a shadda. If دُنْيَا were merged it would be read دُيَّا, and a reader would take the doubled ي for part of the root. Keeping the noon audible keeps the word's shape visible.

Note also that these four words often carry a tanween of their own at the end, and that tanween follows the ordinary rules. In صِنۡوَانٞ وَغَيۡرُ the noon inside the word is clear, while the tanween at its end merges into the following و. Both rules operate in the same word, three letters apart.

definition.technical: Pronouncing the noon sakin clearly before ي or و when both fall inside the same word. Called absolute because it is tied to no particular articulation region, unlike the throat-letter idh-har.

examples.focus: The noon before ي is fully audible. No shadda on the ي.
Clear noon inside the word, then the tanween at the end merges into م.
Clear noon before و inside the word, in an ayah that has it twice.
The fourth and last word of the set.

keyPoints: Only four words, and only inside a single word.
دُنْيَا  بُنْيَان  صِنْوَان  قِنْوَان
Read the noon clearly. Do not double the ي or و.
A tanween at the end of these words still follows the normal four rules.

mistakes.wrong: Reading دُنْيَا as دُيَّا by applying idgham inside the word.

body: This is the smaller sibling of the nun sakin chapter, and it is smaller in a useful way: three rules instead of four, and the sorting question has only two interesting answers. Is the next letter ب? Is it م? If neither, you are done, and the mim is simply said.

Ikhfa shafawi fires before ب. The mechanism is worth doing slowly, because it asks the opposite of what a mim usually asks. Normally a mim seals the lips. Here they come together and rest, without pressure, and the nasal passage carries the sound for two counts before the lips part into the ب. Mim and ba are made in the same place, so a full seal would give you a complete mim and then a second lip closure for the ba: the same gesture twice in a row. Leaving the seal incomplete is what keeps them distinct.

Most scholars classify that reading as ikhfa, which is the position of Tuhfat al-Atfal and the one this course teaches. It is worth knowing that a minority read the mim before ب with idh-har instead, closing the lips fully and holding no hum. The disagreement is real and old, and both readings are recited within Hafs: they differ in what the lips do, not only in what the rule is called, so the difference is audible. This chapter drills the majority reading, ikhfa, throughout.

Idgham shafawi fires before another م. The first mim is dropped and the second is doubled, giving one mim held with two counts of hum. Because the two letters are identical, the classical name for it is إدغام مثلين صغير, the small merge of a pair. The mushaf shows it the way it shows every idgham: no sukoon on the first mim, a shadda on the second.

Idh-har shafawi covers the other twenty-six letters, and it is not a hum with less hum in it: it is a complete mim, lips fully closed, released straight into the next letter, with nothing held. One of the twenty-six can never actually occur there. A soft alif always follows a fatha, so the letter before it is never sakin, which is why al-Jamzuri opens the rule by excluding it.

Two of the twenty-six need guarding, and they are the two the classical texts single out. Before و the danger is sameness: the و is also made at the lips, so a mim that does not fully close simply becomes the beginning of it and the first word loses its ending. Before ف the danger is nearness: the ف is made with the inside of the lower lip against the tips of the upper front teeth, immediately next door, and the lips are already travelling toward it. In both cases the fix is mechanical: close the mim completely, then move.

One last comparison, because the ear cannot separate these two on its own. Iqlab and ikhfa shafawi both produce a concealed mim with two counts of hum, and both do it before a ب. The difference is what you started from. Iqlab starts from a noon or a tanween, and the mushaf prints a small م above it to say the letter has been converted. Ikhfa shafawi starts from a mim that was already written, and carries no extra mark because nothing was converted. In 91:14 the two sit three letters apart: رَبُّهُم بِذَنۢبِهِمۡ has a mim before ب, then a noon before ب.

definition.technical: A mim carrying sukoon, inside a word or at the end of one, whose reading is decided by the single letter that follows. All three of its rules are called شفوي, labial, because the mim itself is made at the lips.

drills.caption: Hum, hum, close, close. The last two are the ones that slip.

Idh-har before و, the harder of the two warnings. The mim must finish before the و starts.

ب gives ikhfa shafawi: lips meet without pressing, two counts of hum.
م gives idgham shafawi: one doubled mim, two counts of hum.
The other twenty-six give idh-har: full closure, released, nothing held.
Guard the mim before و and ف. Those are the two where it stops closing fully.

body: This is the only rule in the course that asks you nothing. Every other nasal rule begins by looking at the next letter. This one looks at the letter in front of you: if it is a noon or a mim and it carries a shaddah, you hum it for two counts. Start of the word, middle, end. Joining on, or stopping. It does not change.

The mechanism explains why it is also the strongest hum in tajweed. A shaddah is not an intensity mark, it is a spelling economy: it records two letters written as one, the first sakin and the second vowelled. نَّ is نْ followed by نَ, and مَّ is مْ followed by مَ. Both halves are nasal letters, so the nose is working across the whole of it, with nothing in between and nothing pulling the sound out through the mouth. In every other rule the hum belongs to a letter that is on its way somewhere else.

Physically, the instruction is to hold still. For نّ the tip of the tongue presses the gum ridge behind the upper front teeth and stays there for both counts. For مّ the lips close and stay closed. Either way the mouth is sealed, so the nose is the only exit the voice has: if the hum stops, the sound stops with it.

Beginners under-hold this one for a specific and slightly unfair reason. Because the mouth is closed, a short hum and a full hum feel almost identical from the inside, and nothing in the word breaks when you cut it. إِنَّ read with a one-count hum is still recognisably إِنَّ, so there is no error to trip over and the habit never gets corrected by accident. The fix is to measure it against something you already read correctly: hold it as long as you hold a madd tabii in the same ayah, and make the two match.

Surat an-Nas is the drill the mushaf built for you. All six of its ayahs close on a word built around a doubled noon: ٱلنَّاسِ in five of them and ٱلۡخَنَّاسِ in the fourth. The hum is not at the stop itself: the waqf falls on the sukoon of the seen, after the long alif, so the doubled noon sits one syllable earlier. That still gives you six measured hums in under a minute, each one landing just before the ayah's closing madd, and any hum you shorten is audible against the five beside it.

definition.literal: the doubled noon and the doubled mim
definition.technical: A noon or a mim carrying a shaddah. The scholars call each of them حرف غنّة, a letter of ghunnah, and give it the complete two-count hum wherever it occurs.

drills.caption: Four doubled letters. Time every hum against the same two counts.
Read Surat an-Nas straight through and hold the doubled noon in all six equally.

examples.focus: Two doubled nuns in one short ayah. Both hums should measure the same.
The hum arrives on the second letter, not the first: a short hamza with a kasra, then two counts of noon.
Doubled mim. Lips shut for the full two counts before the fatha releases them.
A two-word ayah with the doubled mim sitting in the middle of the first word.
Doubled mim then doubled noon, back to back. The second is the one learners miss.
A doubled noon straight after a sun-letter lam, so two rules land on one word.

keyPoints: Trigger: a shaddah on نّ or مّ. Nothing else is required or checked.
A shaddah is two letters in one: نْ + نَ. The hum covers both halves.
Two full counts, and this is the fullest ghunnah there is.
Position, word, wasl or waqf: none of them change the rule.
All six ayahs of Surat an-Nas close on a word built around a doubled noon. Use it as the drill.

mistakes.right: Hold two counts, measured against a madd tabii in the same ayah.

mistakes.wrong: Cutting the hum to a beat or less, so إِنَّ comes out as a slightly long noon.

mistakes.right: Keep the lips shut for both counts, and open only to release into the next vowel.

mistakes.wrong: Opening the mouth partway through the hum, most often on مّ.

mistakes.why: Ghunnah is a measure, not an expressive device. Lengthening it is as much a change as shortening it.
mistakes.wrong: Stretching it well past two counts on words like إِنَّ اللَّهَ for emphasis.

mistakes.right: Look for the shaddah on the letter, not for words you already know.
mistakes.why: The rule is triggered by a mark on the page, so it has to be read off the page rather than recalled from a shortlist.
mistakes.wrong: Humming the familiar words like إِنَّ and ثُمَّ but missing the shaddah inside a long one such as لَتُسۡـَٔلُنَّ.

body: Every other sound in the Qur'an is shaped somewhere you can point to: a tongue position, a lip position, a narrowing in the throat. Ghunnah is not. It is produced in the الخيشوم, the nasal cavity above the roof of the mouth, and the tongue does no work in it at all. The classical definition says exactly that, and it is not a flourish: it is the reason ghunnah behaves unlike every other quality in tajweed.

Here is the mechanism. At the back of the roof of your mouth is the soft palate. For almost every Arabic letter it lifts and seals off the passage to the nose, so all the voice leaves through the mouth. For نون and ميم it drops, and the nasal passage opens. At the same moment the mouth is blocked: by the tongue against the gum ridge for نون, by the lips for ميم. The voice now has exactly one way out. Ghunnah is the sound of it taking that route.

The test takes a second and settles the whole lesson. Pinch your nose shut and hold مـ. The sound dies almost immediately, because you have closed the only exit it had. Now do the same on بـ, which uses the same lips: nothing happens, because the ب never went through the nose. Then try it on words. Hold your nose through إِنَّهَا and the word becomes unreadable. Hold it through قُلۡ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ, stopping at the end of the ayah, and nothing changes at all: there is not one noon or mim in it.

Ghunnah is a permanent quality of those two letters, not something a rule bolts on. Exactly one rule removes it: in idgham bi-ghayri ghunnah, the merge into ل and ر, the noon goes letter and hum together and the nose never opens. Everywhere else it is there. Even a plain vowelled noon, like the one opening نَعۡبُدُ, is nasal. You simply do not hold it. What the rules of this course actually do is decide how much of the letter's mouth position is removed and how long you sit on what is left. Idgham does not add a hum, it deletes the noon's tongue contact and leaves the nose doing the work. Ikhfa does the same without handing that position to anything else. Iqlab moves the position forward to the lips and keeps the nose open. Once you hear it this way, the nasal rules stop being separate things to memorise and become one sound with different amounts of mouth taken away.
Which is what the next lesson does: it orders those amounts from the fullest to the faintest, with a drill for hearing the difference between them.

definition.literal: a resonant sound in the nose
definition.technical: A sound emitted from the الخيشوم, the nasal passage above the roof of the mouth, built into the body of نون and ميم and inseparable from them. The classical wording adds that the tongue has no part in producing it.

drills.caption: Hold each one with your nose pinched. Only the third survives unchanged.
Same vowel, three endings. Feel where each one leaves.

examples.focus: The sound at its clearest: mouth sealed, nose open, nothing else happening.
The same hum, now doing the work of a merge. The noon's tongue contact is gone.
The same hum again, with the mouth already shaping the ص while the nose carries the noon.
The same hum, with the mouth position moved forward to the lips instead of removed.
And once more at the lips. Different rules, different amounts of mouth, one sound underneath all of them.
The control case. Stopping at the end of the ayah there is no noon and no mim in it, so the pinch test changes nothing.

keyPoints: Ghunnah comes from the khaishum, the nasal passage. The tongue does nothing.
Only نون and ميم carry it, and they carry it in every state but one: the merge into ل and ر deletes it.
Pinch your nose: if the sound changes, ghunnah was in it.
The rules do not add the hum; they take mouth away and leave it exposed.
Two counts is the measure wherever a rule calls for full ghunnah.

mistakes.right: Close the mouth, let the soft palate drop, and keep the throat relaxed. The sound should ring in the face, not the neck.
mistakes.why: A throated hum is tiring to sustain, it colours the letters around it, and it does not pass the pinch test.
mistakes.wrong: Producing the hum in the throat, so it comes out as a growl instead of a nasal ring.

mistakes.right: The hum has no vowel. It is one unbroken sound bridging two letters.
mistakes.why: An inserted vowel adds a syllable the word does not have, which is a change to the word and not only to its sound.
mistakes.wrong: Slipping a vowel into the hum, so مِنكُمۡ comes out as min-a-kum.

mistakes.right: Every noon and mim is nasal. The rules change the amount, and only idgham into ل and ر removes it outright.
mistakes.why: Stripping the nasal quality out of plain letters makes ordinary words sound wrong before any rule is involved.
mistakes.wrong: Treating ghunnah as something only certain rules have, and reading an ordinary noon as a dry consonant.

mistakes.right: Hold one level tone for the whole measure, then move.
mistakes.why: A sliding hum reads as melody rather than as a letter, and it makes two ghunnahs in the same ayah impossible to compare.
mistakes.wrong: Letting the pitch slide up or down across the hum.

At the tip of the tongue

At the lips

Whether the sound is leaving through the nose

choices: It has no ghunnah, because no rule applies to it
It has ghunnah, but it is not held

ruleCard.action: Lower the soft palate so the passage to the nose opens, block the mouth (the tongue for نون, the lips for ميم), and let the voice ring out through the nose.

ruleCard.hold: Two counts wherever a rule calls for the full ghunnah. In the states with no rule it is present but never measured.
ruleCard.trigger: Every نون and every ميم, in every state but one. The rules decide only how much of it you hear.

lessons.summary: Ghunnah is made in the nose, not the mouth. It belongs to نون and ميم permanently, and every nasal rule in this course is that one sound with a different amount of mouth taken away.

body: Ghunnah is not a switch that is either on or off. Every noon and mim has it, and none of them have it to the same degree. A reciter who gives the same hum to all of them sounds mechanical, and that is a specific fixable fault rather than a matter of taste. The classical texts sort the states onto a ladder, most often with five rungs.
Rank one is المشدّد, the doubled letter: any نّ or مّ. The mouth is sealed, both halves of the letter are nasal, and nothing competes for the sound. This is the fullest hum there is.

Rank two is المدغم, the merged letter: a noon sakin or tanween merged into ي ن م و, and a mim sakin merged into a mim. The letter has been dissolved into the one after it and the hum carries the merge. When the merge is into ن or م the result is literally a doubled letter, which is why some scholars treat ranks one and two as a single rank. Idgham into ل and ر is not on this ladder at all: it leaves no ghunnah to rank, because the noon and its hum both go.

Rank three is المخفى, the concealed letter: ikhfa, iqlab, and ikhfa shafawi. The letter's own position in the mouth has been taken away, but unlike a merge it has not been handed to anything else, so the hum is fully audible and fully measured while having less body behind it than a merge does.

Rank four is الساكن المظهر, the plainly-pronounced sakin: a noon sakin before one of the six throat letters, a mim sakin before any of its twenty-six. Here the letter keeps its whole articulation, so the mouth is doing most of the work and the nasal part is brief and unmeasured. You do not hold it. A held hum at rank four is a mistake, not a lighter version of the rule.

Rank five is المتحرّك, the vowelled letter: a noon or mim carrying a fatha, kasra or damma. The vowel pulls the sound straight out through the mouth and the nasal component is at its faintest. It has not disappeared: pinch your nose on the م of مَلِكِ and you will still hear it change.

On the disagreement, plainly. The five-rank list above is the one most widely taught and the one this course uses, but it is not the only one in circulation. Some scholars reverse ranks two and three, holding that a concealed letter keeps more ghunnah than a merged one. Some compress the list to four or three by folding the sakin muzhar together with the mutaharrik. Some pull iqlab out of the concealed rank and give it its own. Every version agrees on the two ends: the doubled letter is the fullest and the vowelled letter is the faintest. Learn the ends first; the middle sorts itself out with practice, and no recitation is wrong because its teacher counted the rungs differently.

One more honest caveat, about the number two. The two-count measure used throughout this course for ranks one, two and three is the standard teaching convention, not a duration fixed by unanimous agreement, and the count itself scales with your tempo: a slow reciter and a brisk one both hold two counts and hold them for different clock times. Its job is internal consistency. Every full ghunnah in a given reading should measure the same as every other one in that reading.

The practice routine is the point of the lesson. Read the five examples below in order, once each, then again as one continuous run, listening for the hum shrinking at every step. Then read them bottom to top. Most learners hear rank five for the first time only on the way back up, because the ear needs the contrast with rank four immediately before it. A minute a day for a week is enough to break the habit of humming everything equally.

definition.literal: the levels, or ranks, of the hum
definition.technical: The ordering of the states a noon or mim can occupy, from the one that keeps the most ghunnah to the one that keeps the least. It describes degree; it adds no rule you have not already learned.

drills.caption: Down the ladder. The hum should shrink at every arrow and stop at the last two.
drills.text: ٱلنَّاسِ  ->  فَمَن يَعۡمَلۡ  ->  هُم بِٱلسَّاهِرَةِ  ->  هُمۡ فِيهِ  ->  مَلِكِ

drills.caption: Back up. This direction is what teaches the ear the bottom two rungs.
drills.text: مَلِكِ  ->  هُمۡ فِيهِ  ->  هُم بِٱلسَّاهِرَةِ  ->  فَمَن يَعۡمَلۡ  ->  ٱلنَّاسِ

examples.focus: Rank 1, mushaddad. The fullest hum on the ladder, and your reference for the other four.
Rank 2, mudgham. Nearly as full as rank 1, but the hum belongs to a letter that dissolved into the next one.
Rank 3, mukhfa. Still two counts, with less body: the position was removed and not handed on.
Rank 4, sakin muzhar. The mim is complete, so the nose has little left to do. Nothing is held here.
Rank 5, mutaharrik. The fatha pulls the mim out through the mouth. Nasal, but only just.

keyPoints: Five states, one sound: mushaddad, mudgham, mukhfa, sakin muzhar, mutaharrik.
Ranks one to three are held for two counts. Ranks four and five are not held at all.
Rank is fullness, not duration: the top three all measure the same two counts.
Scholars order and count the middle ranks differently; the two ends are agreed.
Walk the ladder down, then back up. The way back up is what teaches the bottom.

mistakes.right: Hold ranks one to three. Release ranks four and five.
mistakes.why: This is the single habit that flattens a reading, and it is the reason the ranks are taught as a lesson at all.
mistakes.wrong: Giving every noon and mim the same two-count hum, idh-har and vowelled letters included.

mistakes.right: Say the letter normally. Its nasal quality is inherent and needs no attention.
mistakes.why: A deliberately de-nasalised noon is a worse fault than the one it was meant to fix, and much harder to unlearn.
mistakes.wrong: Over-correcting the flat hum by stripping ghunnah out of ranks four and five entirely.

mistakes.right: Strongest means fullest in body, not longest in time. Ranks one, two and three all measure two counts.
mistakes.why: Turning rank into duration invents a length the recitation does not have, and it wrecks the timing of the ayah around it.
mistakes.wrong: Stretching a doubled letter past two counts so that it audibly outranks a merge.

mistakes.right: Attach one short memorised ayah to each rank and practise the sounds, not the names.
mistakes.why: The ranks exist to change what your mouth does. Naming them correctly while humming everything alike is no improvement.
mistakes.wrong: Learning the five ranks as a list to recite back rather than as five sounds to produce.
