lessons.summary: One sound, five strengths. The ladder runs from the doubled letter down to the vowelled one, and walking it is what stops a reciter from humming everything alike.

chapters.subtitle: The lip-based system, and the nasal sound that runs through half of tajweed
chapters.title: Mim Sakin & Ghunnah

body: A madd letter is not a fourth kind of sound. It is a vowel that was allowed to keep going. Say the fatha of هَـ and stop: that is one count. Let the same shape run on without moving your tongue and you have said هَا, which is two. Every rule in this chapter is that one act repeated for longer or shorter, so the mechanism to fix now is the not-moving.

The matching-vowel condition is what makes these three letters madd letters at all. An alif can only ever follow a fatha, so it is always a madd letter. A waw is a madd letter only after a damma, and a ya only after a kasra. Put a fatha in front of either of them and the sound glides instead of stretching, which is a different thing with its own lesson later in this chapter.

In the KFGQPC mushaf the alif is often written as a small vertical stroke above the letter rather than as a full alif on the line: هَٰذَا, بِأَصۡحَٰبِ, عَٰبِدُونَ. That stroke is a dagger alif, and it is a complete alif in every way that matters here. Read it as two counts exactly like a written one. Learners who came to the mushaf from a printed Arabic textbook routinely read straight past it.

A count, harakah, is the time it takes to say one ordinary short vowel at your own reciting pace. It is a relative unit, not a stopwatch: a slow tarteel has long counts and a brisk reading has short ones. What is not relative is that all of your two-count madds must measure the same as each other, because the four and six-count rules are defined as multiples of this one. If your natural madd wobbles, nothing built on top of it can be right.

It is worth knowing how much of the Qur'an this single rule covers. The ground-truth engine finds a natural madd in over four thousand ayahs, which is more than half the mushaf. Get this one length steady and most of your recitation is already correct.

definition.technical: Prolonging the sound of a madd letter for two counts when nothing after it asks for more: no hamzah follows it and no sukoon follows it. Called natural because no reciter's ear will accept it any shorter and no rule asks for it any longer.

drills.caption: The three madd letters on one consonant. Two counts each, identical in length.
All three in one word. Count two on each without letting the middle one shrink.

examples.focus: Two madds in one small word: the dagger alif over the ه, then the written alif after the ذ.
The waw after the damma of دُ. Lips already rounded, hold, do not move.
The ya after the kasra of مِ, held two counts before the ق.
A dagger alif over the ح. Read it as a full alif, not as a short fatha.
Ya madd in the middle of the word, then a dagger alif before the ت. Both are two counts.

keyPoints: Three madd letters: ا و ي, each after its own matching vowel.
Two counts, held without moving the tongue or lips.
The dagger alif is a full alif. Read it, do not skip it.
Natural means nothing follows that asks for more: no hamzah, no sukoon.
This two-count unit is the measure for every other madd in the chapter.

mistakes.right: Keep two counts even at speed. Speed shortens the count, not the number of counts.
mistakes.why: A one-count madd removes the letter, and in Arabic that often removes a meaning: قَالَ (he said) becomes قَلَّ (it became few).
mistakes.wrong: Clipping the madd to roughly one count when reading quickly.

mistakes.right: Two counts here. Save four for muttasil and munfasil, where a hamzah earns it.
mistakes.why: If the baseline is four, the reader has no room left to show the rules that genuinely are four.
mistakes.wrong: Stretching every natural madd to four because it sounds more devotional.

mistakes.right: Treat the small vertical stroke as a written alif: two full counts.
mistakes.why: This is the single most common madd error among readers new to the Uthmani script.
mistakes.wrong: Reading a dagger alif as a plain fatha, so هَٰذَا comes out as haadha with a short first vowel.

mistakes.right: One steady tone across both counts, then move on.
mistakes.why: A wobble turns a held vowel into an ornament, and it makes the length impossible to judge by ear.
mistakes.wrong: Letting the pitch dip or waver during the hold.

As a full alif, held two counts

choices: Because the Qur'an is recited in a fixed rhythm
Because the four and six-count rules are defined as multiples of this unit
Because the mushaf colours them the same
Because otherwise the tanween rules change
quiz.explain: Four counts means twice this, six means three times it. If the unit drifts, every longer madd drifts with it, and no listener can tell your muttasil from your natural madd.
quiz.prompt: Why must all of your natural madds be the same length as each other?

ruleCard.action: Do not move. The vowel has already put your tongue and lips in position; simply keep the sound running on the same shape while the air continues.
ruleCard.hold: Two counts. Always two, never one and never four.

mnemonic.gloss: "We reveal it." One Qur'anic word holding all three madd letters, each after its matching vowel: نُو with damma, حِي with kasra, هَا with fatha.

ruleCard.trigger: ا after a fatha, و after a damma, ي after a kasra, with the madd letter itself carrying no vowel and nothing special after it

lessons.summary: Three letters, each after its own matching vowel, held for two counts. This is the ruler every other madd in the chapter is measured against.

body: The mushaf tells you this rule is coming before your ear does. The small curved sign drawn over the madd letter, the maddah, means one thing: this madd runs longer than its natural two counts. It does not say why. In جَآءَ, وَٱلسَّمَآءِ and ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ the sign sits over the alif and a hamzah is the very next letter, which is the muttasil of this lesson. The same sign sits over the alif of ٱلضَّآلِّينَ, ٱلصَّآخَّةُ and دَآبَّةٖ, where there is no hamzah anywhere and the cause is a shaddah, which is the madd lazim of a later lesson at six counts. So read the sign as an instruction to lengthen, then read the letter after it to learn how far: a hamzah gives 4 or 5, a permanent sukoon or shaddah gives 6.

The reason is articulatory. The hamzah is a hard closure at the deepest point of the throat, the furthest thing there is from an open held vowel. Arriving at it abruptly from a two-count madd makes the join sound chopped. Lengthening gives the throat time to travel, so the closure lands cleanly rather than as a jolt.

This madd is called wajib, obligatory, because it is one of the very few places where all ten qira'at agree that the natural two counts are not permitted. What they differ on is how much longer: Hafs gives it 4 or 5 counts, while Warsh and Hamzah give it 6. So obligatory here means the lengthening is obligatory, not that any single number is.

Between 4 and 5 the choice is yours, but it is a choice you make once. Reciting some muttasils at 4 and others at 5 in the same sitting is not two permitted readings, it is one inconsistent one. The rule of thumb teachers give is simple: pick the length you can hold steadily while breathing normally, and keep it.

One extra case is worth knowing early. When the hamzah is the last letter of the word and you stop on it, as in the ٱلسَّمَآءِ that ends Aal-i-Imraan 5 and Ibrahim 24 and 38, the stop adds a second cause on top of the first. There 6 counts becomes available as well, so the permitted lengths at such a stop are 4, 5 or 6. Reading on, it is back to 4 or 5.

definition.technical: Lengthening a madd letter beyond its natural two counts because a hamzah follows it within the same word. Connected because the madd letter and its cause share a word; obligatory because every reader of the Qur'an lengthens it.

drills.caption: Two counts, then the same alif at your muttasil length with the hamzah after it.
The same rule on all three madd letters. All three should measure identically.

examples.focus: The clearest case in the whole mushaf: alif, maddah sign, hamzah, all in one short word.
The hamzah is the last letter, but this is the opening oath of a run and no reciter stops here, so the 6 of a stop is hypothetical at this spot. Read on and it is 4 or 5.
The same word where a stop is real: it ends the ayah, so 4, 5 and 6 are all permitted here. Join it to the next ayah and it drops back to 4 or 5.
A dagger alif carrying the maddah sign, then the hamzah written on a ya seat. Still 4 or 5.
The waw version. Lips rounded, hold, then the throat closes for the hamzah.
The ya version, and a good reminder that the silent alif in the spelling is not read at all.

keyPoints: Trigger: madd letter then hamzah, inside a single word.
Hafs: 4 or 5 counts. Never 2.
Every qira'ah lengthens it; they differ only over how much (Warsh and Hamzah read 6).
The maddah sign says lengthen; the letter after it says how far (hamzah 4 or 5, permanent sukoon or shaddah 6).
Stopping on a final hamzah opens 6 counts as a third option.

mistakes.right: Hold it to your chosen 4 or 5, then the hamzah.
mistakes.why: This is the one madd on which no qira'ah permits two counts, so a short muttasil is not a lighter reading, it is a wrong one.
mistakes.wrong: Reading جَآءَ with an ordinary two-count alif.

mistakes.right: Close the throat properly on the hamzah. The madd exists to make room for that closure, not to replace it.
mistakes.why: A dropped hamzah changes the word: جَآءَ becomes جَا.
mistakes.wrong: Softening the hamzah into a plain vowel so the word runs smoothly.

mistakes.right: Fix on one length before you start and hold it for the session.
mistakes.why: Consistency is part of the rule, not a matter of taste. Two lengths in one reading is one of the fastest things a teacher hears.
mistakes.wrong: Sliding between 4 and 5 counts from ayah to ayah.

mistakes.right: Learn the condition, not the ornament: madd letter plus hamzah in one word.
mistakes.why: Print sizes vary and some editions are subtle. The condition never varies.
mistakes.wrong: Lengthening only when the mushaf prints the maddah sign large enough to notice.

choices: Because the Qur'an cannot be recited without it
Because every qira'ah lengthens it past the natural two counts
Because it is the longest madd there is
Because the mushaf always marks it
quiz.explain: The ten readings differ on how long: Hafs 4 or 5, Warsh and Hamzah 6. None of them permits 2. The obligation is on the lengthening, not on a particular number.
quiz.prompt: Why is this madd called wajib, obligatory?

choices: 2 counts
4 or 5 counts
6 counts only

Lengthen this madd beyond two counts
The letter is silent
Double the letter
quiz.explain: The maddah is a lengthening instruction and nothing more. The letter after it supplies the cause: a hamzah gives muttasil or munfasil at 4 or 5, while a permanent sukoon or shaddah, as in ٱلضَّآلِّينَ, gives madd lazim at 6.
quiz.prompt: What does the small curved maddah sign over a madd letter mean?

ruleCard.action: Hold the madd letter longer than a natural madd, then release cleanly into the hamzah from the bottom of the throat.

ruleCard.hold: 4 or 5 counts in Hafs. Choose one and keep it for the whole recitation.
ruleCard.trigger: A madd letter ا و or ي, then a hamzah ء, both inside one word

lessons.summary: A madd letter with a hamzah after it inside one word. Hafs holds it 4 or 5 counts, and no qira'ah in the ten shortens it to two.
lessons.titleEn: Madd Muttasil: Hamzah in the Same Word

body: Mechanically this is the same act as muttasil: a held vowel, then a hamzah. The only difference is bookkeeping, and it is the bookkeeping that changes the ruling. Here the madd letter finishes one word and the hamzah opens the next, so the two are separable: stop between them and the cause is simply gone.

That separability is the whole reason the rule is classed as ja'iz, permissible, rather than obligatory. Several imams read it at the natural two counts, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr among them, precisely because the cause is not welded to the madd letter. Hafs by the tariq of ash-Shatibiyyah, which is what this app recites, reads 4 or 5. By the tariq of at-Tayyibah, Hafs also has the two-count reading, but that is a different tariq and not what you are reading here.

Because it only exists while you are joining the two words, munfasil disappears the moment you stop on the first one. Stop on وَمَآ and it is just an ordinary two-count alif with a sukoon after it. This makes munfasil the only long madd in the chapter that you can make appear and disappear by deciding where to breathe.

Two constraints tie this lesson to the last one. First, whatever number you choose here, use it for every munfasil in the session. Second, your muttasil must never be shorter than your munfasil: a reader on 5 for munfasil cannot be on 4 for muttasil. The safest pairing for a learner is 4 and 4.

One trap deserves naming now, because it produces a wrong madd rather than a missing one. The rule needs a hamzat qat', the hamzah that is always pronounced. It does not fire before a hamzat wasl, the connecting alif of ٱلۡ and of words like ٱسۡمُ. In مَا ٱلۡقَارِعَةُ the wasl hamzah drops when you join, the alif of مَا then meets the sakin lam, and the alif is dropped altogether: you read mal-qaari'ah with no madd at all.

definition.technical: Lengthening a madd letter at the end of a word because the following word begins with a hamzat qat'. Separated because the madd letter and its cause sit in two different words; permissible because the qurra' differ over whether it is lengthened at all.

drills.caption: The same word مَا before a qat' hamzah and before a wasl. Long, then nothing.
Munfasil, then a natural madd, then a stop. Three lengths in four words.

examples.focus: Written as one block, but يَٰٓ and أَيُّهَا are two words. The maddah over the ya, then the hamzah.
The alif of وَمَآ carried across into the hamzah of أَدۡرَىٰكَ, 4 or 5 counts.
The ya version. Same length as the alif version, no shorter.
A short ayah for drilling. Hold the alif of كَلَّآ, then the hamzah of إِنَّ.
Two very short words, so the join is easy to hear. Do not put a gap between them.
The counter-case: ٱلۡ opens with a wasl hamzah, so there is no madd and the alif of مَا is dropped.

keyPoints: Trigger: madd letter ending a word, hamzat qat' beginning the next.
Hafs by Shatibiyyah: 4 or 5 counts. By Tayyibah, 2 is also his.
Stop on the first word and the madd reverts to a plain two counts.
One length for the whole session, and muttasil never shorter than munfasil.
No madd before a hamzat wasl: مَا ٱلۡقَارِعَةُ is read mal-qaari'ah.

mistakes.right: Decide the length before you open the mushaf and hold it all the way through.
mistakes.why: Both lengths belong to Hafs, but by different turuq. Mixing them within one recitation belongs to neither.
mistakes.wrong: Reading munfasil at 4 in one ayah and 2 in the next, depending on the pace.

mistakes.right: At a stop the cause is gone. Read two counts and stop.
mistakes.why: The hamzah that earned the extra length is in a word you are no longer reading.
mistakes.wrong: Lengthening the alif after stopping on the first word.

mistakes.right: Check whether the hamzah is a qat' or a wasl. Before a wasl there is no madd, and often no alif either.
mistakes.why: The connecting hamzah is not pronounced when you join, so there is nothing for the madd to prepare for.
mistakes.wrong: Lengthening before ٱلۡ, as in مَا ٱلۡقَارِعَةُ.

mistakes.right: Keep one continuous stream of air across the boundary.
mistakes.why: A gap between the words is a stop, which cancels the very rule you were trying to apply.
mistakes.wrong: Breaking the two words apart to make room for the hamzah.

lessons.summary: A madd letter ends one word and a hamzah begins the next. Hafs by Shatibiyyah reads 4 or 5 counts, and the whole rule vanishes if you stop on the first word.
lessons.titleEn: Madd Munfasil: Hamzah in the Next Word

body: Badal means substitution, and the name records where these words came from. Arabic does not tolerate two hamzahs in a row when the second one carries a sukoon, so the second one was converted into a madd letter matching the vowel of the first. أَأْمَنَ became ءَامَنَ. أُؤْتُوا became أُوتُوا. إِإْمَان became إِيمَان. The alif, waw and ya you see are substitutes standing in for a hamzah that is no longer pronounced.

The reason it is not lengthened is the whole point of this lesson, and it is worth stating as a mechanism rather than a fact to memorise. Extra length exists to give the throat room to reach a hamzah. In muttasil and munfasil the hamzah is ahead of you, so the madd is a run-up. In badal the hamzah is behind you: it has already been said, the throat has already done the hard work, and there is nothing left to prepare for. So the madd letter takes its ordinary natural length.

This is a place where the qira'at differ visibly and Hafs is on the short end. Warsh reads badal at 2, 4 or 6 counts, and hearing a Warsh recitation is the fastest way to notice how many badal words there are. Hafs reads 2, and only 2.

One refinement for accuracy. Strictly, badal is only the words where the madd letter really did replace a hamzah. Words where a hamzah simply happens to sit before an original madd letter, such as وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ or مَسۡـُٔولٗا, are called shabih bil-badal, resembling badal. Scholars keep the two apart when explaining the derivation, but in Hafs both are read at two counts, so the distinction never changes what you do with your mouth.

definition.technical: A madd letter preceded by a hamzah, where the madd letter is itself a substitute for an original second hamzah. Read at two counts in Hafs, the same as a natural madd.

drills.caption: Hamzah first, then the matching madd letter. Two counts on each.

A shabih bil-badal word: the alif is original, not a substitute, and it is still two counts.

Two counts in Hafs, exactly like a natural madd.

mistakes.right: Look at which side the hamzah is on. Before the madd letter means two counts.
mistakes.why: The eye sees a hamzah and reaches for the muttasil habit. The rule depends on order, not on presence.
mistakes.wrong: Lengthening ءَامَنُواْ to four counts because a hamzah is visible.

mistakes.right: Full hamzah, then a full two-count alif.

mistakes.wrong: Reading the hamzah softly because it is followed by a long vowel.

body: Iwad means compensation, and the transaction is literal. Stopping on a word means giving its last letter a sukoon, and a tanween cannot survive that: the n-sound goes. What replaces it, for fatha-tanween only, is an alif: usually the one already written under the two fatha marks, and still pronounced in the words whose spelling leaves it out. You get an alif in exchange for the noon you lost, and it is read as an ordinary two-count madd.

The restriction to fatha-tanween is not arbitrary. Fatha-tanween is the one of the three that is compensated by an alif when you stop; damma-tanween and kasra-tanween simply take a sukoon, so stopping on them produces no lengthening at all: you stop on خُسۡرٍ as khusr, not khusree.

That alif is usually written into the word, as in ضَبۡحٗا, but not always, and what you say does not depend on whether it is drawn. After a hamzah that already sits on an alif the second alif is left out of the spelling: بِنَآءٗ, مَآءٗ, دُعَآءٗ, نِسَآءٗ and the ayah-final إِنشَآءٗ all end at the hamzah with the tanween mark and nothing after it, and stopping on them still gives a full two-count alif: binaa'aa, inshaa'aa. Words ending in alif maqsura behave the same way. هُدٗى and فَتٗى have no written alif either, and the maqsura is the supporting letter the stop lengthens: hudaa, fataa.

There is one exception in pronunciation, and it is about the letter under the tanween rather than the tanween itself. When the fatha-tanween sits on a ta marbutah, ةً, stopping converts the ta marbutah into a sakin ha instead. لَٰغِيَةٗ is stopped as laaghiyah, not laaghiyaa. Nothing is lengthened, because the ta marbutah takes the stop for itself.

Everything above is conditional on stopping. Read straight on and there is no iwad at all: the tanween is fully pronounced and behaves under the ordinary nun sakin rules, hiding or merging or converting according to whatever letter comes next.

Surat al-Adiyat is the natural drilling ground. Its first five ayahs all end in fatha-tanween, so every ayah-end is an iwad if you pause there, and reading it through without pausing is a clean test of the opposite behaviour.

definition.technical: Reading a fatha-tanween at the end of a word as a two-count alif when you stop on that word, the alif compensating for the dropped noon of the tanween.

drills.caption: Stop on each: an alif, a bare sukoon, a sakin ha. Three different endings.

examples.focus: Stop here and you say dabhaa with a clean two-count alif and no n-sound.
The same ending one ayah later. Both stops should measure the same two counts.
The other written form of fatha-tanween. The two marks sit differently, the stop is identical.
Two madds when you stop: the natural ya inside the word, then the iwad alif at the end.
The ta marbutah exception. Stopped, this is laaghiyah with a sakin ha and no added alif.

keyPoints: Fatha-tanween only. Damma and kasra-tanween just take a sukoon.
Only when you stop. Reading on, the tanween is fully pronounced.
The result is a plain two-count alif, no longer.

mistakes.right: The noon is gone completely. Say the alif and stop.
mistakes.why: Half a tanween is neither the joined reading nor the stopped one.
mistakes.wrong: Keeping a trace of the noon before the stop, as dabhan-aa.

mistakes.wrong: Lengthening a kasra or damma tanween at a stop, reading خُسۡرٍ as khusree.

mistakes.why: This is the single exception to the rule and it appears constantly, since so many feminine nouns end this way.
mistakes.wrong: Reading the ة of لَٰغِيَةٗ as an alif at a stop.

mistakes.right: No stop, no iwad. Apply the ordinary tanween rules instead.
mistakes.why: The compensation only exists because the noon was lost, and joining does not lose it.
mistakes.wrong: Applying iwad in the middle of an ayah while continuing to read.

body: Start from what a madd letter needs: a vowel that matches it. A waw is a madd letter after a damma, a ya after a kasra, because in each case the vowel and the letter are the same shape held longer. Put a fatha in front of them instead and the match is broken. The mouth has to travel from an open fatha to a rounded waw or a spread ya, and travelling is a glide, not a hold. That is a leen letter, and there are exactly two of them.

Because it is a glide, a leen letter is not lengthened on its own. كَيۡفَ, يَوۡمَ, عَلَيۡهِمۡ, بَيۡنَ are all read straight through at ordinary speed with no hold whatsoever. This is the half of the rule learners most often get wrong, usually by importing the habit from madd tabi'i.

What gives a leen letter length is a sukoon immediately after it, and in the overwhelming majority of cases that sukoon comes from stopping. Read on through قُرَيۡشٍ and there is nothing to hold. Stop on it and the ش takes a sukoon, the glide now has a wall in front of it, and you may hold it 2, 4 or 6 counts. As with madd arid, the number is your choice and it should be the same choice every time in one sitting.

Surat Quraysh is the cleanest drill in the mushaf for this, because all four of its ayahs end on a leen letter: قُرَيۡشٍ, وَٱلصَّيۡفِ, ٱلۡبَيۡتِ, خَوۡفِۭ. Three ya and one waw, four stops, one length.

There is one family of cases where the sukoon after a leen letter is permanent rather than borrowed from a stop: the letter عٓ in the openings كٓهيعٓصٓ and عٓسٓقٓ. Its name is spelled عَيْنْ, a leen ya with a sakin noon behind it that never goes away, so this is madd leen lazim. It is read 4 or 6 counts, and 2 is also narrated; among reciters 4 and 6 are the two you will actually hear.

definition.technical: A waw or a ya carrying sukoon with a fatha on the letter before it. Called soft because the sound comes out with no effort from the mouth, gliding rather than stretching.

drills.caption: Read on, then stop on the same word. The first is a glide, the second is a held glide.
Ya and waw at a stop. Same length on both.

examples.focus: Stop here: the ya glides, then holds for your chosen 2, 4 or 6 counts.
The same soft ya one ayah later. It should measure exactly the same as the last one.
Third leen stop in the same short surah. Three in a row is the drill.
The waw version, closing the surah. Lips round for the glide, then hold and stop.
The counter-case: mid-ayah, nothing sakin after it, so nothing is held.

keyPoints: Two leen letters: و and ي, each with sukoon and a fatha before it.
Not madd letters: the vowel before them does not match them.
No sukoon after them means no lengthening at all. كَيۡفَ is not held.
A stop supplies the sukoon: then 2, 4 or 6 counts, consistently.
The عٓ of كٓهيعٓصٓ and عٓسٓقٓ is a permanent case: 4 or 6.

mistakes.wrong: Holding the ya of كَيۡفَ or the waw of يَوۡمَ while reading on.

body: This rule is a companion to madd iwad in one respect: it is created by the reader, not by the word. Nothing in ٱلنَّاسِ asks for extra length. The س ends the word carrying a kasra, and if you read on into the next ayah the alif before it is an ordinary two-count madd. It is only when you decide to stop that the س takes a sukoon, a sukoon now stands immediately after a madd letter, and the length becomes available.

Because the cause is borrowed, the length is not fixed. Three readings are permitted and all three are correct: 2 counts (qasr), 4 counts (tawassut), and 6 counts (ishba'). What is not permitted is drifting between them. Reciters choose one according to the pace they are reciting at, generally 6 for slow tarteel, 4 for a middle pace, 2 for a brisk hadr, and then hold that choice for the whole session.

The same applies when the letter before the final one is a leen letter rather than a madd letter, which is the case covered in the previous lesson. The two are the same rule wearing different letters, which is why your leen stops and your ordinary arid stops should measure the same.

Practically, madd arid is the most frequently used length decision in recitation, because most ayahs end in a long vowel plus one consonant. The ground-truth engine finds it at the end of roughly three and a half thousand ayahs. Every one of those is a place where an inconsistent reader will be heard.

definition.literal: the stretch made temporary by a sukoon
definition.technical: Lengthening a madd letter when the letter after it takes a sukoon only because the reader stopped on the word. Called 'arid, accidental, because the cause belongs to the reader's pause and not to the word.

drills.caption: Joined, then stopped. Two counts becomes your chosen 2, 4 or 6.
Three stops in a row. They must all measure the same.

examples.focus: The last word of the mushaf. Stopping makes the س sakin, so the alif may be 2, 4 or 6.
Waw madd, then a stopped noon. The same ayah ending repeats in the next ayah, so mismatched lengths are audible immediately.
Ya madd, then a stopped lam. Read on into the next ayah and it is a plain two counts.
Waw madd, then a stopped ra. Joined, the ra is light because of its kasra; stop and the kasra is gone, so the sakin waw hands the ra back to the damma before it and the ra turns heavy.

keyPoints: Cause: a sukoon that exists only because you stopped.
2, 4 or 6 counts, all correct. Pick one and keep it.
Read on and the madd goes straight back to two counts.
Leen letters at a stop follow the same three-way choice.
The names are qasr (2), tawassut (4), ishba' (6).

mistakes.right: One length for the whole session, chosen to match your pace.
mistakes.why: All three are permitted individually; switching between them inside one recitation is not one of the three.
mistakes.wrong: Stopping at 6 counts on one ayah and 2 on the next.

mistakes.right: Joined, it is an ordinary two-count madd.
mistakes.why: The sukoon that earned the length only exists while you are stopped.
mistakes.wrong: Keeping the long stop-length when reading on through the ayah end.

mistakes.why: Confusing arid with lazim erases the distinction between a borrowed cause and a permanent one, which is the whole architecture of the chapter.
mistakes.wrong: Treating it as six counts because six sounds more correct.

body: Every other madd in this chapter has a soft edge. Muttasil is 4 or 5, arid is 2, 4 or 6, leen the same, munfasil depends on the tariq. Madd lazim is the fixed one: six counts in Hafs, six in every other qira'ah, and no narrated alternative to the length. That single fact is why it is worth learning as its own category rather than as a long version of madd arid. One exception sits inside the category and is spelled out below rather than smoothed over: the عٓ of كٓهيعٓصٓ and عٓسٓقٓ, whose name holds a leen letter rather than a madd letter, is read 4 or 6. A second wajh, the tas-heel of ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ described in the last paragraph of this lesson, is not a shorter madd lazim but a different way of reading the hamzah altogether.

The reason it is fixed is the reason for the name. Lazim means binding, and the sukoon that causes it is written into the word. In ٱلضَّآلِّينَ the lam is doubled whether you stop or continue. In ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ the lam is sakin whether you stop or continue. There is nothing accidental for the reader to decide about, so nothing is left to the reader.

The four sub-types come from crossing two questions. First: is the madd inside an ordinary word (kalimi) or inside the name of a letter in a surah opening (harfi)? Second: is the sukoon merged into a shaddah (muthaqqal, heavy) or standing on its own (mukhaffaf, light)? Two answers each gives four types, and all four are six counts.

Kalimi muthaqqal is the common one: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ, ٱلصَّآخَّةُ, ٱلطَّآمَّةُ, دَآبَّةٖ, وَٱلصَّٰٓفَّٰتِ. Kalimi mukhaffaf is the rare one: it occurs in a single word, ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ, and only in the two places where that word appears, Yunus 51 and Yunus 91. Learn that word once and the whole sub-type is finished.

The harfi types live in the disjointed letters that open twenty-nine surahs. The trick is that those letters are read as their names, not as their sounds: الٓمٓ is alif, laam, meem. Spell each name out and the madd rules apply to the spelling. لَامْ is three letters with a madd alif in the middle and a sakin meem at the end, which is a madd lazim harfi. When the next opening letter is مِيمْ, that sakin meem merges into it and gains a shaddah, which makes it muthaqqal. The final مِيمْ of الٓمٓ ends in a plain sakin meem with nothing to merge into, so it is mukhaffaf. One three-letter opening carries both harfi types.

Not every opening letter is six counts, and getting this wrong in the other direction is just as audible. Of the fourteen letters that appear in these openings, collected in the line نَصٌّ حَكِيمٌ قَاطِعٌ لَهُ سِرٌّ, the alif has no madd at all because its name أَلِفْ contains none. Five of them, ح ي ط ه ر, have two-letter names ending in a madd letter with nothing after it, so they are simply two counts. Seven, ن ق ص س ل ك م, have three-letter names of the shape consonant-madd-sakin, and those are the six-count ones. That leaves عٓ, whose name عَيْنْ holds a leen letter rather than a madd letter, and which is therefore read 4 or 6 counts.

One narrated choice belongs here rather than being smoothed over. In the six places where an interrogative hamzah meets a hamzat wasl, ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ twice, ءَآللَّهُ twice and ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ twice, Hafs by ash-Shatibiyyah has two permitted wajhs: converting the second hamzah into a six-count alif, which is the madd lazim reading, or facilitating it as a light hamzah between two sounds (tas-heel). The printed mushaf draws the first, and it is what most reciters read, but both are his.

definition.technical: Lengthening a madd letter for six counts because the letter after it carries a permanent sukoon, whether that sukoon stands alone or has been merged into a shaddah. Called lazim because the cause never leaves the word, so the length never varies.

drills.caption: الٓمٓ spelled out. No madd, six, six, with the lam's meem merged into the next.
Three kalimi muthaqqal words. Count six on each and check they match.

examples.focus: Kalimi muthaqqal: six counts on the alif, then the doubled lam. The most-recited madd lazim there is.
Kalimi muthaqqal again, mid-ayah, so the six counts cannot be blamed on a stop.
A short, common word carrying the same rule. Six counts, then the doubled ب.
Kalimi mukhaffaf: a plain sakin lam after the alif. This word and Yunus 51 are the entire sub-type.
Both harfi types in three letters: the لَامْ merges into the مِيمْ (muthaqqal), the final مِيمْ stands alone (mukhaffaf).
يَا is two counts, سِينْ is six. Two different lengths inside one two-letter opening.
Harfi mukhaffaf on its own: قَافْ, six counts, then the pause mark.
Every category at once: كَافْ six, هَا two, يَا two, عَيْنْ four or six, صَادْ six.

keyPoints: Cause: a sukoon or shaddah that is part of the word, not one you created by stopping.
Six counts, with no choice, in any qira'ah. The one exception is the leen-lazim عٓ, at 4 or 6.
Four sub-types: kalimi or harfi, crossed with muthaqqal (shadda) or mukhaffaf (plain sukoon).
Kalimi mukhaffaf is one word only, ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ, in Yunus 51 and 91.
In the surah openings: ا has no madd, ح ي ط ه ر are 2, ن ق ص س ل ك م are 6, and ع is 4 or 6.

mistakes.right: Six counts, then the doubled lam.
mistakes.why: The shaddah is written in the word. Nothing about your stopping created it, so nothing about your pace may shorten it.
mistakes.wrong: Reading ٱلضَّآلِّينَ at four counts because the arid habit is four.

mistakes.right: The stop changes nothing. Six counts either way.
mistakes.why: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ ends Surat al-Fatiha, so this error is repeated in every prayer a learner makes.
mistakes.wrong: Shortening a lazim that falls at the end of an ayah, where a stop is expected.

body: The ha in question is one specific ha: the suffix meaning his or its, as in لَهُ (to him), إِنَّهُ (indeed he), كِتَابُهُ (his book). It is not any ha that happens to end a word. The ha of وَجۡه and of فَقِهَ is a root letter of the word and has nothing to do with this rule, and neither does the feminine هَا.

In the KFGQPC mushaf the rule is drawn for you rather than left to be deduced. A small superscript waw ۥ after a damma, or a small superscript ya ۦ after a kasra, is the silah: it is a real madd letter that is pronounced but not written on the line. Where the mushaf prints a bare damma or kasra on the ha with no small letter after it, there is no silah, and that is a deliberate signal rather than a printing accident.

The condition behind the marking is that the ha must sit between two vowelled letters. If the letter before it is sakin, the silah does not apply: مِنۡهُ, عَنۡهُ, فِيهِ, إِلَيۡهِ are all read with a short vowel on the ha. If the letter after it is sakin, it also does not apply, which is why لَهُ ٱلۡمُلۡكُ has no silah: joining drops the wasl hamzah and leaves the ha facing a sakin lam. And stopping on the ha removes it too, because the ha then takes a sukoon of its own.

The split between the two silahs is decided by one thing: whether the next word begins with a hamzat qat'. If it does not, this is silah sughra, the lesser connection, and it is two counts, exactly a natural madd. If it does, this is silah kubra, the greater connection, and it takes the ruling of madd munfasil: 4 or 5 counts in Hafs by ash-Shatibiyyah. That is not a coincidence but the same rule from a different angle, since the silah is a madd letter ending a word with a hamzah beginning the next.

Hafs then has a small set of words that do not follow the general condition, and they are worth memorising as a list because there is no pattern to derive. فِيهِۦ مُهَانًا in al-Furqan 69 receives a silah even though the ha is preceded by a sakin ya, and it is the only place in the Qur'an where that happens. يَرۡضَهُ لَكُمۡ in az-Zumar 7 receives no silah even though both neighbours are vowelled. أَنسَىٰنِيهُ in al-Kahf 63 keeps a short damma. عَلَيۡهُ ٱللَّهَ in al-Fath 10 is read by Hafs with a damma on the ha rather than the kasra the ending would normally take. And in أَرۡجِهۡ, at al-A'raf 111 and ash-Shu'ara 36, and in فَأَلۡقِهۡ at an-Naml 28, Hafs gives the ha a plain sukoon.

definition.technical: Connecting the ha of the third-person masculine singular pronoun to a waw after a damma or a ya after a kasra, when the ha falls between two vowelled letters and the reader does not stop on it.

body: Everything in this chapter comes from one branch structure, and once you can see it the ten lessons collapse into three questions you ask in order.

First: is there a madd letter at all? An alif after a fatha, a waw after a damma, a ya after a kasra. If there is not, there is no madd, with one qualification: a waw or ya after a fatha is a leen letter, which behaves like a madd letter only at a stop.

Second: what follows the madd letter? Only two things in the language lengthen it. A hamzah, which gives you muttasil if it is in the same word, munfasil if it is in the next, and silah kubra if the madd letter is the unwritten one after a pronoun ha. Or a sukoon, which sends you to the third question. And if a hamzah sits before the madd letter rather than after it, that is badal, and Hafs leaves it at the natural two counts.

Third, only if a sukoon follows: is that sukoon permanent or borrowed? Permanent, written into the word, means madd lazim and six counts with no choice. Borrowed from your decision to stop means madd arid, and the choice of 2, 4 or 6 is yours as long as you keep it. Madd iwad is the same borrowing seen from the other side: you stopped, the tanween's noon was lost, and its alif is left holding two counts.

If neither question two nor question three applies, the madd is natural and it is two counts. That is the case in more than half the ayahs in the mushaf, which is worth remembering when the chart below starts to look like a lot of rules.

examples.focus: Three mudood in four words: munfasil here, natural on the alif of ٱلۡكَٰفِرُونَ, arid if you stop on it.
Permanent cause, so six counts, and stopping on the noon does not change it.
No madd letter at all: a leen ya, glided through with no lengthening until a stop supplies the sukoon.

keyPoints: Only two causes lengthen a madd: a hamzah, or a sukoon.
Hamzah after the madd letter lengthens it. Hamzah before it does not.
A permanent sukoon means six counts and no choice. A borrowed one means your choice.
Every count value in the chapter is a multiple of the natural two.
Consistency across a session is part of every rule that offers a choice.

body: Arabic letters divide by whether the sound can keep running once you have made them. Eight letters block it completely, and they are gathered in the phrase أَجِدُ قَطٍ بَكَتْ: ء ج د ق ط ب ك ت. These are the shadeed letters, and while you are holding one of them nothing at all comes out.

Two of those eight, ك and ت, are mahmoos: the vocal cords are open, so when you release them a puff of breath escapes and you hear it. The hamza is set apart, because its articulation is a closure of the vocal cords themselves and its release is simply the letter. That leaves five: ق ط ب ج د, which are shadeed and majhoor together. Sound is blocked and breath is not running, so a sakin one has nothing to make it audible. Qalqalah is the fix: instead of a vowel, the letter is given a sharp separation, and the pop of the articulators parting is what you hear.

Feel it letter by letter and the rule stops being abstract. For د and ط the tongue tip is pressed against the gum ridge and then flicked off it. For ب the lips are sealed and then popped apart. For ج the middle of the tongue is pressed against the roof of the mouth and released. For ق the back of the tongue is against the soft palate and drops away. In every case the bounce is the release, not an extra sound stuck on afterwards.

Reciters divide qalqalah by where the sukoon came from. It is sughra (lesser) when the sukoon belongs to the word and you carry on reading past it, as in لَمۡ يَلِدۡ or ٱلۡقَدۡرِ. It is kubra (greater) when the letter is only sakin because you stopped on it, as when you stop on فَٱرۡغَب at the end of Surat ash-Sharh. Nothing about the mechanism changes; the bounce is simply more audible at a stop, because there is silence behind it.

Whether there are two levels or three is a real disagreement, and it is only about naming. Most classical texts describe the two above. A number of contemporary teachers add a third, akbar, for stopping on a doubled qalqalah letter such as وَتَبَّ or بِٱلۡحَقِّ, where you hold the shadda and then release, which produces the strongest echo of all; others keep two names and simply note that the bounce there is stronger. Your mouth does the same thing under either scheme.

The instruction that matters more than any of the naming: the bounce carries no vowel. قَدْ is not qada, not qadi, and not qad-eh. The echo is a single sharp release and then silence or the next letter. Teachers differ over whether it leans a hair toward a fatha or is entirely neutral, but nobody permits a full vowel, and nobody permits lengthening it. Keep the heaviness of the letter, though: ق and ط are letters of isti'la, so their echo is thick, while ب ج د stay light.

mistakes.right: One sharp separation, then nothing. The echo is a release, not a syllable.
mistakes.why: A vowel added to a sakin letter invents a syllable that is not in the mushaf, and at the end of a word it changes the grammatical ending.
mistakes.wrong: Letting the echo grow into a vowel, so أَحَدْ becomes ahada and قَدْ becomes qad-eh.

mistakes.right: Only a sakin one bounces. A vowelled ق ط ب ج د is an ordinary letter.
mistakes.why: The whole reason for the rule is that a sakin one would be inaudible. A vowel already makes it audible.
mistakes.wrong: Bouncing a qalqalah letter that is carrying a vowel, such as the ب of بَعۡدِ.

mistakes.right: Go straight into the doubled ب with no release in between.
mistakes.why: That ب is merged into the one after it, so it has no articulation of its own left to release. A merged letter is never bounced.
mistakes.wrong: Bouncing the ب of ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ before the doubled ب.

mistakes.right: Release and stop. The silence after the bounce is part of the stop.
mistakes.why: Qalqalah has no count. Stretching it is the audible sign of a reader performing the rule rather than applying it.
mistakes.wrong: Holding the echo at the end of an ayah, turning it into a hum or a stretch.

body: Arabic does not begin a word on a sakin letter, and a good many words do begin with one. ٱسۡمٌ starts with a sakin س, ٱقۡرَأۡ with a sakin ق. The solution is a disposable hamza at the front, carrying a vowel, whose only job is to get you started. Once the word is reached from something before it, that job is done and the hamza is dropped without a trace.

The mushaf tells you which hamza you are looking at. Hamzat al-wasl is printed as a bare alif carrying a small ص head, the head of the word وصل: ٱ. It never carries a hamza sign. If you see أ or إ or ء, that is hamzat al-qat', which is a real letter of the word and is pronounced every time, connected or not. The أَ of أَنۡعَمۡتَ and the ٱ of ٱهۡدِنَا look similar at a glance and behave in opposite ways.

When you do start on one, its vowel is decided by three cases, and only three. First, the definite article ٱلۡ takes a fatha, with no exceptions anywhere in the Qur'an. Second, a verb takes a damma if the third letter of the word carries a damma that belongs to the verb, and a kasra otherwise: count the hamza as one, the sakin letter as two, and look at three. ٱسۡجُدُواْ has a damma on the ج, so it begins usjudu; ٱهۡدِنَا has a kasra on the د, so it begins ihdina; ٱنطَلَقَ has a fatha on the ط, so it begins intalaqa. Third, the seven nouns take a kasra.

The phrase belongs to the verb is doing real work in that rule. Four verbs in the Qur'an carry a damma on the third letter that is on loan from the plural waw rather than from the verb itself: ٱمۡشُواْ، ٱقۡضُوٓاْ، ٱبۡنُواْ، ٱئۡتُواْ. Their own vowel is a kasra, so you begin imshu, iqdu, ibnu, i'tu, even though a damma is printed in front of you. This is the one place in the rule where reading off the page misleads you.

The classical list of nouns that take hamzat al-wasl runs to ten; seven of them occur in the Qur'an: ٱبۡن، ٱبۡنَة، ٱمۡرُؤ، ٱمۡرَأَة، ٱثۡنَان، ٱثۡنَتَان، ٱسۡم. All seven begin with a kasra, which is why بِٱسۡمِ رَبِّكَ read from a stop is ismi rabbik and never usmi.

In connection the drop is total, and the word before often takes a helping vowel so that two sakins do not collide. That is why the mushaf writes قُلِ ٱللَّهُ, إِنِ ٱمۡرُؤٌاْ, أَنِ ٱمۡشُواْ, وَقَالَتِ ٱمۡرَأَتُ: the kasra on the preceding word is there to carry you over the vanished hamza. وَنَادَىٰ نُوحٌ ٱبۡنَهُۥ is read nuhu-bnahu in one breath, not nuhun ibnahu.

Two further cases are worth recognising when they appear. If the letter after hamzat al-wasl is itself a sakin hamza, starting on the word turns that second hamza into a letter of madd matching the vowel: ٱؤۡتُمِنَ begins utumina with a long u, and ٱئۡتُواْ begins itu with a long i. And when the questioning hamza runs into the article's hamza, the two are written merged and the reading lengthens, which happens in three words and six places: ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ twice in Surat Yunus, ءَآللَّهُ in Yunus and an-Naml, and ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ twice in al-An'am.

definition.technical: An extra hamza placed in front of a word whose first letter is sakin, so that the word can be begun at all. It is sounded when you start on the word and dropped entirely when you connect to it.

body: The two names come from the two examples and nothing more. ٱلشَّمۡس, the sun, has a lam that disappears; ٱلۡقَمَر, the moon, has one you hear. Surat ash-Shams opens with both words in consecutive ayahs, which is the cheapest way to fix the pair in memory.

Most of the fourteen sun letters are made with the tip or the front of the tongue, in the same neighbourhood as the lam itself, and two sounds made that close together collapse into one very readily. The moon letters are made in the throat, at the lips, or in the middle and back of the tongue, too far from the lam to pull it in. The split is not perfectly derivable from the makharij, though, so treat the mnemonic as the authority and the makhraj story as the reason it mostly works.

The practical point is that you never have to hold either list while reading, because the mushaf marks the rule on every single word. If the letter after the lam carries a shadda, the lam is silent and that shadda is the merge. If the lam itself carries a sukoon, you pronounce it. Look at وَٱلشَّمۡسِ and وَٱلۡقَمَرِ side by side and the difference is visible before it is audible.

The sun merge is complete. Nothing of the lam survives, not a trace of it, and what you hear is one doubled letter: ash-shams, ar-rahman, an-nas. When the letter after the article is itself a lam, as in ٱلَّذِي or ٱلَّيۡل, the two letters are identical, which makes it the mutamathilayn merge of the last lesson in this chapter.

One neighbouring case, so it does not confuse you later: the name ٱللَّه is written with the same doubled lam, but the question people ask about it is a different one, namely whether that lam is read heavy or light, which is decided by the vowel before it and has a lesson of its own.

definition.literal: the lam of definition, the lam of ال
definition.technical: The lam of the prefix ال. It is called شمسية when it is not pronounced but merged into the following letter, doubling it, and قمرية when it is pronounced with sukoon. The following letter decides which.

body: The previous lesson covered one lam out of five. Classical books count them as the lam of the definite article, the lam of a noun, the lam of a verb, the lam of a particle, and the lam of a command. Four of the five are far simpler than the article, and the whole point of this lesson is recognition: work out which lam is in front of you first, then you already know what to do with it.

The lam of a noun is part of the word itself, sitting inside it: سَلۡسَبِيلٗا، ٱلۡأَلۡبَٰب، أَلۡوَٰنُهُۥ. It is always read clear, and nothing ever merges it. There is no case to memorise here at all.

The lam of a verb is part of a verb: قُلۡ، جَعَلۡنَا، يَلۡتَقِطۡهُ، أَلۡهَىٰكُمُ. It is read clear too, with one exception: when a ل or a ر follows it, it merges into that letter and is not pronounced. قُل لَّا is read qul-la with a doubled ل and no lam of its own, and وَقُل رَّبِّ is read wa-qur-rabbi. It is a common pattern, and every instance is printed as a merge.

The lam of a particle means the sakin lam in هَلۡ and بَلۡ. Same rule, same two triggers: clear before everything else, merged before ل and ر. The merge with ل happens in four places for هَلۡ and a good many for بَلۡ, and the merge with ر happens in exactly two places for بَلۡ: بَل رَّفَعَهُ in Surat an-Nisa and بَل رَّبُّكُمۡ in al-Anbiya. Counting the lam of قُلۡ as well, a verb or particle lam merges into a following ر in twelve places in the whole Qur'an.

There is a third place where بَلۡ meets a ر, and it does not merge: كَلَّاۖ بَلۡۜ رَانَ in Surat al-Mutaffifin. Hafs, by the way of ash-Shatibiyyah, reads a sakt there, a brief cut of the voice without taking a breath, and a merge cannot cross a silence, so both the ل and the ر are heard. It is one of the four sakts read in this riwayah, along with عِوَجَاۜ in al-Kahf, مَّرۡقَدِنَاۜ in Ya-Sin, and مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ in al-Qiyamah. The mark ۜ printed above the line is what tells you. A fifth place, مَالِيَهۡ running into هَلَكَ at the end of al-Haaqqah, is related two ways, and the next lesson takes it up.

The lam of a command is the لِ prefixed to a verb to give an order. Standing alone it carries a kasra, but after وَ، فَ or ثُمَّ it becomes sakin, and that is how the mushaf writes it: فَلۡيَعۡبُدُواْ، وَلۡيَتَّقِ، فَلۡيَنظُرِ. It is always clear. Some books fold it into the lam of a particle rather than counting it separately; the reading is identical either way, so the disagreement is about tidiness, not about sound.

As with the article, none of this needs to be recalled at speed, because the merge is written into the page in exactly the same way: no sukoon on the lam, a shadda on the letter that swallowed it. What the lists are actually for is the other direction: they stop you inventing merges Hafs does not read, and they tell you when a lam that looks like an article is not one.

definition.technical: A lam carrying sukoon in a noun, a verb, a particle, or a command. Classified by the kind of word it belongs to, because that is what decides whether anything may happen to it.

A noun's lam and a command's lam are always clear.

mistakes.why: Its hamza is a qat' with a fatha printed on it, not the connecting alif, and the article never attaches to a verb. The hamza is the giveaway.
mistakes.wrong: Reading the أَلۡ at the front of أَلۡهَىٰكُمُ as a definite article and looking for a sun or moon rule.

mistakes.right: qur-rabbi, with a doubled ر and no lam at all.
mistakes.why: This merge is complete, exactly like the sun lam. A half-said lam is neither the merge nor a clear reading.
mistakes.wrong: Leaving a faint lam audible in قُل رَّبِّ.

mistakes.right: Cut the voice briefly on بَلۡ without breathing, then say رَانَ.
mistakes.why: Hafs reads a sakt there, and a sakt prevents idgham. Merging it belongs to other ways of reading, not to Hafs by ash-Shatibiyyah.
mistakes.wrong: Merging بَلۡ into the ر of رَانَ in Surat al-Mutaffifin, because the two other بَلۡ + ر places do merge.

mistakes.right: fal-ya'budu, with a sakin lam.
mistakes.why: The command lam takes a kasra only when nothing precedes it. After وَ or فَ it is written sakin, and the mushaf shows exactly that.

body: The nun sakin chapter taught one idgham, the one triggered by يرملون. These three are the rest of them, and they behave differently: instead of a rule that fires across the whole Qur'an, most of them are a handful of named places you can learn in an afternoon. The names describe distance. Two identical letters are متماثلان. Two letters from the same articulation point with different qualities, like د and ت, are متجانسان. Two letters from neighbouring points, like ل and ر, are متقاربان. The closer the pair, the harder it is to keep them apart, which is why they merge.

Identical letters merge wherever they meet, with no list to memorise: ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ, وَقَد دَّخَلُواْ, يُدۡرِككُّمُ, يُسۡرِف فِّي. The one thing that blocks it is a letter of madd. In ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ the و of ءَامَنُواْ is a madd letter carrying two counts, so it is not merged into the و after it; the same goes for فِي يَوۡمٖ. Merging there would delete a length the mushaf writes out, so the two letters stay separate.

The متجانسان of Hafs are a closed list, pair by pair. د into ت is by far the commonest, the أَرَدتُّمۡ and قَد تَّبَيَّنَ type. ت into د occurs twice, in أَثۡقَلَت دَّعَوَا and أُجِيبَت دَّعۡوَتُكُمَا. ت into ط occurs seven times, and every single one of them is before a form of the word طَآئِفَة. ط into ت occurs four times: أَحَطتُ، بَسَطتَ، فَرَّطتُمۡ، فَرَّطتُ. ذ into ظ occurs twice, both of them إِذ ظَّ. ث into ذ occurs once, in يَلۡهَث ذَّٰلِكَ. ب into م occurs once, in ٱرۡكَب مَّعَنَا, and most books count that pair here because both letters are made at the lips.

Those four ط words are the interesting ones, because the merge is incomplete. The ط gives up its articulation point to the ت but not its itbaq, the pressing of the tongue up against the roof of the mouth, so what you hear is a thickened, emphatic ت rather than a plain doubled one. The mushaf says so: in all four of them the ت carries no shadda at all, while every complete merge in this lesson has one printed. Reading بَسَطتَ as a clean doubled ت is the standard error here, and the missing shadda is the standing reminder.

The متقاربان of Hafs are two pairs. ل into ر is the merge you already met in the previous lesson, the lam of قُلۡ and بَلۡ before a ر, twelve places in all. ق into ك occurs once, in أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم. That single word carries a genuine disagreement: ash-Shatibiyyah has Hafs merging the qaf into the kaf, and what is disputed is whether the qaf's isti'la survives the merge, making it incomplete, or does not, making it complete. Both are related from Hafs, so a teacher may correct you toward either; the printed shadda reflects the complete reading, which is what most teach today. What is not read by anyone is a plain sakin qaf pronounced in full.

Two identical letters do not always merge either, and Surat al-Haaqqah has the case worth knowing: مَالِيَهۡ at the end of one ayah runs into هَلَكَ at the start of the next. Hafs is related two ways there, with a sakt that keeps both ha's audible, or with an idgham that merges them, and the mushaf prints the sakt mark to flag it. When a riwayah has two faces, say so and pick one deliberately rather than drifting between them.

The reason to learn this lesson is not to recall the lists while reciting. Every merge above is written into the page the same way, the first letter stripped of its sukoon and the second given a shadda, so reading what is printed already gives you the merge. The lists are for the other direction: recognising that a bare letter is bare on purpose, and not inventing merges in the many places where two close letters simply sit next to each other and are both pronounced.

definition.literal: to insert one thing into another
definition.technical: Joining a sakin letter to the vowelled letter after it so that the two are pronounced as one doubled letter. It is called متماثلان when the letters are identical, متجانسان when they share a makhraj but differ in their sifat, and متقاربان when their makharij are merely close.

ت into ط. All seven places of this pair look like this one.
Incomplete: no shadda on the ت, because the ط's heaviness stays behind.

The only ق into ك, and a place where Hafs is related two ways.
متقاربان: the lam is gone and the heavy ر is doubled.
Two identical letters that must not merge. The first و is a madd of two counts.
Read on into هَلَكَ and Hafs allows either a sakt or a merge. Choose one and keep it.

keyPoints: Identical letters merge wherever they meet, unless the first is a letter of madd.
متجانسان in Hafs: د/ت, ت/د, ت/ط, ط/ت, ذ/ظ, ث/ذ, ب/م. Nothing else.
متقاربان in Hafs: ل into ر, and ق into ك once, in أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم.
أَحَطتُ، بَسَطتَ، فَرَّطتُمۡ، فَرَّطتُ keep the ط's heaviness, and print no shadda.
Every merge is marked: no sukoon on the first letter, shadda on the second.

mistakes.right: The د is not pronounced at all. Begin on a doubled ت.
mistakes.why: A merge is not a softening. Half-saying the first letter is the same error as half-saying the noon in idgham with ghunnah.
mistakes.wrong: Sounding the first letter faintly, so a د can still be heard in قَد تَّبَيَّنَ.

mistakes.right: Keep the tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth through the merge, so the ت comes out thick.
mistakes.why: The ط's makhraj merges but its itbaq does not. The absent shadda in those four words is the printed reminder that something of the ط survives.
mistakes.wrong: Reading بَسَطتَ with a plain doubled ت.

mistakes.right: Give the و of ءَامَنُواْ its two counts, then say the next و separately.
mistakes.why: The first و is a letter of madd, and merging it would erase a length the mushaf spells out. Identical letters merge only when the first is a plain sakin.
mistakes.wrong: Merging ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ into one doubled و.

mistakes.right: Go straight into the doubled ب with nothing in between.
mistakes.why: Qalqalah is the release of a sakin letter at its own makhraj. A merged letter has no makhraj of its own left to release.
mistakes.wrong: Bouncing the ب of ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ, because ب is a qalqalah letter.

body: There is a habit that separates a reader who has memorised rules from one who can actually use them. The first meets a word, retrieves the rule from memory, and applies it. The second looks at the word and sees that something is already marked. Both arrive at the same recitation, but only the second is reading. This lesson is about the second habit, and it costs nothing to learn: the marks are already on every page you have ever opened.

Start with the single most useful observation in the whole script. A sukoon (ۡ) printed on a letter means that letter is pronounced closed, plainly, and then it is over. In أَنۡعَمۡتَ the nun carries a sukoon and nothing at all happens to it: you close the nun, you say the ع, you move on. That is idhhar, and the mark is the reason you did not have to think about it.

Now the useful half. If a nun or a tanween does NOT carry a sukoon, and it is not a madd letter, the omission is deliberate. The scribes did not forget. A missing sukoon is the script telling you that the sound does not simply close: it is going to be hidden, merged, hummed, or swapped. In يُنفِقُونَ the nun is bare and a ف follows, and that bareness is the whole announcement of ikhfa. Once you have seen this once you cannot unsee it, and it turns the nun rules from four things to recall into one thing to notice.

The second mark is the shadda (ّ), and it is best read as a receipt. A shadda is written where a letter is doubled, and one of the ways a letter gets doubled is that something merged into it. In هُدٗى مِّن the meem of مِّن carries a shadda that the word does not own by itself: it is there because the tanween before it was absorbed. So a shadda on the first letter of a word, right after a bare nun or tanween, is idghaam already recorded in the ink. The same reading works inside the definite article, which is the next mark.

The laam of ٱل is either given a sukoon or not, and that one difference is the whole of the shamsiyyah and qamariyyah distinction. ٱلۡحَمۡدُ has a sukoon on the laam, so the laam is a real letter and you pronounce it. ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ has no sukoon on the laam and a shadda on the ر, so the laam is not read at all and the ر is doubled instead. You do not need the fourteen-letter lists to read the word correctly; you need to look at whether the laam was pointed.

The last mark is the least subtle, because it is not a hint at all but an instruction. In أَلِيمُۢ بِمَا there is a small meem (ۢ) printed above the line where the tanween's nun would have been. Iqlab is the one nun rule where the script simply prints the letter you are meant to say. Nothing is being implied and nothing needs to be inferred: the meem is there, so you say a meem.

Read this way, the page divides into two kinds of place. Marked and closed: sukoon on the letter, nothing to do. Marked and open: no sukoon, or a shadda ahead, or a small letter overhead, and a rule is running. Neither kind requires you to recall a letter list at speed, which is exactly why reciters who read fluently are rarely reciting from memorised tables.

drills.caption: Same two letters. The first is closed and plain; the second is waiting on what follows.
Sukoon on the laam and you read it. No sukoon and you do not.

examples.focus: The sukoon on the nun: closed, plain, and nothing to apply before the ع.
No sukoon on the nun, and a ف after it. That bareness is the whole announcement.
The shadda on مِّن is the receipt: the tanween before it was absorbed into the meem.
A sukoon on the laam, so the laam is a letter you pronounce.
No sukoon on the laam and a shadda on the ر: the laam is not read at all.
The small meem above the line is not a hint. It is the sound, printed.

keyPoints: A sukoon on a letter means it closes plainly. Nothing to apply.
No sukoon on a nun or tanween, and no madd: a rule is running.
A shadda opening the next word is a merge already recorded.
The laam of ٱل: with a sukoon you read it, without one you do not.
The small meem of iqlab prints the sound you are meant to make.

mistakes.right: Treat the missing sukoon as the signal. Look at the letter after it and apply the rule that follows.
mistakes.why: The Uthmani script is pointed deliberately. An absent mark carries as much information as a present one.
mistakes.wrong: Reading a bare nun as though the sukoon were simply left off by mistake.

mistakes.right: Check the laam for a sukoon. There is none, and the ر carries a shadda, so the laam is silent.
mistakes.why: The script is showing you a merge. Reading the laam undoes it and doubles a letter that should have been absorbed.
mistakes.wrong: Pronouncing the laam in ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ because the alif-laam is written there.

mistakes.right: See the small meem, say a meem. It is the one rule the script spells out for you.
mistakes.why: Recalling a rule under time pressure is where mistakes come from. This one asks nothing of your memory.
mistakes.wrong: Working out iqlab from the rule instead of reading the meem that is printed above the line.

The nun is merged into the next letter
The nun is hidden into the next letter
The nun is replaced by a meem

Do not read the laam. The next letter is doubled instead
Read the laam with a light ghunnah
Stop and begin again from the alif

lessons.summary: The Uthmani script is not a neutral recording of the letters. It was pointed by people who knew how the words are recited, and almost every rule you have learned is visible on the page before you have remembered its name.

table.title: What the mark is telling you

body: A tanween is a doubled vowel sign standing in for a nun sakinah that is pronounced but not written. That is the whole reason the four nun rules apply to it: there is a nun in the sound even though there is no nun on the page. What the Uthmani script adds is a way of telling you, from the shape of the two strokes alone, whether that hidden nun is going to be said plainly or not.

When the two strokes sit squarely one above the other, in the ordinary stacked shape, the hidden nun is pronounced clearly. عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٞ opens with exactly that: a plain dammatayn, a throat letter after it, and a full clear nun sound between the two words. Nothing is being concealed, so nothing is being signalled.

When the two strokes are staggered, offset, or drawn in the slanted forms ٗ ٞ ٖ, the script is telling you that the hidden nun is not plain. Which rule it is depends, as always, on the letter that follows, but the shape has already told you to stop treating it as a clear nun. In عُمۡيٞ فَهُمۡ the dammatayn is the slanted form and a ف follows, so the nun is hidden: ikhfa. In هُدٗى مِّن the fathatayn is the slanted form and the next word opens with a doubled meem, so the nun is absorbed: idghaam with ghunnah.

Iqlab is the exception that proves the system, because it does not use a shape at all. Instead of leaving you to infer the sound, the script deletes one of the two strokes and prints a small meem where the nun would have been. صُمُّۢ بُكۡمٌ shows both conventions in five letters: a small meem on the first word, and a plain stacked dammatayn on the second.

One honest caveat. Not every printing draws these marks the same way, and the slanted forms belong to the Madinah Uthmani tradition this app renders rather than to every mushaf in the world. The principle survives the difference: if a tanween does not look like the ordinary stacked pair, slow down, look at the next letter, and apply the rule. A reader who has that instinct will read an unfamiliar printing correctly too.

drills.caption: Stacked and slanted, side by side. The first is a clear nun; the second is not.
Clear, then hidden or merged, then swapped for a meem.

examples.focus: The ordinary stacked dammatayn before a throat letter: the hidden nun is said in full.
The slanted dammatayn, and a ف after it. The nun is hidden, not spoken.
The slanted fathatayn, and a doubled meem opening the next word: the nun is absorbed.
Both conventions at once: a small meem on the first word, a plain stacked pair on the second.

keyPoints: A tanween is a written vowel plus an unwritten nun, so the nun rules apply to it.
Stacked, ordinary strokes: the hidden nun is said clearly.
Staggered or slanted strokes: the hidden nun is hidden, merged, or hummed.
Iqlab does not use a shape. It prints a small meem instead.
Printings differ. The instinct to slow down at an unusual shape is what transfers.

letterSets.label: Ordinary, stacked: read the nun clearly
letterSets.note: Idhhar. The hidden nun is pronounced in full.

letterSets.label: Staggered or slanted: a rule is coming
letterSets.note: Ikhfa, idghaam, or a ghunnah, decided by the letter after it.

letterSets.label: Replaced outright
letterSets.note: Iqlab. One stroke is dropped and a small meem is printed instead.

mistakes.right: Look at whether the strokes are stacked or staggered before deciding. It is a glance, not a calculation.
mistakes.why: Idhhar is only one of four outcomes. Applying it everywhere flattens three of the nun rules out of the recitation.
mistakes.wrong: Reading every tanween as a clear nun because the two strokes look roughly alike at speed.

mistakes.right: Fall back to the letter after the tanween, which decides the rule in every printing.
mistakes.why: The shapes are a convenience of one printing tradition. The rule itself never depended on them.
mistakes.wrong: Expecting the slanted marks in every mushaf and being thrown when they are absent.

mistakes.right: The nun is gone. Say the meem, hold the ghunnah, and go to the ب.
mistakes.why: The stroke was removed precisely so that no nun would be pronounced. Saying both doubles a sound the script deleted.
mistakes.wrong: Saying a nun before the small meem of iqlab, then a meem as well.

choices: A full clear nun, then the ف
A hidden nun with ghunnah, running into the ف
A meem, then the ف
Nothing. The tanween is dropped
quiz.explain: ف is one of the fifteen ikhfa letters, and the slanted shape had already told you the hidden nun would not be plain. The nun is concealed into the ف while the ghunnah is held.
quiz.prompt: A word ends in a tanween drawn in the slanted form, and the next word begins with ف. What do you say?

choices: Because the shapes were not available in early printings
Because iqlab replaces the nun sound outright, so the script writes what you say
Because iqlab is not a nun rule
Because the meem marks where to breathe
quiz.explain: The other rules alter how the hidden nun is produced, so a shape can hint at them. Iqlab substitutes a different letter entirely, and the script simply prints that letter.
quiz.prompt: Why does iqlab print a small meem instead of using a distinct tanween shape?

lessons.summary: Every tanween ends in a hidden nun, so every tanween is subject to the nun rules. The Uthmani script draws the two marks differently depending on which rule is coming, and that difference is readable at a glance.
