chapters.subtitle: The marks that tell you a rule is coming, before you name the rule
chapters.title: Reading the Page

body: Two different systems are at work on the page, and confusing them is the reason most readers never really use the marks. The first system is a classification the scholars of waqf built by reading the meaning: is this sentence finished, and is it still attached to what comes next. The second is the set of marks a committee derived from that classification and printed above the line. The marks are guidance, not part of the revealed text, and different printed mushafs mark different places, which is exactly what you would expect of a judgement rather than a recitation.

The classification has four grades. تام (complete) is a finished sentence with no attachment, in grammar or in meaning, to what follows: most ends of ayahs, and the seam between two subjects. كافٍ (sufficient) is finished and grammatically independent, but still tied in meaning to what follows. In both you stop, breathe, and begin again from the next word.

حسن (good) is the one to watch. The words so far give a sound meaning on their own, but they are still grammatically hooked into what follows: a noun waiting for its adjective, a verb waiting for its object. Stopping at ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ before رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ is the textbook case: the sense stands on its own, and the noun is still waiting for the description that follows it. You may stop there, but when you begin again you should go back and take the phrase from its start rather than resuming on the next word. The exception is an end of an ayah, where you may go on from the next word, because stopping at an ayah end is itself something the Prophet is reported to have done ayah by ayah.

قبيح (ugly) is a stop that leaves no meaning or leaves the wrong one. Nobody chooses it. It happens when breath runs out, and the fix is not to hold your breath longer but to go back: a forced stop (اضطراري) is excused, resuming from the wrong place is not.

Now the marks. مـ is waqf lazim: stop. It does not mean continuing is forbidden as an act; it means that if you run the two sides together the sense fuses and comes out wrong. This mushaf prints it at 21 places. لا means do not stop here, and if you did stop, go back and take the phrase again from before it; it is not a claim that stopping is forbidden in some absolute sense, and if you have run out of air you still breathe, you simply return. One caveat about لا: the Madinah text this app renders does not use it at all, and its marks are مـ قلى صلى ج plus the معانقة dots. لا belongs to the Indopak layout this app also ships, which prints it nearly three thousand times, and to the Egyptian printings, so you will meet it in a mushaf but not on this page. قلى is الوقف أولى, both are allowed and stopping is the better of the two. صلى is الوصل أولى, both are allowed and carrying on is the better. ج is waqf ja'iz, with nothing to choose between them.

One mark comes in pairs. Three dots printed twice, a few words apart, is المعانقة: the phrase between them belongs equally to what is before and to what is after, so if you stop, you stop at one of the two and not at the other; you may also read straight through both, which is what most reciters do. The text this app renders prints the pair at three places: 2:2, 5:26 and 5:41.

Two marks that look like instructions are not stop marks at all. ۩ marks a place of prostration, at 15 places in this text. ۞ marks the start of a quarter of a hizb, and is a navigation aid for a reciter working through the mushaf in portions. A large ع in the margin, which the Indopak layouts print and the Madinah layout does not, marks the end of a ruku' section. None of the three says anything about your breath.

definition.technical: Cutting the sound at the end of a word for about the length of a breath, intending to carry on afterwards. Cutting it with no intention of carrying on is قطع; cutting it without taking a breath at all is سكتة.

examples.focus: The مـ after يَسۡمَعُونَ: stop, or the dead are heard as joining the ones who respond.
قلى after ٱلۡأَرۡضِ: both are open to you, and stopping is the better of the two.
صلى after ٱلۡحَقُّ: both are open to you, and carrying on is the better of the two.
ج after ٱلسَّمَآءُ: stop or carry on, with nothing to choose between them.
The three dots twice: if you stop, stop at رَيۡبَ or at فِيهِ, at one of them and never at both.
Stop here on its own and you have said do not come near the prayer. That is what قبيح means.

keyPoints: Two systems: the scholars' four grades, and the marks that summarise them.
تام and كافٍ: stop, then start from the next word.
حسن: you may stop, but go back and repeat the phrase unless it was an ayah end.
On this page: مـ stop, قلى better to stop, صلى better to go on, ج either. لا, do not stop, belongs to other printings.
۩ and ۞ are not stop marks.

letterSets.label: Marks in this mushaf
letterSets.note: Stop / stopping is better / carrying on is better / either

letterSets.label: Marks in other printings
letterSets.note: Do not stop. The Indopak layouts and the Egyptian printings use it; the Madinah text does not.

letterSets.label: Not stop marks
letterSets.note: A prostration, and the start of a quarter-hizb. Neither concerns your breath.

mistakes.right: Breathe. Then go back a few words and take the phrase again from a place the meaning can start from.
mistakes.why: The mark is about the meaning, not about your lungs. A forced stop is excused; a strained, shaking recitation helps nobody.
mistakes.wrong: Treating لا as an absolute prohibition and holding your breath past the point of control.

mistakes.right: Read through both, or stop at exactly one of them, never at both.
mistakes.why: The whole point of معانقة is that the middle phrase can belong to either side but not to both at once.
mistakes.wrong: Stopping at both of the three-dot marks.

mistakes.right: ۞ marks a quarter of a hizb, ۩ marks a prostration. Read on unless a stop mark says otherwise.
mistakes.why: Both are printed in the same margin space as the stop marks, which is the entire reason they get confused.
mistakes.wrong: Reading ۞ or ۩ as a signal to stop.

mistakes.right: Stop where the meaning closes and where your breath needs it, and let صلى and ج pass most of the time.
mistakes.why: Three of the four marks permit continuing. A reader who stops at all of them is following the ink, not the sense.
mistakes.wrong: Stopping at every mark on the page, so the recitation comes out in fragments.

choices: Nothing. The stop is invalid and the recitation is broken
Carry on from the next word, since the stop is already made
Go back and take the phrase again from before that word
Repeat only the word you stopped on
quiz.explain: لا means do not stop here. It does not make a stop sinful or a recitation void; it tells you that resuming from the next word would leave the sense wrong, so you back up and read the phrase through.
quiz.prompt: You stopped on a word printed with لا. What do you do?

choices: Both
At most one
Exactly one, always
Whichever is nearer the ayah end
quiz.explain: المعانقة marks a phrase that can attach to either side, so it must not be cut off from both at once. The mark never obliges a stop: carrying straight on through both is the ordinary reading, and it is only the double stop that is forbidden.
quiz.prompt: The three dots appear twice, a few words apart. At how many of the two may you stop?

choices: حسن is at an ayah end and كافٍ is not
A كافٍ stop is grammatically independent; a حسن one is still attached in grammar
حسن stops are marked and كافٍ stops are not
One takes a breath and the other does not
quiz.explain: Both leave a sound meaning. كافٍ has cut the grammatical tie and only the sense carries over, so you begin from the next word. حسن still has the grammatical tie, so you go back and take the phrase again.
quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a حسن stop and a كافٍ stop?

lessons.summary: Scholars grade a stop by what it does to the meaning. The small letters printed above the line are a shorthand for those grades, put there so you do not have to make the judgement afresh on every line.

rows: Finished, and unattached to what follows
Finished, but still linked in meaning
Sound on its own, still attached in grammar
Go back and repeat, unless it was an ayah end
table.title: The four grades

body: There is one governing fact: in the Qur'an you never stop on a vowel. Whatever the last letter was carrying, at a stop it carries a sukoon. Say that out loud a few times on ٱلۡفَلَقِ and ٱلنَّاسِ and the rest of this lesson stops being a list and becomes a single habit.

Tanween splits three ways. Damma-tanween and kasra-tanween simply go: أَحَدٌ becomes ahad, لَهَبٖ becomes lahab, and the n-sound is not heard at all. Fatha-tanween does not go. It turns into an alif held for two counts, which is why the alif is already printed on the page: دِهَاقٗا read on is dihaaqan, and stopped on is dihaaqaa. Scholars call that replacement مدّ العوض, the madd of compensation, and unlike the madd later in this lesson its two counts are not optional. The one exception is a fatha-tanween sitting on a ta marbutah, which gives no alif at all.

That is because the ta marbutah has a rule of its own. ة is a ت when you read on and a ه with sukoon when you stop: ٱلۡقَارِعَةُ becomes al-qari'ah, and رَحۡمَةٗ becomes rahmah rather than rahmatan or rahmataa. The letter closes at the throat instead of at the tongue, and you should be able to hear which one you did.

Once the final letter is sakin, two rules that were dormant wake up. If that letter is one of ق ط ب ج د it now has a sukoon it did not have a moment ago, so it bounces: this is qalqalah kubra, and it is the reason ٱلۡفَلَقِ read on has no bounce and ٱلۡفَلَقْ stopped on does. And if the letter before it is a madd letter, that madd is now followed by a sukoon, so it stretches: مدّ عارض للسكون, held 2, 4 or 6 counts. All three lengths are read in Hafs. Choose one and keep it for the whole sitting, because what is wrong is not the number, it is changing it from ayah to ayah.

Two smaller changes finish the picture. A shaddah on the last letter is held before it is released, so وَتَبَّ stopped on is wa tabb with a pressed, doubled ب that then bounces. And the pronoun ه loses its silah: لَهُۥ read on is lahoo, stopped on is lah, and بِهِۦ is bih.

One refinement is worth knowing exists even if you leave it for a teacher. The full drop of the vowel is not the only permitted way to stop: الرَّوم sounds about a third of a damma or kasra, and الإشمام rounds the lips toward a damma without letting any sound out. Both are taught face to face, because a written description of a third of a vowel is close to useless. Until then, stop on a clean sukoon.

drills.caption: The same word joined, then stopped. The kasra goes and the ق bounces.
Two tanweens, two different outcomes at the same stop.
Fatha-tanween on a ta marbutah gives no alif at all. The ة closes into a ه.

examples.focus: Read on it is al-falaqi; stop and the kasra goes, leaving a sakin ق that bounces.
The damma-tanween is not heard at a stop: ahad, not ahadun.
Fatha-tanween at a stop becomes the alif already on the page, held two counts.
The ة closes into a ه with sukoon: al-qari'ah, never al-qari'at.
The kasra drops, the س is left sakin, and the alif before it stretches 2, 4 or 6 counts.
Press and hold the doubled ب, then release it with a bounce: wa tabb.

keyPoints: You never stop on a vowel. Every stop is a stop on a sukoon.
Damma- and kasra-tanween go silent; fatha-tanween becomes a 2-count alif.
ة closes into a ه with sukoon, and لَهُۥ becomes lah.
A final ق ط ب ج د bounces, and a final shaddah is held before it is released.

mistakes.right: Cut the vowel off. The last letter you say is sakin.
mistakes.why: This is the most common error in the whole chapter, and it is audible from across a room.
mistakes.wrong: Stopping with the vowel still sounding: al-falaqi, an-naasi.

mistakes.right: It becomes the alif already printed after it, held two counts: dihaaqaa.
mistakes.why: The alif is on the page precisely so you can see what the stop turns the tanween into.
mistakes.wrong: Reading a fatha-tanween as -an at a stop: dihaaqan.

mistakes.right: Close it into a ه with sukoon: rahmah, al-qari'ah.
mistakes.why: The two letters share a shape but not a stopping rule, and the ت version is a different word ending.
mistakes.wrong: Sounding a ta marbutah as a ت when stopping: rahmat, al-qari'at.

mistakes.right: Choose 2, 4 or 6 and hold that choice for the whole recitation.
mistakes.why: All three are correct readings in Hafs. Mixing them inside one sitting is what is not.
mistakes.wrong: Stretching madd arid four counts in one ayah and two in the next.

choices: dihaaqan, with the tanween
dihaaqaa, with the alif held two counts
dihaaq, with a plain sukoon
dihaaqi
quiz.explain: Fatha-tanween is the one tanween that does not disappear at a stop. It is replaced by the alif written after it and held for two counts, which is مدّ العوض.
quiz.prompt: You stop on دِهَاقٗا. What do you say?

choices: Because ق is a heavy letter
Because it sits at the end of an ayah
Because the stop removes the kasra and leaves the ق sakin
Because the ل before it is sakin
quiz.explain: Qalqalah needs a sukoon. Read on, the ق carries a kasra and there is nothing to bounce; stopped on, it is sakin, and a sakin ق bounces. That is qalqalah kubra.
quiz.prompt: Why does ٱلۡفَلَقِ carry a qalqalah only when you stop on it?

choices: Always 2 counts
Always 6 counts
2, 4 or 6, chosen once and kept consistent
4 counts, unless the letter is heavy
quiz.explain: Hafs permits all three. The rule is consistency: whichever you choose, every madd arid in that recitation gets the same length.
quiz.prompt: How long is madd arid held?

ruleCard.action: Take the vowel off the final letter and leave it sakin. Everything else in this lesson follows from that one move.

fragments.caption: read al-falaq, with a bounce on the ق
read ahad: the tanween is gone
read dihaaqaa: two counts of alif

ruleCard.hold: The pause itself lasts a breath. What is worth studying is what happens to the word, not to the silence.
ruleCard.trigger: You stop on a word, at a mark, at an ayah end, or because your breath ran out.

lessons.summary: A stop is never just silence. The final letter loses its vowel, and five other rules fall out of that single change: the tanween, the ta marbutah, the qalqalah, the madd, and a shaddah at the end.

table.title: The ending you see, the ending you say

body: Three things can happen at the end of a word: you carry on, you stop and breathe, or you do this third thing. A sakta is a gap in the sound with the breath still held. Mechanically you close the voice at the larynx and simply do not open it for a moment; the air never leaves. A listener hears a clean seam and hears no intake, and that is the whole test.

Hafs by the tariq of ash-Shatibiyyah has four of them. In Al-Kahf 18:1 to 18:2 the sakta comes after عِوَجَا and before قَيِّمٗا, so that the denial of any crookedness does not run straight into the word describing the Book as straight, which read together sound like one contradictory phrase. In Ya-Sin 36:52 it comes after مَّرۡقَدِنَا, keeping the sleepers' question separate from the answer they are given in هَٰذَا مَا وَعَدَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ.

The last two exist for a reason of sound rather than sense. In Al-Qiyamah 75:27, مَنۡ is a noon sakin and رَاقٖ begins with a ر, which is idgham without ghunnah: joined normally the noon would vanish into a doubled ر and you would hear مَرَّاق, one word. The sakta blocks the merge and keeps مَنْ audible. Al-Mutaffifin 83:14 is the same shape one letter over: بَلۡ ends in a lam sakin and رَانَ begins with a ر, so joined it would come out as بَرَّانَ and بَلْ would be gone.

The mark is a small س, from the word سكتة, printed above the line. Read it as an instruction only where a sakta actually belongs, because the same glyph does a second, unrelated job elsewhere: it also sits over the ص of بَصۜۡطَةٗ, وَيَبۡصُۜطُ and ٱلۡمُصَۜيۡطِرُونَ, where it records an alternative letter and not a pause. Those three belong to the next lesson.

A sakta only exists when you are joining. If you stop at عِوَجَا, take a breath and begin again at قَيِّمٗا, there is no sakta to make: you have made a waqf, which is permitted, and the moment for the cut has passed.

There is a fifth place where the same mark appears and where the transmission genuinely differs: Al-Haaqqah 69:28 to 69:29, مَالِيَهۡ followed by هَلَكَ. Two accepted wajhs are read from Hafs. One is the sakta, which keeps the two ه distinct; the other merges the first ه into the second. The mushaf prints the mark, so it records the first. Scholars did not fix a count for the sakta's length either, and teachers commonly measure it at about two counts; what is not negotiable is that no breath is taken.

body: The scholars of waqf make one asymmetry the centre of this topic. A stop can be forced: breath runs out, a cough arrives, and the reader had no choice. A start is never forced, because you decide when and where to open your mouth. So the excuse that covers a broken stop does not extend one word further, and where a stop can be graded from complete down to ugly, a start is only ever good or ugly.

That gives the practical rule. When you run out of air mid-phrase, do not resume on the word you happened to reach. Go back: to the head of the sentence if it is short, or at least to a word that carries no grammatical dependency on what came before it, so the phrase can begin there and stand. An ayah opening, a وَ that starts a new clause, a subject before its verb: any of these is a place a listener can pick the meaning up from.

The second half of starting is mechanical, and it is the reason the connecting hamza exists at all. Arabic does not begin a word on a sakin letter, but plenty of words do begin with one. همزة الوصل is a hamza written ٱ that appears only so you have something to start on, and it vanishes the moment the word is joined to what precedes it: وَٱلۡعَصۡرِ has no hamza sound in it, and ٱلۡعَصۡرِ begun on does.

What vowel does it take? Before the definite article it is always a fatha: ٱلۡحَمۡدُ begun on is al-hamdu. On one of the seven heard nouns that carry it, always a kasra: ٱسۡمَ begun on is isma. Those seven are not the whole story: the masdars of five- and six-letter verbs carry a connecting hamza too, and they also begin with a kasra, so ٱبۡتِغَآءَ, ٱخۡتِلَٰفِ and ٱسۡتِكۡبَارٗا are ibtigha, ikhtilaf and istikbaran. On a verb, you look at the third letter, counting the connecting hamza itself as the first. If that letter carries a damma, begin with a damma; anything else, begin with a kasra. ٱدۡخُلِي has a damma on the خ, so you begin udkhulee. ٱرۡكَبُواْ has a fatha on the ك, so you begin irkaboo, not urkaboo.

One refinement catches nearly everyone. The damma has to belong to the letter. In ٱمۡشُواْ and ٱقۡضُوٓاْ the third letter carries a damma only because a plural waw follows and the original kasra had to shift to accommodate it. That damma is borrowed, so you still begin with a kasra: imshoo and iqdoo, never umshoo or uqdoo. Compare ٱدۡخُلِي, where the damma is the letter's own from the verb itself, and the start really is a damma.

Two conventions frame the whole thing. Beginning a session, you say the isti'adhah; if you are beginning at the head of a surah you follow it with the basmalah, and at the head of Surat at-Tawbah there is no basmalah to say. Beginning in the middle of a surah, the isti'adhah is said and the basmalah is optional. And starting mid-ayah is allowed and often necessary in a long ayah, but prefer a clause boundary to an arbitrary word: the question to ask is not where did I stop, it is where can a listener start understanding.

body: Hafs is a remarkably regular reading. Almost everything in it follows a rule you can state in a sentence and apply everywhere. What follows is the short list of places where that stops being true, and the reason each one is worth memorising is that they are exceptions: no rule will generate them for you.

الإشمام, in تَأۡمَ۬نَّا at Yusuf 12:11. The word underneath is تَأۡمَنُنَا, two noons that merged. Hafs is read with two accepted wajhs here. In the first you make the merge fully, and while saying the doubled noon you round your lips toward the damma that was dropped: a gesture with no sound in it, meant to be seen rather than heard. In the second, الاختلاس, you sound most of the dropped damma, about two thirds of it, on the first noon, so the merge is only partial and the ear catches a trace of it. This is not the الرَّوم of the previous lesson: الرَّوم is a way of stopping and sounds about a third of the vowel, while الاختلاس belongs to a joined reading. Both are read; a teacher will tell you which one is being taught. Note that this is a different thing from the ishmam that may be used at any stop, which the previous lessons mentioned.

الإمالة, in مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا at Hud 11:41, and nowhere else. The fatha on the ر and the alif after it lean toward a kasra and a ya, so the syllable lands between raa and ree without arriving at either. Hafs by ash-Shatibiyyah has this one imalah and no taqleel anywhere, which is why the mushaf can afford to mark it with a small sign under the ر: it only has to do the job once.

التسهيل, in ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ at Fussilat 41:44, also one place. Two hamzas meet here, the questioning hamza and the hamza of أَعۡجَمِيّ. Hafs eases the second into a sound between a hamza and an alif: neither a clean glottal stop nor a plain long vowel. A full second hamza is transmitted by other routes; ash-Shatibiyyah, which is the tariq this app follows, reads tasheel.

النقل, in بِئۡسَ ٱلِٱسۡمُ at Al-Hujurat 49:11, one place. The hamza of ٱسۡم is dropped and its kasra is carried back onto the lam of ٱل, so you read bi'sa-lismu rather than bi'sa al-ismu. The page shows you exactly this: the lam carries a kasra and the hamza written after it carries nothing at all.

The sin and sad words. Four words are written with ص where the root has س: وَيَبۡصُۜطُ at 2:245, بَصۜۡطَةٗ at 7:69, ٱلۡمُصَۜيۡطِرُونَ at 52:37 and بِمُصَيۡطِرٍ at 88:22. In this riwayah the ص is the letter carrying the vowel or the sukoon, so the ص is the letter you read. In the first three the mushaf also prints a small س beside it, recording the reading with س that other transmissions carry; 88:22 is printed with a bare ص. Reciters differ over how far the س may be used within Hafs, 52:37 being the place it is argued over most, so this is a genuine disagreement rather than a settled point. What the page itself indicates is the ص.

Silent letters, which use two different marks and are constantly confused. A small rounded zero on a letter means it is never sounded, whether you join or stop: the alif closing قَالُواْ, the waw inside أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ, the alif of قَوَارِيرَاْ at 76:16. A small upright rectangular zero means the letter is silent when you carry on and sounded when you stop: أَنَا۠, ٱلظُّنُونَا۠ at 33:10, قَوَارِيرَا۠ at 76:15. Surat al-Insan sets the pair in consecutive ayahs, with a different mark on each, which is the clearest illustration of the difference anywhere in the mushaf.

One nearby word is worth flagging as unsettled. سَلَٰسِلَاْ at 76:4 is printed with the rounded zero, so the page says the alif is not sounded even at a stop. Teachers differ, and stopping on it with the alif is also transmitted. Follow whoever is teaching you; the mark records one of the two.
